#3424. ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: They Shoot Franchises, Don’t They?

A grimmer, gloomier “Hunger Games” is on the horizon with “Sunrise on the Reaping,” adapted from Suzanne Collins’ prequel novel about the origin story of the hardened alcoholic Haymitch Abernathy. Here, the teenage version of Woody Harrelson’s character in the original films is played by Australian actor Joseph Zada, the blond, ringletted Adonis who also starred as the moody Cal Trask in the recent “East of Eden” series.

Franchise fans might be riveted by Francis Lawrence’s latest installment — points for consistency, as he’s directed all the films dating back to 2013’s “Catching Fire” — but those audiences not already invested in the dystopian material and tales of tributes will find themselves left out in the cold by an overlong (it’s 158 minutes, so get comfortable), visually soupy, and narratively morose reprisal. But no matter, as this new slice of bankable I.P. is likely to rake in a hysterical amount of money, and perhaps launch Zada’s career as a face of new Hollywood stardom. Related Stories ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ First Reactions: Quentin Tarantino and David Fincher Deliver a ‘Pure Riot’ of a Hangout Movie ‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier

The film is set during the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell. Only 16 years old, Haymitch is thrust into games that are rigged from the start — and whose broadcasting is ultimately edited and deepfaked to look like pro-Capitol propaganda. (The film nudges a little bit toward the ethics of state surveillance and how footage can be manipulated or even fabricated for political ends.) His pastoral, if impoverished, life in District 12 is small but happy, with girlfriend Lenore (Whitney Peak) and a mother and younger brother (Kara Tointon and Smylie Bradwell) with whom he shares close affinity, plus a best friend we’ll eventually find out will become the father of Katniss Everdeen (Lawrence) in the later films.

After a reaping (refresher: that’s when tributes are selected ceremonial-style, here as by a grotesquely pulled-tight-in-the-face Glenn Close as Drusilla Sickle) turns bloody, long-shot Haymitch ends up being selected at only 16. Violence follows him everywhere, as during the subsequent Tribute Parade, tragedy strikes Haymitch’s childhood friend (Molly McCann) during a horse-drawn Tribute chariot ride. Sequences meant to be thrilling often lack connective tissue to the rest of the material, or are devised in such a maelstrom of CGI (as goopy and cacophonous as a Marvel battle) that it’s difficult to feel engaged. It’s also unhelpful that most of the supporting cast is so wildly over the top, especially Capitol residents played by Close and a smarmy and mannered Kieran Culkin. Jesse Plemons as a Hunger Games camera operator brings a shade of moral dimension to the proceedings, but as with his “Digger” role, the actor feels woefully underused. Ralph Fiennes as Capitol president Snow, meanwhile, is given but scraps of material to work with.

The by-the-book script by Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie appears to stick faithfully to Collins’ 2025 novel, with plenty of potential for visual appeal that goes largely unrealized. The Hunger Games arena Haymitch is thrust into is rife with hidden dangers: poisonous streams, a deadly force field, and other trippy flora and fauna that vibe like a dark mirror version of “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory,” but again, “Sunrise on the Reaping” trips up on the CGI fakery.

The movie’s stacked young cast of tributes and mentors (those victors of previous Hunger Games tournaments) includes Mckenna Grace as a District 12 tribute who’s not to be trusted, the endearingly wily Ben Wang (recently excellent in the SXSW film “Brian”), plus a gravely underused Maya Hawke as the winner of the 49th Hunger Games, Kelvin Harrison Jr. as victor of the 34th, and the great Lili Taylor as a legacy tribute played previously by Lynn Cohen (aka Magda on “Sex and the City”) in the second film. These characters mostly exist to introduce themselves to Haymitch, be established as good or evil or helpful or unhelpful, and then be shuffled out of the scene. Elle Fanning is rather amusing, however, as the Capitol stylist Effie Trinket, styled and nearly drowned out by extremely outré fashions. Glenn Close also (with a visage channeling Katherine Helmond as Ida Lowry in “Brazil”) could’ve been used to better effect.

The specter of death looming over the film should not be confused for much in the way of actual depth, and while Zada’s performance is charming enough, his character lacks the gravitational charisma or arc that, say, Jennifer Lawrence brought to the original films. He feels like a cog or a function to get this prequel to line up with the prior films — and isn’t that what he is? Which makes the movie, and ergo probably the book, feel a little bit like a cold cash grab rather than a necessary deepening of the series’ lore. When Haymitch comes home from Second Quarter Quell and descends into depression and alcoholism, that’s when the movie gets most interesting. Not a great sign when your film’s tepid coda is also its best moment.

And equally worrying is a series of cameos tacked onto the film’s end that smack of depressing fan service. These movies seem to be mostly critic-proof and hugely appealing to their core audience, but “Sunrise on the Reaping” is a dreary slog, another death-march “They Shoot Horses, Don’t They?” riff with a pretty Gen Z cast, and one that mistakes new layers of darkness (and trauma!) for the sort of profundity that its filmmakers hope will burnish a creatively withering property.

“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” opens in theaters on Friday, November 20.

#3423. Three Ways to Avoid CAPTCHA Prompts When Using a VPN

VPNs make it harder to track your online activity across websites, but it also makes them suspicious about your origins. When you borrow an IP address that hundreds of other people are also using for any number of reasons, you’re much more likely to get repeat verification requests from online firewalls.

CAPTCHAs are simple puzzles that websites use to filter out bots and spam. They’re supposed to be easy for people but hard for robots, such as simple object recognition tasks or audio-visual challenges. However, they can still disrupt your browsing experience if they happen too frequently.

Most modern CAPTCHA providers, like Google's reCAPTCHA v3 or Cloudflare Turnstile, start working long before they give you a puzzle to solve. It usually starts with a risk score that studies your IP address, browser and device signals, or recent online activity.

If the CAPTCHA provider can’t confidently identify your request as human based on those signals, it requests that you complete a puzzle before deciding if the request should be blocked. That means when you get repeat CAPTCHA requests, there’s something affecting your browser’s risk score. For example, popular VPN servers spread the same IP address across any number of users, which can easily make a website mistake you for a bot farm. If you change your IP address frequently by switching servers often, that might look suspicious too.

Luckily, there are ways to deal with frequent CAPTCHA requests using tools and services available with your browser and VPN. Cloudflare has already cut its CAPTCHA requests by 91% using its Managed Challenge platform. Apple has also been shipping token-based verification on devices since iOS 16 and macOS Ventura. In June 2026, Cloudflare even announced a joint effort called the Private Access Control Tokens (PACT) standard with Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Shopify.

While there’s no direct off switch for CAPTCHAs, you can use different fixes to improve your browser’s trust signals when using the internet. That way, you’re less likely to be hounded by verification requests.

The easiest fix for repeat CAPTCHAs is to stop connecting to whichever server your VPN app picks automatically. Proton recommends choosing servers with lower traffic load. In fact, its apps display load as a percentage to help you avoid the most crowded options. I'd also skip big traffic hubs like New York or London, since that's where most traffic originates from. Servers in smaller cities located nearby are often just as fast but never as populated.

You should also avoid changing IP addresses too frequently, which can look suspicious on its own. Pick a server that seems to behave well, then continue using it for at least one session. Also remember you’re more likely to get premium server options if you’re on a paid VPN plan. Major platforms like ExpressVPN, Surfshark, Proton, and Nord are particularly likely to have a larger server collection to pick from.

Costs nothing more than your current subscription

Hopping between servers often can backfire

Private Access Tokens (PAT) let you verify the authenticity of your request using your device rather than an IP address. Apple calls it Automatic Verification, where an Apple server validates your device and Apple Account to assign you an anonymous token.

To enable Automatic Verification on an iPhone or iPad, go to Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification. On a Mac, open System Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification.

Unfortunately, there’s no equivalent feature for Windows, Android, and Linux users. That said, Cloudflare offers the Silk extension for Chrome, Firefox, and Edge that serves a similar function. A quick look at the ratings will tell you it’s not as effective, but Cloudflare’s upcoming cross-browser standard called PACT seems promising once it is released.

Doesn’t share personal details with websites

Chrome and Firefox extensions can be unreliable

If you pay a bit extra for a dedicated IP add-on, VPN providers can assign you a unique IP address that isn’t shared with anyone else. For example, NordVPN offers dedicated IPs in 30 countries for $2-5 a month and Surfshark charges $3.75 a month for it.

There are also dedicated providers like Private Internet Access, which charges $3.99 per month for a zero-trust setup so not even their employees know which IP address is assigned to you. On the other hand, Proton VPN offers dedicated IPs only to business plan users, so you’ll need to be on the Workspace Standard, Premium, or Enterprise plans to get one.

That said, there is a trade-off here too. NordVPN itself admits that a dedicated IP makes it easier to link online activity back to a single user. Also, many websites can still tell that the IP address originated from a VPN data center rather than a consumer’s device.

Get unique IP addresses with pristine reputation

Works across desktop, mobile, and even smart TVs

Also functions as an allowlisted address for work

Add-ons cost more on top of the VPN subscription

Offers less anonymity than shared VPN servers

#3422. Desire, Death, and a Breakthrough Year for Queer Cinema

A willingness to die for sex is a familiar bargain for queer people. Born in the twentieth century at the wrong place and time? Beware of Nazis, AIDS, and other mortal dangers. Hollywood has at times depicted these threats in ways that emphasize the humanity of LGBTQ+ people, as when Tom Hanks played a lawyer dying of AIDS in “Philadelphia,” during the height of the epidemic in 1993. The industry also has a history of finding ever more creative ways to kill off and scapegoat queer characters, a trope that as recently as 10 years ago seemed to be running amok.

But a more twisted and nervy dance between desire and death has unfolded in this year’s spate of particularly macabre queer films. After years of what felt like permanent advances in rights and representation, LGBTQ+ people have been stung by backlash, including attacks on gender-affirming care, legal threats to marriage equality, and cuts to suicide prevention. Amid a reduced perception of safety, anxieties about the possibilities and consequences of nonnormative desire are spilling out onscreen like so much fake blood. Even so, their formulation is evidence of social and creative progress. Related Stories ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: They Shoot Franchises, Don’t They? ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ First Reactions: Quentin Tarantino and David Fincher Deliver a ‘Pure Riot’ of a Hangout Movie

This alarm has played out, perhaps most obviously, in horror films. In Adrian Chiarella’s “Leviticus” and Jane Schoenbrun’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” same-sex attraction engenders extreme and potentially deadly terror, be it from detractors or the people it consumes. Both films explore not the evils of queerness — an argument that belongs to the tradition of queer-coded villains — but the horrors of having one’s desires villainized.

The year’s queer history films also subvert conventional narratives around sexuality and deadly fates. In Andrew Scott’s awards-season vehicle “Elsinore,” Ian Charleson’s dying wish to play Hamlet is one many actors would share; the film doesn’t focus on how or why he has AIDS, but what he wants to do before it kills him. The Spanish epic “La Bola Negra” depicts forbidden romance, but desire isn’t what dooms its multiple generations of queer men. The fact that they’re swept up in the currents of history, just like everyone else, is part of the film’s revolutionary power.

The era for combatting the notion that being gay is a no good, very bad thing in a straightforward way finally seems to have passed. Usually such sermons were preaching to the choir anyway. Gone is the teary earnestness of a conversion therapy drama like “Boy Erased,” from 2018, in which much of the trauma wrought on Lucas Hedges’ character derives from the church but is carried out by earthly messengers. In “Leviticus,” when a healer tries to pray the gay away from a pair of lovesick adolescents, he conjures supernatural and murderous doppelgangers.

After rituals of deliverance are performed over the convulsing bodies of a pair of schoolmates (played by Joe Bird and Stacy Clausen), each one is haunted by an illusion of the other that tries to kill them. The concept of “Leviticus,” named for the Old Testament book that forbids man to lie with man, partly functions as a wry play on the idea that you never get over your first crush. It also takes the fear that so many queer people know well — that what you desire most will be your downfall — to literal and horrifying extremes. Imagining the bigotry of organized religion as a senselessly violent supernatural force is a radical reversal. The boys aren’t the problem; the boogeymen that torment them spring from the so-called good book.

Schoenbrun’s meta queer fantasia “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” likewise performs a canonical revision. The nonbinary killer in the campy franchise within the film were themselves killed and sunk to the bottom of a lake by their comically gender-panicked peers. A victim seeking revenge, the TV-headed slasher is called Little Death, a nod to a French term for orgasm, la petite mort. Hannah Einbinder’s millennial filmmaker is on a quest to reboot the franchise, but more significantly, to achieve her own “little death.” In order to grow more comfortable with sex, and give into her own desires, her fear of intimacy — one that, again, many queer people know well — needs to be killed.

The movie ultimately intertwines fear of death with the fear of intimacy in a way that demonstrates the stakes — how you can feel so afraid of getting close to someone you could just die. But what must be slaughtered in this case is fear itself — so that same-sex desire, which has so often been pathologized and villainized, can flourish. (The trail of straight people extravagantly dispatched along the way, like so many gays before them, is one of the film’s many deranged and delightful flourishes.)

There is a potent realignment evident in the year’s period films as well, which center the desires and fates of queer characters on their own terms, rather than taking their oppression or disease as subjects unto themselves. “Elsinore” leans a bit heavily on obvious sentiment while leaving much of the thematic richness of “Hamlet” on the table. But Charleson’s determination to play the part before he dies is what drives the film, while the indignities of succumbing to AIDS are mostly a secondary plot.

Contrast that with recent period dramas on TV, like “It’s a Sin” (2021) about young people facing the AIDS crisis in London, or “Fellow Travelers” (2023) about the Lavender Scare in the U.S., and focusing on Charleson’s dream itself rather than the injustice of what threatens it marks a distinct shift.

The broad sweep of the canvas in “La Bola Negra” heralds another major turn of the page. The play of the same name by Federico García Lorca that partly inspires the movie, and appears in one of its several timelines, is about a young man denied access to an elite social club because he’s presumed to be gay. But homophobia isn’t the primary struggle (or a harbinger of death) for the film’s other gay characters. It certainly doesn’t help two doe-eyed young men (played by Miguel Bernardeau and Guitarricadelafuente) brought together and kept apart by the Spanish Civil War. But the forbiddenness of their infatuation is just one current swirling around them, the most pressing of which is, well, the Spanish Civil War.

Weaving the fates of queer characters into the broader scope of history, and suggesting a lineage of ancestry and shared desire, as “La Bola Negra” so marvelously does, feels like a kind of imaginative reparations. And it marks a bolder, more robust tactic in humanizing queer lives; the film traces generational ties and uncovers untold histories, rather than contending with acute crises like religious doctrine or deadly disease.

There is a stranger and more expansive creative palette evidenced in these films, one that suggests the unnerving climate for queer people in the real world is only furthering the reaches of the imagination. In carrying forward the legacy of queer cinema, it seems the gays presumed buried by the trope are finally rising up.

#3419. Movie Theaters Are Back, but the Rest of Hollywood Seems to Be Crumbling

Movie theater owners have been through hell.

The pandemic forced many of them to shut their doors for months. When they could finally turn their marquees back on, Omicron and other variants made audiences skittish about returning to cinemas. Then the writers’ and actors’ strikes upended production, leaving them with fewer movies to screen. A promised moviegoing revival kept getting delayed or disrupted, often by circumstances outside of the exhibition industry’s control.

At long last, things are finally changing. Domestic ticket sales are up 20 percent year over year, and with potential blockbusters like “Dune: Part Three,” “Avengers: Doomsday,” and “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” on the horizon, analysts expect revenues to easily eclipse $10 billion for the first time since COVID. Grosses in North America currently sit at $8.76 billion through November 15, fueled by franchise fare such as “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “Toy Story 5,” but also by unconventional hits ranging from “Project Hail Mary” and “The Odyssey” to “Obsession” and “You Can See Everything.” Related Stories Desire, Death, and a Breakthrough Year for Queer Cinema ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: They Shoot Franchises, Don’t They?

Audiences are showing up for superhero movies and three-hour documentaries about a convicted felon. And media companies, which treated the theatrical business as the sick man of the entertainment industry, are finally seeing the value in cinemas, with the likes of Amazon MGM Studios and Skydance committing to making more movies for the big screen than most major studios did over the last decade. Better yet, younger viewers are driving the comeback, with studies showing that Gen Z members are the most frequent moviegoers.

That’s the good news. Elsewhere, Hollywood seems to be crumbling. Netflix, which has done more to reshape the entertainment industry this century than arguably any other company, is teetering, having jettisoned both chief content officer Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin in a brutal purge. Ted Sarandos, who is clearly feeling the heat after the company’s stock has fallen 35.6 percent year-to-date, has brought in Peter Rice, a well-regarded former Fox and Disney exec whose calm demeanor and unthreatening good looks are out of c-suite central casting, to steady the ship.

As Hollywood has stumbled around trying to develop a better business model, the solution that many companies have landed on is to get bigger, fast. Thus, Fox sold to Disney, MGM was auctioned off to Amazon, and David Ellison’s Skydance bought Paramount and then quickly merged it with Warner Bros. Others, such as Comcast, spun off assets to make themselves more digestible. Has it worked? That’s the $80 billion question at Skydance, where executives have pledged to make 30 movies a year and turn a combined Paramount+ and HBOMax into a true Netflix challenger. Yet Ellison must pull this off while paying down a massive amount of debt.

So far, their early moves haven’t inspired much confidence. Executives like CBS News chief Bari Weiss have embraced the Silicon Valley ethos of “move fast and break things,” but what they’ve built instead, such as a simulacrum of “60 Minutes,” doesn’t seem better than what they’ve replaced. And if, as a recent Variety story about Skydance’s post-merger strategy suggests, part of their cost savings involves making sure executives don’t send out for “sandwiches and green juices” from Erewhon, they’re in for a world of pain. They can have Jimmy John’s cater lunch, and it won’t make a dent in their debt.

Skydance has already laid off most of Warners’ leadership and offered buyouts to the rank-and-file. Another wave of layoffs is expected at the company any day now. And across town, those types of cuts are the default move, with everyone from Disney and NBCUniversal to Amazon and Sony slashing hundreds of jobs. Are some of these layoffs in anticipation of what a leaner, AI-assisted future might bring? Probably. But with many of these companies’ share prices flatlining or falling, they aren’t being enacted out of foresight or a position of strength.

“I can’t remember a time when things have felt so scary,” an entertainment executive confessed to me recently.

And they’re right. It’s always popular to say the movie business is dying or the television industry is collapsing, and those doomsayers have been proven wrong time and time again. People want to be entertained. It’s just that making money entertaining them has never been harder for Hollywood.

#3417. 8 Strongest Villains In The Lord Of The Rings & The Hobbit Movies, Ranked By Power (& Sauron Isn't #1)

J.R.R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings features some of the best villains in fantasy history. Modern fantasy often plays on humanized villains, ensuring we can empathize with the bad guy's motivation. Tolkien cared little for that; his grandest villain, Sauron, became the Dark Lord who set the pattern for every Dark Lord afterward. Smartly, though, so many of the other villains were tied to the corruptive power of the One Ring; it gave the story a wonderful thematic strength.

It's actually surprisingly difficult to rank the villains of The Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit. That's largely because there are so many different forms of "power" in this saga; physical strength, magical ability, military skill, and even political influence. Still, playing all those variables against one another, here are the eight most powerful villains of this saga.

Let's start with a character who possesses absolutely none of the traditional Tolkien powers: Grima Wormtongue. Saruman's agent, he became the "power behind the throne" for King Théoden; spinning a web of lies that ensnared the monarch and brought the entire kingdom of Rohan to the brink of destruction. It's easy to underestimate Grima, but he was a ruthless, manipulative man skilled in all the arts of manipulation. Words are his weapon, and he knows how to cut deep with them.

Interestingly, Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings weakens Wormtongue by suggesting he's drawing on Saruman's power. That's explicitly visible when Gandalf frees Théoden from the lies binding him, and Saruman himself experiences the backlash. Tolkien's books make Grima the mastermind in his own right, stressing how dangerous (and powerful) a manipulator he is.

Now let's move from political and manipulative power to something a little more physical: Gothmog, Sauron's senior military commander. The Orcs are far stronger than any human, and can endure a lot more punishment too. Given Orc society, we can assume he was considered one of the Orcs' greatest fighters, although we sadly never see him going up against powerful Elves like Legolos or Dwarves like Gimli.

Viewers tend to underestimate the Orcs, treating them as mindless brutes. But Gothmog's power is demonstrated by his military skills, and he is a proven master tactician. He recognizes that the capture of Minas Tirith requires more than brute force, and he adapts effectively. As formidable as the Orcs may be, they would be far less effective and dangerous without Gothmog.

The Witch-King of Angmar is probably the most powerful agent of Sauron, a mortal Man who received one of the Rings of Power and was corrupted by Sauron. He became the most dangerous of the Nazgûl, transforming him into a near-immortal spirit whose existence is tied to the One Ring. A powerful sorcerer, his very presence weakens the resolve of his opponents, and he inspires overwhelming fear in normal soldiers.

The Witch-King of Angmar is a skilled warrior, and he goes head-to-head with some of The Lord of the Rings' most skilled fighters. He is, however, not truly invincible; his eventual defeat proves there's a limit to his power and his endurance. The Witch-King remains one of Tolkien's most sophisticated villains—a blend of sorcerer, spirit, and monster—but he can be defeated.

Saruman is one of the most powerful wizards in The Lord of the Rings, an immortal Maia sent to Middle-earth by Eru (Tolkien's version of God). He's basically a fallen angel, and indeed was easily the most powerful of all the wizards until Gandalf too ascended to become a White. Aragorn gives a sense of Saruman's raw power in the books:

"Once he was as great as his fame made him. His knowledge was deep, his thought was subtle, and his hands marvelously skilled; and he had a power over the minds of others. The wise he could persuade, and the smaller folk he could daunt. That power he certainly still keeps. There are not many in Middle-earth that I should say were safe, if they were left alone to talk with him, even now when he has suffered a defeat. Gandalf, Elrond, and Galadriel, perhaps, now that his wickedness has been laid bare, but very few others."

As powerful as Saruman may be, though, note that Gandalf implies Saruman's corruption—his turn to wickedness—has diminished him. Although Saruman's ego would reject this idea, he is far less powerful than he was originally.

This next placement is actually pretty tricky, because the comparison between Saruman and the Balrog is somewhat imprecise. The Balrog is one of several Maiar who turned from the Valar and followed Morgoth, Sauron's own master. Little is known about the process by which a Maiar became a Balrog; it's unknown whether Morgoth turned all his Maiar into them, or whether he only did it with his most devoted followers. Regardless, the Balrogs were absolute powerhouses.

The Balrog possesses immense physical strength, extraordinary combat abilities, and mastery of fire and shadow. The creature's duel with Gandalf is a stunning one, pushing both to their limits (and beyond). It's difficult to say how the Balrog compares with Saruman, but I'm choosing to place it higher, given it has even more experience working with its dark magic than the fallen White.

Smaug is a Great Dragon, descended from the dragons bred by Morgoth during the First Age. He demonstrates a very different kind of power to some of the other entries on this list; he's another physical powerhouse, a being of phenomenal destructive potential. In Tolkien's lore, dragons aren't simply gigantic beasts; they are incredibly intelligent, and this allows them to use their powers—flight and breathing fire—with tremendous skill.

Smaug is large enough to destroy buildings and to crush most enemies, and he's arguably more dangerous than any other villain in the fantasy saga. I'd tentatively place Smaug above the Balrog, given his intelligence and aerial agility. But it would certainly be a fight to behold; it's just a shame Tolkien never really gave us a sense of how it would play out.

The Dark Lord is undoubtedly the most powerful villain of the Third Age, the one whose malevolent evil inspires the entire saga. Sauron is another Maia, one of their greatest, but he was corrupted by service to Morgoth back in the First Age. Sauron is not simply a powerful wizard or monster; he's a cosmic being in his own right, one even the other wizards could not stand against. He's a phenomenal sorcerer, a skilled manipulator, and (in earlier ages) was a potent shapeshifter.

It doesn't matter what form of power you're talking about; Sauron excels in it. Most significant of all, though, is the fact he is bound to the One Ring. Using this, he can exercise control over the will of others, and could easily have conquered all Middle-earth had he managed to acquire it. Sauron appears in many forms throughout this saga, each more dangerous than the last. But, surprisingly, he isn't the most dangerous character. That distinction lies with a villain who I have already mentioned, and who is discussed a great deal in The Lord of the Rings, but who was never seen.

Morgoth, originally called Melkor, was the most powerful of the Valar; the godlike beings who created the entire world. He's essentially a class above Sauron in power, which explains why Sauron became his servant after Morgoth corrupted him. "Morgoth" means "the Black Foe of the World," which gives a sense of just how monstrous he really was.

In truth, there is nothing in all of Lord of the Rings to compare with Morgoth. He's as far beyond Sauron as Sauron is beyond Wormtongue; although his powers diminished during the First Age due to grievous injuries, he'd still have far outclassed any of the other characters and creatures in the list. Sauron represents domination, but Morgoth stands for corruption; Sauron could conquer, but Morgoth could transform. He's easily the greatest villain in all Tolkien's lore.

#3416. Netflix Officially Confirms ‘The Witcher’ Will Not End in 2026

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Geralt of Rivia made up the “of Rivia” part because he thought it would get him more work. Four seasons into The Witcher, a queen finally makes the name official, and the person who’d appreciate that story most is Ciri. Back at Kaer Morhen, Geralt had already once let her in on a secret that’s a little embarrassing for a man who makes his living killing monsters: when he was a boy, he wanted to be a knight. By the time he gets his wish, he’d trade it for an afternoon with his daughter.

It’s been more than a year since Liam Hemsworth took over for Henry Cavill, and one of the stranger consequences of the timing is how little of his run he’s gotten to spend with Freya Allan, because Geralt and Ciri were already separated when Hemsworth picked up the sword. With Netflix filming the final two seasons back-to-back, the expectation was that viewers who saw his first season in October 2025 would get the rest of that story this year.

Netflix has officially slated The Witcher Season 5 onto its release schedule for 2027 or later. In its November 16 announcement from the Texas Book Festival, the streamer listed Geralt’s final outing among the book adaptations coming in “2027 and beyond,” alongside Bridgerton Season 5 and Narnia: The Magician's Nephew. Netflix has yet to announce an exact premiere date for The Witcher's fifth and final season.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

Geralt has spent the better part of a season looking for Ciri, and even if somebody handed him a map with her whereabouts marked on it, he’d still be working with bad information. The girl he remembers training at Kaer Morhen has fallen in love, found a home with the Rats, and watched Leo Bonhart (Sharlto Copley) murder every last one of them, ending with Bonhart taking Ciri alive. Whatever Geralt imagines he’ll need to do for his daughter when he finds her, he has no idea yet what happened to Mistle or what Ciri had to see.

Then there’s Ciri’s biological father, who has come to an ugly conclusion about the man who raised her. Emhyr (Bart Edwards) once owed Geralt his life. By the end of Season 4, his advisers have convinced him that the bond between Geralt and Ciri is the reason he keeps failing to find his daughter. The emperor closes the season by walking up to a cell and giving the creature behind the bars Geralt’s name. After four seasons of people hunting Ciri for what her blood can do, someone has finally figured out what makes her father vulnerable. Everybody on the Continent knows who he’ll come for.

The first four seasons of The Witcher are streaming on Netflix. Stay tuned with Collider for future updates on the release of Season 5.

#3415. Skydance Sets Film Leadership Team: Don Granger and Kira Goldberg to Head Paramount Motion Picture Group, Jesse Ehrman Promoted to WB Pictures Chief

Skydance has set its film leadership team.

Don Granger, a veteran Skydance executive, and Kira Goldberg, a leader of Netflix’s film team, have been tapped as presidents of Paramount‘s Motion Picture Group.

As part of the moves, Jesse Ehrman has been promoted to president of Warner Bros. Pictures, while Mikey Ireland will remain as president of production. Their task will be to stabilize Warner Bros.‘ film output while rejuvenating or extending franchises like “The Lord of the Rings” and “The Conjuring.” Skydance executives have been horrified by the extent of the losses racked up by Pam Abdy and Michael De Luca, with sources estimating them in the hundreds of millions of dollars. David Ellison, who orchestrated Warner Bros.’ merger with Paramount, was more diplomatic on a recent earnings call, though he said the WB film division has “underperformed this year.” Related Stories ‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic Movie Theaters Are Back, but the Rest of Hollywood Seems to Be Crumbling

As part of this restructuring, Jeff Goldstein, who oversaw Warner Bros. distribution for many years, will retire, and Bill Damaschke will exit Warner Bros. Pictures Animation, which he led. Skydance said that in the interim, Jennifer Dodge and Traci Balthazor will oversee all animation across both Paramount and Warner Bros. Pictures. Richard Brener, a survivor of several mergers, will remain as president and chief content officer of New Line, where he guided hits like “Weapons.”

Others remaining include: Lia Buman, EVP, head of global acquisitions and Republic Pictures; J.D. Lifshitz and Raphael Margules, heads of the genre division, Paramount Primal; and Christian Parkes, head of the indie label Clockwork; and Charlie Tabesh, SVP and general manager of Turner Classic Movies.

Last week, Skydance announced that James Gunn and Peter Safran, who had led DC Studios, were leaving the company. Jeremy Latcham, a former Marvel executive, replaced them. It wasn’t the only overhaul at the top. Last month, as Skydance took full control of Warner Bros., Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy were ousted. De Luca and Abdy were beloved by the creative community, but they spent liberally and accumulated too many flops, including “Digger” and “The Bride!”

Both Granger and Goldberg will report to Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, the co-chairs of Skydance’s Motion Picture Group. Across Paramount and Warner Bros., the mandate will be to get more films into production. To get the merger over the finish line, Skydance founder David Ellison agreed to make more than 30 films annually, far exceeding the output of any traditional studio.

In a memo to staff, Goldberg and Greenstein praised Granger as “a great partner as we’ve repositioned the studio, bringing in key talent relationships and nearly doubling output.” They noted that at Netflix, Goldberg “oversaw a slate that included ‘Don’t Look Up,’ starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence, and the upcoming ‘Bad Day,’ with Cameron Diaz, and ‘The Take’ starring Denzel Washington and Robert Pattinson. Goldberg was also an executive at Fox, working on films such as “The Greatest Showman” and “Bohemian Rhapsody.”

“Together, Don and Kira will work hand in hand going forward,” Goldberg and Greenstein wrote, adding, “We have both an incredible legacy to build upon and an enormous opportunity ahead of us: to champion the world’s best filmmakers, invest in ambitious storytelling and deliver an unparalleled slate of films that captivate audiences everywhere.”

Ehrman is a WB veteran who has worked on hits such as “A Minecraft Movie” and “Sinners.” Ireland joined Warner Bros. after years at Paramount. He left the studio after it was sold to Skydance in 2025.

“This team brings deep knowledge of our businesses, strong creative instincts and longstanding relationships across the industry,” Goldberg and Greenstein wrote. “We have tremendous confidence in these leaders and are grateful for their partnership.”

#3414. I Played Wendy's RPG, and It's Actually Worth It for the Free Food

November is a huge month for video games. Nintendo dropped its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 last week, and the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is right around the corner. But the game we've been waiting for most of all also launched this month: WendyQuest, the free RPG from Wendy's. (No, this is not a joke.)

Despite the absurdity of a hamburger chain making a full video game (complete with Wendy's-themed puns), the thing is, this game is pretty solid—even if it is a promotion at the end of the day. WendyQuest's main purpose is to offer customers coupons they can use toward purchases in real life, though it's a bit of a commitment. It took me just under an hour of gameplay before I earned my first coupon, and Wendy's says it takes roughly 15 hours to beat. All that to say, this is a pretty unique marketing campaign.

I was surprised booting up WendyQuest on my iPhone. This doesn't necessarily feel like a thrown-together product. On the flip side, the production quality is quite high. The music is solid and very much traditionally RPG; there are even three save slots, in case you plan to return to this RPG again and again.

There's even a story, albeit cheesy (no pun intended): As the game explains, the "Four Great Spirits of Flavor" created Savoria, "a food-rich paradise." All was well until Mech Corp, led by the evil Dr. MechBorg, built robots to take over Savoria. The plot is far from compelling, and the writing can be a little over the top, but hey, I'll give them credit: They thought through a full story here.

You play as Wendy, the "representation of true culinary excellence and taste as dictated by the four ancient spirits of flavor." Wendy (or The Wendy, as some call her) is tasked with saving the world, traveling between villages and picking up new characters along the way. The game world even has "real" Wendy's locations you can visit. These act like inns and shops in other RPGs, giving you a chance to heal while also buying equipment.

Like other RPGs, WendyQuest uses turn-based combat. You have to charge up your attacks, but stop before they hit 100%, or you'll miss. (It took me a while to master the timing.) I'm pretty impressed with how challenging some of these battles can be, though you are quickly given the option of an amulet that gives you a huge leg-up in combat. You don't have to take it, but it makes fights easier if you're only in it for the coupons. That, combined with the spatulas the game encourages you to buy, lets you mow down enemies. You can also utilize your companions here: "Frygor," for example, can either attack enemies with a barrage of fries, or use those fries to build a shield to protect you.

While there are tons of enemies to fight, the key baddies are the "mechs." There are five in total, and after you defeat each, you get a coupon. Spoiler alert: The first mech drops the "Fry Stone," which nets you a coupon for a free order of medium fries—though you need to buy something in tandem, as well as use the Wendy's app. While I stopped my gaming here for this article, the other four coupons are:

Free biscuit or croissant (I didn't even know Wendy's sold biscuits and croissants)

Again, it's wild that WendyQuest has a 10+ hour campaign, with over 1,000 lines of dialogue to boot. I'm not sure this is a game I'm going to see through to the end, but I'll admit, it's a fun marketing approach from Wendy's. Sure, they could have run a promotion in the Wendy's app to give people coupons, but instead, they built an entire RPG. I respect it. You can download the game for iOS, Android, or Steam.

#3412. ‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic

“Madden” is technically a David O. Russell film, but all involved seem to want to downplay that fact. Amazon MGM Studios, in their infinite wisdom, has decided to emphasize star Nicolas Cage’s performance as the larger-than-life NFL coach and sports broadcaster in its scant promotional material. While the trailer includes an obligatory “From the director of ‘Silver Linings Playbook’ and ‘American Hustle’” title card, the poster features Cage and Christian Bale, who plays Oakland Raiders coach Al Davis, flashing their Super Bowl rings, and no mention of Russell. Even the PR flack at the sparsely-attended press screening introduced the film by saying, “Please enjoy Nicolas Cage’s ‘Madden’!” Related Stories Skydance Sets Film Leadership Team: Don Granger and Kira Goldberg to Head Paramount Motion Picture Group, Jesse Ehrman Promoted to WB Pictures Chief Movie Theaters Are Back, but the Rest of Hollywood Seems to Be Crumbling

To be fair, this isn’t the worst promotional strategy. Russell may be a problematic figure, but it wasn’t so long ago when starring in one of his films almost guaranteed an actor awards attention. During a brief five-year period in the 2010s, his work garnered Oscar wins for Christian Bale and Jennifer Lawrence, and nominations for Amy Adams, Bradley Cooper, and Robert De Niro. Putting aside the uneven quality of his work, Russell certainly afforded actors the opportunity to “make choices” in lavish studio productions, which often amounted to adopting broad accents and wearing flashy costumes, and receive acclaim for their efforts. It’s probably why people keep working with him in spite of the numerous incidents of on-set mistreatment (on top of a sexual assault allegation) that have continued to this day.

Russell may shifted to streaming but his commitment to allowing actors to go big or go home remains sacrosanct. In “Madden,” Cage wore 30 pounds of prosthetics on top of the 25 pounds he gained for the role. He certainly resembles the man, at least if you ignore Cage’s actual face. Ditto Bale, who adopts Davis’s Noo-Yawk accent and bold fashion sense. But it’s all in service of a film so milquetoast that it will make you beg for the sheer personality exhibited in “Amsterdam,” which at least had the decency to have a narrative and occasionally spark tension and generally be about something.

Here’s what happens in Russell’s eleventh feature: head coach John Madden leads the Oakland Raiders to finally beat their longstanding rivals Pittsburgh Steelers in the 1976 AFC Championship, after which they win the Super Bowl. Following his diagnosis of a bleeding ulcer in his stomach, Madden permanently retires from his coaching career to be with his family. Realizing he’s a stranger in his own home after spending too much time away, he quickly transitions into sports broadcasting where he becomes a television mainstay. To secure his legacy and pass on his legendary playbook, he eventually lends his likeness to EA Sports for the “Madden” video game franchise, which becomes one of the most profitable on the market. He then lives happily ever after.

If that sounds like a film with little-to-no conflict, you would be correct. Part of the problem is that Madden, while being an American institution and a legendary NFL coach, isn’t really suited to be the subject of a biopic, largely because the details of his life are fairly free of drama or intrigue. He’s the kind of figure who should be the lead of a Saturday-morning cartoon where he helps kids solve mysteries using the power of his football mind. Rather than impose a zany plot onto his life or make up outlandish shit for entertainment purposes, which he’s known to do, Russell dutifully relates the major events in his life.

The bare-bones emotional foundation of “Madden” takes the form of the two loves in the eponymous character’s life. The first is with his wife Virginia (Kathryn Hahn), who longs for John to recommit to fatherhood and their marriage, at least until it becomes clear that he needs football to be a functioning human being. Hahn’s established joie de vivre ensures Viriginia is slightly more interesting than an archetypal long-suffering wife character, but, alas, her general lack of chemistry with Cage dampens their tender scenes together, and their intermittent marital troubles are too fleeting and half-hearted to make any dramatic purchase.

The second, and arguably most pivotal, is with Davis, whose slightly-problematic bromance with Madden serves as the film’s primary source of drama. Russell’s film briefly flirts with an interesting thread by portraying Davis as a devil on Madden’s shoulder, someone who seemingly wants him to continue coaching forever, his health and family life be damned. He constantly tries to pressure Madden into returning to the league long after he retires in the vein of an old buddy who wants you to stay out for “just one more beer.” Despite his size, Madden frequently shrinks in Davis’s presence, who knows just what to say to get him to do what he wants.

But while Russell gestures towards connecting Davis’s “maverick” professional style, which made him uniquely qualified for the world of sports ownership but nevertheless created controversy within the league, and his friendship with Madden, he ultimately chickens out from characterizing him as a truly malign influence. (“Madden” just isn’t set up to be a film with a villain or an antagonist of any kind.) Instead, Russell depicts John and Virginia Madden and Al and Carol (Sienna Miller) Davis as tightknit couple friends, admittedly a type of relationship that rarely receives the big-screen treatment, whose ups and downs are manageable because, well, they really just love each other.

It’s worth noting that “Madden” is technically a comedy. It certainly presents as one, featuring well-proven settings for laughter in sports comedies like the sidelines, the locker room, and the announcing booth. Intermittent jokes pop up in these spaces, though I’m genuinely hard-pressed to remember anything specific because much of it suffocates under Cage’s affectionately-caricatured performance. Russell trusts that the sight of the actor in a full-body fat suit is enough for audiences. Granted, Cage seems to palpably enjoy embodying Madden’s flamboyant energy and imposing figure, even if his inconsistent voice acting, complete with slurred speech and vowel-swallowing, occasionally threatens to tip into outright cruelty. (“Madden” features the real article speaking at the film’s end and it’s downright absurd how much Cage exaggerates his diction.)

If there’s one semi-sophisticated bit in the film, it’s that Madden’s one-track mind sees the world entirely through football strategy. He literally can’t write “XOXO” to his future wife in their yearbook without turning it into a play design. But Russell doesn’t really develop the idea any further and instead defaults to broad humor that tends to blend together and subsequently die on the vine. These often materialize as sight gags, like Bale’s increasingly ridiculous haircuts, or John Mulaney, who plays Electronic Arts founder Trip Hawkins, costumed to resemble Steve Jobs. Sometimes it amounts to Shane Gillis delivering Shane Gillis-style lines, sometimes with a perm or donning a wizard’s outfit, or former running back Marshawn Lynch dressed like a nerd.

On paper, Russell is actually a neat fit for a film like “Madden.” He made his bones directing abrasive ensemble screwball comedies. He’s directed period biopics, including one that’s also a sports drama, and one of his most acclaimed films involves football fandom. Sadly, “Madden” features few Russellisms beyond tacky ’70s and ’80s fashion and some mild domestic discord. He’s replaced his typically messy, chaotic atmosphere for an overly genial one.

Anyone who has some familiarity with screen passes or end-arounds likely learned it downwind from Madden, who used whiteboards to make complicated play schemes accessible to the viewing public. His impact extends well into the realm of pop culture, like the Miller Lite commercial where he breaks through the wall, the custom-manufactured bus in which he drove around the country due to his well-documented fear of flying, and his famous turducken. “Madden” covers all of that material without offering any insight other than the security of the man’s legacy. The Russell who made “I Heart Huckabees” has long faded away, but it’s still a shame that he’s been reduced to directing one of the oddest and blandest examples of brand management in recent memory.

Amazon MGM Studios will release “Madden” in select theaters and on Prime Video on Wednesday, November 18.

#3410. 10 Longest-Running Comic Strips Of All Time

Comic strips have occupied newspaper pages for more than a century, and a surprising number have outlived the artists who created them. Some evolved from topical jokes into multigenerational family sagas, while others kept familiar characters in circulation through successive cartoonists. Their histories reveal how newspaper humor adapted to changing audiences, publishing habits and generations of readers.

This selection combines exceptionally long publication histories with some of the most recognizable comics ever created. It is not a strict statistical ranking as The Far Side, for example, had a considerably shorter original run than the century-old newspaper classics. However, its influence, alongside the 50-year publication history of Peanuts, makes both important additions to any discussion of the medium's most long-lasting titles.

Rudolph Dirks launched The Katzenjammer Kids on December 12, 1897, in the New York Journal. Inspired by German illustrator Wilhelm Busch's Max and Moritz, the strip followed mischievous twins Hans and Fritz as they tormented adults. Its early use of speech balloons, sound effects and sequential action helped establish visual conventions that later comic strips adopted.

While some works failed to secure a place in the collective memory, the most iconic comic strips shaped generations and changed pop culture forever.

The feature lasted through generations of cartoonists and changes in publishers, although a legal dispute eventually split its history. Dirks left Hearst and created a competing strip with the same characters, eventually titled The Captain and the Kids. New Katzenjammer Kids installments ended on January 1, 2006. King Features has continued circulating reprints rather than producing new episodes.

Frank King introduced Gasoline Alley on November 24, 1918, initially focusing on a group of automobile enthusiasts who gathered to discuss cars. Its premise changed dramatically in 1921, when bachelor Walt Wallet found an abandoned baby named Skeezix on his doorstep. That decision transformed a gag strip into an unusually ambitious chronicle of family life.

Unlike most comic-strip characters, the residents of Gasoline Alley age as time passes. Readers have followed marriages, children, careers and old age across generations. King's successors included Dick Moores and Jim Scancarelli, who took over in 1986. The strip remains in publication, making it one of the oldest American newspaper comics still producing new material.

Billy DeBeck began Barney Google in July 1919 as Take Barney Google, F'rinstance. Its title character was a cigar-smoking sports fan who loved horse racing, poker and betting. The strip became popular enough to inspire a hit song in 1923, but its cast and focus changed considerably when DeBeck introduced another character during the following decade.

Snuffy Smith arrived on November 17, 1934, bringing a rural setting and a different style of comic mischief. His growing popularity eventually pushed Barney into the background and gave the strip its familiar double-barreled title. Fred Lasswell, initially DeBeck's assistant, continued the comic after DeBeck's death in 1942. John Rose subsequently took over in 2001.

E.C. Segar launched Thimble Theatre on December 19, 1919, years before its most famous character appeared. The early strip centered on Olive Oyl, her brother Castor and Olive's suitor Ham Gravy. Popeye entered the story on January 17, 1929, as a supporting character during an adventure involving a voyage to an island.

The sailor quickly became the strip's biggest attraction, thanks to his distinctive speech, stubborn courage and extraordinary strength. Popeye's popularity was so overwhelming that many newspapers and readers began using his name for the feature. Segar died in 1938, but other cartoonists continued the property, keeping one of America's most recognizable comic characters in circulation.

The comic now known as Nancy began in 1922 as Fritzi Ritz, created by Larry Whittington. Ernie Bushmiller took over in 1925 and introduced Fritzi's niece Nancy in 1933. Readers quickly gravitated toward the outspoken youngster, and by 1938 the strip had been renamed Nancy to reflect its new main character.

Bushmiller developed an instantly recognizable style built around crisp lines, economical backgrounds and carefully timed visual jokes. The strip has continued through several generations of cartoonists, despite a brief pause in the early 1930s. It currently appears in more than 100 newspapers, with Caroline Cash beginning her tenure on January 1, 2026.

Chic Young introduced Blondie on September 8, 1930, as a dating comedy about a carefree flapper and her wealthy boyfriend, Dagwood Bumstead. The strip found its lasting direction when the couple married on February 17, 1933. Dagwood was disinherited, and the feature shifted toward the everyday complications of married life and raising a family.

The perspective of a mischievous six-year-old boy and his imaginary tiger has resulted in some of the greatest quotes in comic strip history.

That change gave newspapers a durable domestic comedy, complete with Dagwood's enormous sandwiches, frantic journeys to work and clashes with his boss, Mr. Dithers. Young continued the strip until his death in 1973, after which his son Dean and other cartoonists carried it forward. Blondie remains syndicated more than 96 years after its debut.

Chester Gould's Dick Tracy debuted on October 4, 1931, introducing a hard-edged detective whose cases contrasted with the lighter family humor found in many newspaper comics. Gould built the strip around elaborate criminals, high-stakes investigations, and cool police technology. One of its best-known devices, Tracy's two-way wrist radio, appeared in 1946.

Gould retired on December 25, 1977, after writing and drawing the strip for more than 46 years. Other creative teams continued the detective's adventures, preserving its combination of crime stories, unusual villains and gadgets. Dick Tracy is still in syndication, giving a character created during the Great Depression a place in modern newspaper comics.

V.T. Hamlin introduced Alley Oop on December 5, 1932, bringing a prehistoric caveman and his pet dinosaur Dinny to newspaper readers. The strip takes place in the fictional Kingdom of Moo, where Alley encounters characters including his girlfriend Ooola, friend Foozy and King Guz. Its original premise combined prehistoric slapstick with adventures involving dinosaurs and other unusual creatures.

The strip briefly lost its original syndication after Bonnet-Brown folded in 1933, but the Newspaper Enterprise Association picked it up that August. Hamlin eventually introduced a time machine, allowing Alley to travel beyond the Stone Age and encounter different historical periods. The feature passed through several cartoonists and remains a recognizable example of adventure-oriented newspaper comics.

Charles M. Schulz's Peanuts debuted on October 2, 1950, in seven American newspapers. Its small cast of children and animals turned schoolyard worries, family tensions and everyday disappointments into a comic strip with surprising emotional depth. Charlie Brown, Snoopy, Lucy, Linus and the rest of the gang gradually became familiar figures far beyond the newspaper page.

Schulz wrote, drew and lettered all 17,897 original strips himself, an extraordinary achievement across five decades. He announced his retirement in December 1999, and the final Sunday strip appeared on February 13, 2000, one day after his death. Reprints remain widely available, but no new original Peanuts newspaper strips have been produced since.

Gary Larson's The Far Side debuted in January 1980 and quickly stood apart from traditional newspaper comics. Rather than relying on recurring characters or multiframe stories, Larson usually delivered a complete joke in a single illustration. His surreal scenarios often involved animals, scientists, parents and children, with familiar situations pushed into bizarre and unexpected territory.

Gary Larson's twisted takes on pop culture were the engine that drove The Far Side; these underrated referential jokes are him at his best.

Larson announced his retirement in October 1994, and the final syndicated cartoon appeared on January 1, 1995. Its original run lasted approximately 14 years, far shorter than most comics here, but its influence was considerable: it reached more than 1,900 newspapers worldwide and inspired numerous book collections. Its continued popularity makes it one of the most recognizable newspaper comics of its era.

#3408. The 8 Heaviest Family Movies, Ranked

There's an assumption that family movies are meant to be the safe option, whether that be from its colorful worlds, lovable characters, or stories that leave you feeling warm and fuzzy. But that's not always the case, as some of the films we grew up watching were considerably heavier than we might remember.

From devastating losses and childhood trauma to religious persecution, and the threat of nuclear destruction, these movies tackle some surprisingly bleak subject matter without softening its blow. Sure, they might be made appropriate for younger audiences, but that doesn't mean they're afraid to break (and horrify) a few hearts along the way. To buckle up because this is going to be a heavy watch.

Under the watchful eye of his mother (Paula Winslowe), Bambi begins to explore the world around him, until his idyllic childhood is quickly shattered by the actions of a hunter. Now growing older, Bambi (Donnie Dunagan) must learn to navigate the dangers of the wilderness, while also learning about friendship, love, and the realities of life—alongside his companions Thumper (Peter Behn) and Flower (Stan Alexander).

For a film often remembered as a sweet childhood classic, Bambi doesn't pull its punches when it comes to loss. The death of Bambi's mother remains one of Disney's most heartbreaking moments, made all the more devastating by how suddenly it happens and how little the young deer understands. It's also a surprisingly mature and profound story about growing up, with the changing seasons reflecting the joys and hardships that come with each stage of life.

In Don Bluth's animated fantasy, Mrs Brisby (Elizabeth Hartman) is a widowed field mouse facing an impossible dilemma: her family must leave their home before the farmer plows the field, but her youngest son, Timothy (Ina Fried), is too sick to make the journey. Desperate to save him, she seeks help from a group of highly intelligent rats living beneath a rose bush.

There's a surprising amount of darkness packed into The Secret of NIMH, from its eerie atmosphere and unsettling imagery to its exploration of grief, sacrifice, and mortality. Mrs Brisby's determination to save her family gives the story its emotional heart, but the film never pretends that doing the right thing comes without risk. Its willingness to tackle genuinely frightening ideas makes it a far more intense watch than its talking-animal premise might suggest—proving that you don't have to underestimate what younger audiences can handle.

Set during the summer of 1972, 11-year-old Vada Sultenfuss (Anna Chlumsky) is a precocious hyperhondriac girl growing up in a funeral home run by her widowed father. Her closest companion is Thomas J. Sennett (Macaulay Culkin), an equally awkward boy who shares her curiosity about the world. But as Vada navigates her first crushes, family changes, and the tribulations of growing up, she's forced to confront a loss far more devastating than anything she could've imagined.

My Girl is a deceptively gentle coming-of-age story that builds such a warm connection between its young characters that its emotional gut punch feels almost unfair. Chlumsky and Culkin are wonderfully natural together, capturing the innocence and intensity of a childhood friendship. But it's the film's treatment of grief that's particularly affecting because it doesn't offer easy explanations or try to make tragedy feel meaningful. Instead, it shows the messiness of a young person beginning to process something well beyond their years.

Based on Louis Sacher's bestselling novel, Stanley Yelnats (Shia LaBeouf), a teenager who's wrongly convicted of stealing a pair of shoes, is sent to Camp Green Lake, a juvenile detention facility in the middle of the desert. There, he and the other boys are forced to dig enormous holes everyday under the watch of the intimidating Warden (Sigourney Weaver). The official explanation is that the digging builds character, but as Stanley uncovers the camp's secrets, he also begins to unravel a family curse stretching back generations.

For all its quirky humor and mystery-solving, Holes has a surprisingly bleak view of justice as its characters are dealing with abandonment, prejudice, and the consequences of choices made long before they were born. Luckily, Stanley's friendship with Zero (Khleo Thomas) gives the film its emotional center, particularly as the pair find solidarity in a place designed to break them down. Consider this a clever, satisfying adventure, but one that also understands how much a little kindness and loyalty can matter in an unfair world.

Quasimodo (Tom Hulce) is a young man who has spent his entire life hidden away in the bell tower of Paris' Notre Dame Cathedral. Raised by the treacherous Judge Claude Frollo (Tony Jay), who convinces him that the outside world will reject him because of his appearance, Quasimodo longs to experience life beyond the cathedral walls. Thankfully, the Festival of Fools takes place, where he finally ventures into the city and befriends Esmerelda (Demi Moore), a Romani dancer whose compassion challenges everything he's been taught about the world and those within it.

As one of Disney's darkest films, The Hunchback of Notre Dame tackles prejudice, religious hypocrisy, persecution, and the abuse of power with a seriousness that still sets it apart from the studio's other family classics. All of this stems from the chilling villain Frollo, whose treatment of Quasimodo remains a sustained exercise in emotional abuse, while his persecution of the Romani people escalates into imprisonment, torture, and genocide. Even its final show-stopping number becomes an unsettling exploration of lust and self-righteous cruelty, making the film's dark themes hard to miss.

Set in 1950s America at the height of Cold War paranoia, young Hogarth Hughes (Eli Marienthal) discovers a gigantic robot that has crash-landed near his small town. And despite its enormous size and mysterious origins, the Giant (Vin Diesel) is gentle and curious, leading the two to quickly form an unlikely friendship. But when a government agent becomes convinced the machine is a threat to national security, Hogarth must find a way to protect his new friend before fear and suspicion turn into something much more dangerous.

Beneath its charming adventure lies a surprisingly moving story about identity, empathy, and the choice between destruction and compassion. Sure, The Giant may have been built as a weapon, but Hogarth teaches him that he doesn't have to be defined by what he was made to do. That message gives the film a powerful emotional core, particularly as the threat of nuclear war hangs over the story. Its final moments are among the most affecting in animated cinema, proving that even a giant robot can deliver one of the most human tales about sacrifice and love.

DreamWorks' epic animated musical retells the biblical story of Moses (Val Kilmer), who is raised as an Egyptian prince alongside his brother Rameses (Ralph Fiennes), both unaware of his true heritage. But when he discovers the truth about his birth and the suffering of his people under Egyptian rule, Moses leaves the palace and eventually returns with a divine mission: to convince Rameses to free the enslaved.

For a so-called family film, The Prince of Egypt doesn't soften the brutality of the story it tells. For one, its opening depicts soldiers tearing infants from their mothers and throwing them into the Nile, while the eventual plagues bring increasingly devastating consequences, including the deaths of Egypt's firstborn children. The spectacle is truly impressive, but the film's real weight comes from the personal cost of the conflict, particularly the painful divide between Moses and Rameses. There's no doubt that this is an ambitious family film that takes the themes of faith and suffering very seriously.

Based on Katherine Paterson's classic novel, Jess Aarons (Josh Hutcherson) is a lonely young boy who struggles to fit in at school and feels overlooked at home. But his life changes when he befriends Leslie Burke (AnnaSophia Robb), a new girl with a vivid imagination and a knack for seeing magic in the ordinary. Together, they create an imaginary kingdom called Terabithia, where they can escape their everyday troubles and become the heroes of their own adventure. Sadly, their friendship is put to the ultimate test when tragedy strikes.

What makes Bridge to Terabithia so heartbreaking is the way it captures the intensity of childhood friendship before suddenly confronting its audience with a devastating loss. What can we say? The film's reputation for making audiences cry is well-earned as it beautifully showcases grief from a child's perspective. By allowing Jess to struggle with guilt and anger, the story doesn't offer an easy way out. As a result, Terabithia becomes more than an imaginary escape—it's a way for Jess to hold onto his friend and carry something of her with him. What a devastating reminder that childhood doesn't always protect you from utter heartbreak.

#3407. ‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Christmas Special Trailer: Can Mary Bennet Still Be Herself and ‘the Perfect Wife’?

Any news about the upcoming “The Other Bennet Sister” Christmas special — three episodes released in time for Christmas, but not set at Christmas — is worthy of celebration, but the first trailer for the upcoming BritBox treat also packs one heck of a wallop for fans of breakout character Caroline Bingley. Brace yourselves!

Following the first 10 episodes of the smash hit series, based on Janice Hadlow’s novel of the same name, these three new episodes pick up after the very happy ending of the first season finale. But while the marriage of Mary Bennet (Ella Bruccoleri) and Tom Hayward (Dónal Finn) was an unabashedly joyous occasion, the special dares ask: well, now what? Or, more appropriately, how does someone like Mary retain her unique qualities and serve as a “perfect wife”? Related Stories Movie Theaters Are Back, but the Rest of Hollywood Seems to Be Crumbling ’14th’ Trailer: Ava DuVernay Unpacks the Necessity of Another Essential Constitutional Amendment

That’s a tall enough order, and that’s before (gasp) the return of Caroline Bingley (Tanya Reynolds) and Mr. Ryder (Laurie Davidson), who return back to London from their jaunt to Italy with lots of big reveals. We won’t spoil anything that the trailer doesn’t, but the three episodes look to already have plenty of drama long before the Ryders (yes, you read that correctly) come back into the fold with a baby in tow. We’re scandalized and delighted.

Also returning for the special are Ruth Jones as Mrs. Bennet, Varada Sethu as Ann Baxter, Poppy Gilbert as Lizzie Darcy, Maddie Close as Jane Bingley, Grace Hogg-Robinson as Lydia Wickham, Molly Wright as Kitty Buncock, and Anna Fenton-Garvey as Charlotte Collins. Nerys Amber Stocks also joins the cast as Mary’s housemaid Lucy. Screenwriter Sarah Quintrell also returns, writing all three additional episodes of the special. Asim Abbasi has also returned to direct.

BritBox also announced today that its podcast series “On the Box” will launch “On the Box with The Other Bennet Sister” video companion episodes. Following each installment of the special, executive producer Jane Tranter and stars Bruccoleri, Finn, Reynolds, and Davidson join hosts Edith Bowman and Michelle Collins to “unpack the episode, share behind-the-scenes stories, and discuss key moments from the series.” The official companion podcast episodes will be available to watch and listen on BritBox and wherever podcasts are available as soon as each episode premieres.

#3405. Michael Connelly’s Bosch Replacement’s Next Release Is Just 6 Months Away

Cher Thompson is a Senior Staff Writer at Screen Rant, where she covers everything from explosive reality TV moments to cast interviews about the twists and turns of scripted dramas. With a background in creative writing, marketing, and teaching, Cher knows how to spot both the storytelling genius and the guilty pleasures in pop culture. Her work blends wit with insight, making readers feel like they’re chatting with a friend who just happens to know way too much about TV.

Over the past several decades, Michael Connelly has taken his time establishing Harry Bosch as one of crime fiction's most recognizable figures, but his closest replacement character's next release is sooner than you'd think. While Bosch was first introduced in the early 1990s with The Black Echo, Connelly has worked with the character and continued to build the universe for well over 30 years, bringing him into the present day. While the author's Bosch was a successful series in the literary world, nothing has helped boost the character into the cultural lexicon more than the Prime Video live-action TV adaptation.

When Prime Video began adapting Bosch into a series in 2014, the character broke containment and became one of the most popular TV investigators of the modern streaming era. With a specific point of view of policing in today's world and an incredible portrayal of the character from Titus Welliver, the series quickly rose in the rankings and stayed on the air for seven seasons before transitioning into a secondary series, Bosch: Legacy, which ran for another three seasons. With Bosch coming to a close in 2025, the decade that the series was on the air did wonders for the books, which have sold more than 92 million copies worldwide.

Connelly's tremendous character may be his most notable, and while the Bosch series continues on the page, the author's most promising replacement character has another release coming out in just six months. With his newest character in the Catalina series, Connelly's introduced his readers to a whole new detective in Steve Stilwell.

Although Bosch himself is still alive and well in the literary world, Connelly has branched out into other characters consistently throughout his career, most notably writing The Lincoln Lawyer series with Mickey Haller at the center, as well as the Ballard series, which follows detective Renée Ballard. Both The Lincoln Lawyer and Ballard have been adapted into successful TV projects as well, but his newest work is still finding its footing, despite already getting the green light for a TV adaptation of its own. The Catalina series, which follows detective Steve Stilwell as he solves cases in a sleepy California island town, is a much different swing than his previous work.

Connelly's Catalina series, which will be adapted for HBO Max by Connelly and TV legend David E. Kelley, currently consists of two novels: 2025's Nightshade, which introduced the character and brought his first intense investigation to life, and 2026's Ironwood, which introduced Stilwell to Renée Ballard. Connelly's larger interconnected universe of characters does mean that eventually, Stilwell and Bosch could come face to face. In building a very different franchise, the author has brought Stilwell to a more remote, rustic location on Catalina Island, and has made his work feel vastly different than the intensity of Bosch's, or the pace of Ballard's.

With Connelly's Catalina series kicking off on the right foot, another piece of the larger puzzle will be coming out in 2027, just six months from now. Stilwell is set to return in Daybreak, Connelly's next title within the series, which will explore another case on the island that's changed the detective's life. Daybreak is set to release on May 25, 2027, and while there hasn't been much news about what to expect from the plot, the novel will continue Stilwell's story, which is setting him up to be the prime Bosch replacement as he continues the series in sunny Catalina.

While Stilwell and Bosch share some commonalities because of their work, both investigators have a vastly different approach to what they do. With Connelly having explored Bosch as a character for decades, there's far fewer surprises on the table for readers when it comes to learning things about his past or his process. Stilwell, on the other hand, is a far newer character for Connelly to dive into. This means that novels like Daybreak are working hard to establish who he is, how he works, and why readers should invest themselves in his stories. Thankfully, Connelly's newest Bosch replacement isn't far off from releasing new material.
