#3404. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.

#3403. Sean Connery Wasn’t the First James Bond: Meet Barry Nelson in the ‘Casino Royale’ You’ve Never Seen

Ever since George Lazenby first replaced Sean Connery as James Bond in 1969’s “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” fans have argued over who makes the best 007 — and those arguments are likely to resume once Robert Pattinson takes the screen as the latest Bond in director Denis Villeneuve’s new iteration. Although Craig has his partisans, Connery tends to be the consensus choice for the best Bond, though I’ve argued here for the merits of 1970s and ’80s Roger Moore. All the Bonds have their virtues, but Connery benefited from being there first — for anyone who discovered the series in its initial heyday, Connery simply is James Bond. Related Stories ‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Christmas Special Trailer: Can Mary Bennet Still Be Herself and ‘the Perfect Wife’? ‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic

Yet Connery actually wasn’t the first actor to play Bond. That honor goes to journeyman MGM contract player Barry Nelson, who played Bond in a “Casino Royale” adaptation eight years before Connery made the character famous in “Dr. No.” Connery may have been the first 007 to grace the big screen, but Nelson established Bond on the small screen in an episode of the CBS anthology series “Climax!” opposite Peter Lorre in the Le Chiffre role that would later be inhabited by Orson Welles (in the goofy 1967 “Casino Royale”) and Mads Mikkelsen (in the 2006 adaptation that introduced Craig to the series).

The 1954 “Casino Royale” is a fascinating artifact that includes elements that would go on to characterize future James Bond movies, while also going in a few other very different directions. The key difference is in the scale, stripped down by necessity for television production. The hour-long “Climax!” episode is all interiors, taking place entirely in the hotel and casino of the title. It’s more a James Bond play than a movie, with Bond and Le Chiffre facing off in a series of verbal — and ultimately physical — jousts in confined spaces, and it’s surprisingly effective.

It’s also a very strange beginning for a franchise that would come to be known for its globetrotting locales and elaborate action set pieces. Not that this “Casino Royale” was officially part of the James Bond franchise as we know it. In fact, although there have been three adaptations of Ian Fleming’s first James Bond novel, only the third incarnation with Daniel Craig was from EON Productions, the company that controlled the character from “Dr. No” through the Craig era before selling the rights to Amazon.

The 1954 “Casino Royale” came about when producer Gregory Ratoff optioned the rights to Fleming’s novel in May of that year. The novel wasn’t yet a hit, and Fleming was sorely in need of cash, which led him to make one of the worst deals in movie-rights history when he sold the book outright to Ratoff for $6,000 after the TV episode aired. This left “Casino Royale” out of the deal when EON secured the screen rights to James Bond as a character, so Bond producers Albert Broccoli and Harry Saltzman could only sit back and grit their teeth when Ratoff turned “Casino Royale” into a comedy in 1967 and cast Peter Sellers, David Niven, Woody Allen and others as rotating Bonds.

EON ultimately made a deal to bring “Casino Royale” under their umbrella and used the novel to reboot the franchise with Craig, but in 1954 it served as the source for a much more modest affair. The biggest similarities between the 1954 “Climax!” episode and the Daniel Craig movie come in the time spent on extended gambling sequences, and the centering of a brutal torture scene. Given censorship restrictions of the time, Nelson’s torture in a bathtub is considerably less graphic than the mallet to the testicles inflicted on Craig, but it’s rough enough stuff for a 1950s TV production.

Certain aspects of Nelson’s characterization, like Bond’s mix of sexual swagger and icy indifference, would later be adopted by most future 007s, to varying degrees. The biggest difference between Nelson and future Bonds is a simple one: He’s American. Although Broccoli and Saltzman flirted with the idea of an American Bond throughout the series’ history (going so far as to cast James Brolin in “Octopussy” before Moore decided to return at the last minute), to date they’ve never actually pulled the trigger on casting outside the UK.

Nelson is probably best known to modern audiences as the affable hotel manager Stuart Ullman in Stanley Kubrick’s “The Shining,” but in the 1950s he was a sturdy character actor and occasional leading man who bounced around television after an initial sojourn as a studio contract player. As a young man, he appeared in several important MGM films, including “Shadow of the Thin Man,” “Bataan,” and “A Guy Named Joe” (the source material for Steven Spielberg’s “Always”). Later on, he popped up in “Airport” and had a successful Broadway career. He was nominated for a Tony acting opposite Liza Minnelli in Martin Scorsese’s 1977 production “The Act.”

In 1954, though, he was in the middle of a prolific and productive era as a TV stalwart, both as a series regular (on “The Hunter” and “My Favorite Husband”) and a frequent guest star. He doesn’t exhibit a ton of range as American “Combined Intelligence” agent “Jimmy” Bond, but that too is in keeping with the overall conception of the character, at least until Craig tried to bring a little more emotional depth to the role.

In Americanizing Bond, the “Climax!” edition of “Casino Royale” ends up making a number of related changes that are small but make the film feel just a bit off for fans of the EON productions. American Felix Leiter (later played by Jeffrey Wright) becomes Brit Clarence Leiter, for example. Although there’s none of the Bond gadgetry that would become famous later, there are hints of what’s to come in the form of props like a villain’s cane that hides a gun, and the opening credits for the “Climax!” series itself feature a gun barrel pointed at the viewer that predicts the iconic graphics of later Bond title sequences.

The 1954 “Casino Royale” is noteworthy for another reason: its composer, Jerry Goldsmith, who would ultimately score hundreds of major films, including “Planet of the Apes,” “Chinatown,” “Basic Instinct,” and most of Joe Dante’s work. Yet in some ways what’s fascinating about “Casino Royale” is how unremarkable it is — it’s a decent, solid piece of entertainment from an era when proliferating anthology shows provided similar programs every week.

If Fleming had his way, it would have only been the start for 007 on television; he wrote several outlines for episodes of a James Bond series before CBS canceled the project. Luckily, he repurposed most of what he wrote as short stories for his 1960 book “For Your Eyes Only,” and television’s loss was cinema’s gain. By 1962, James Bond belonged to the movies — and to Sean Connery.

#3402. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

Chase bank appears to be suffering an online banking outage. On the outage tracking site, Down Detector, reports slowly starting rolling in this morning before suddenly spiking around 10 am Pacific.

Chase released a pair of statements throughout the nearly eight hour outage. The bank claimed that a technical issue brought its services down and was clear that it did not consider the issues a cyberattack.

Tom's Guide tried to confirm with the company but customers claimed that tellers at Chase locations couldn't operate their systems either. At least one support tweet on X seemed to confirm this.

Chase never said if its non-digital locations were compromised.

Here's what we learned throughout the day.

@veeramarni We saw your post and want to reach out. I do apologize, it appears that we are currently working to resolve an issue with online banking. Please try again at a later time. We're sorry for any inconvenience, and appreciate your patience. ^RRNovember 16, 2026

So far, I haven't seen Chase say anything on any official channels as a formal post.

The best I've come across is from Chase Support on X where the company said that it is "working to resolve an issue with online banking."

Over on Down Detector reports started rolling in around 6:30 am Pacific/9:30 am ET but didn't really start spiking until 9:00 am PT. As of this posting there are more than 4,000 reports on the site.

I am seeing hundreds of reports for Bank of America, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo and Zelle, but based on the amounts and the ability to log in to accounts with those banks, I currently believe this incident is isolated to Chase.

However, if you're trying to send or receive money from or to a Chase account, you will likely have problems.

According to posters on Reddit, people have said that after attempting online transactions they ended up going to their location branch.

Multiple people said that the Chase tellers told them all their systems were down and they couldn't do anything.

"Then went to branch to ask about it they said they can’t do anything because their system is down smh," said one representative poster.

Tom's Guide has reached out to Chase for comment.

I'm seeing reports and comments that people are having trouble logging into other banks including Bank of America and Wells Fargo.

I've been able to login into Wells, but that may not be universal.

Lets u know, are you having problems with your bank?

Chase has not responded to Tom's Guide as of this posting; however, a spokesperson did give a statement to the San Francisco Chronicle.

“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete, but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” a Chase spokesperson told the paper. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”

This does seem to contradict users on social media claiming they can't log in.

Analyst Bruce Schneier (Security Technologist; Fellow at Harvard Kennedy School) is an internationally renowned security technologist.

We asked him why companies don't have redundancies to prevent outages:

"Redundancies reduce profitability, and it is the goal of shareholders these days to wring all excess profits out of any and every company. Thatreduces resilience in general, and redundancy in particular.”

With the Outlook outage last week, and more every day, Schneier expects more will come.

"I guess I’m not surprised. Our systems are very fragile these days. Fragile systems are the most profitable in the near term. And there is no incentive to focus on the long term.”

Reports are starting to go Down Detector, though as of this posting they are still around 4,000 after a peak of 5,000 reports about 30 minutes ago.

A Chase spokesperson has responded to our inquiries with a similar statement as the one received by the San Francisco Chronicle.

“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds. We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible."

However, our statement had one extra line saying that the issue was not cyber-related, meaning it is something in the Chase systems and not a malicious attack.

"This is a technical issue, not cyber related.”

The spokesperson did not indicate how long it would take to resolve the issue or any potential causes.

Yahoo! Finance is tracking statements from different banks. Wells Fargo and Bank of America have received some outage reports, but not as many as Chase, which again suggests that it's an issue between Chase and other banks.

"You can still access your accounts through our ATMs, banking locations, and customer service," the Wells Fargo website reportedly reads.

I have a Wells Fargo account and could not find that statement, but I've also had no issues logging in or using my accounts online, so my experience may not be the same.

Bank of America has not released a statement.

After an initial decline, reports on Down Detector hit a momentary plateau. For the last half an hour, they've started a slow but steady decline.

Let me know if you're able to access your Chase account since reports started going down.

As of this writing, reports are under 3,200 for the first time since 10 am PT, about 3 hours ago.

Chase has been suffering a technical outage for more than 4 and a half hours.

Again, we saw an initial stream of reports around 7 am PT/10 am ET, with the real spike hitting two hours later.

Chase has said in statements that the problem is a technical one, not an attack. It's not clear what the issue is and it appears to affect both online banking and in-person transactions at their banks.

Reports have declined but not enough to declare the outage over. People are still reporting that they can't access their accounts.

We have asked Chase for clarification but haven't received any updates since the first statement.

I just received an update from Chase. Here's what the bank is saying now.

Per the bank's spokesperson, JPMorganChase apparently experienced a software bug in "on-premise hardware system", which the spokesperson reiterated there is "no evidence this is cyber-related."

The statement claims that customers still have access to their accounts and funds. They did not respond to questions about issues affecting brick-and-mortar banks.

"We’re working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today." It's unclear which timezone that end of day actually refers to.

Reports on Down Detector have halved in the last hour dropped from about 3,800 to 1,780.

Its been a slow decline but it appears things are coming back online for people.

People who've regained access have said they've been able to use Zelle, withdraw money and successfully login to the app or the browser.

For awhile it seemed reports were in steady decline, but things have remained study for the last hour.

I am seeing mixed comments from people saying they have access, while others say they still can't login to the app.

From what I can tell, the Chase outage finally appears to be over. Reports are still over 500 but most comments and social posts are indicating that people have access to their accounts again.

I have not a seen a "We're back" post from Chase or JPMorgan.

#3400. ‘Supernatural’ Star Officially Lands in Netflix’s Next Mega Hit

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

One of the perks of being married to Jared Padalecki is that when your book club finds a romance you’d like to see him star in, you can take it up with him at home. In 2022, Genevieve Padalecki, who played Ruby opposite her future husband on Supernatural, picked up a book by fellow Texan Katherine Center. Four years later, the movie adaptation starring Padalecki is just hours from premiering on Netflix.

It’s easy to see what she had in mind for him. Between fifteen seasons of saving people as Sam Winchester and four more carrying a Texas Ranger’s badge on Walker, Padalecki looks like a pretty safe bet to get somebody home in one piece. This time, however, he plays the other half of that dynamic, and the person qualified to keep him alive is Leighton Meester.

Padalecki and Meester star in Guarding Stars, which premieres Wednesday, November 18, on Netflix. Based on Center’s 2022 novel The Bodyguard, the holiday rom-com follows action star Jack Stapleton (Padalecki), who has picked up a stalker just in time for Christmas at his family’s ranch. Bringing a bodyguard home would mean telling his family why he needs one, but bringing home a girlfriend buys him a perfectly good excuse to keep Hannah Brooks (Meester) close, provided nobody asks the happy couple too many questions.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

Jack makes the mistake of questioning whether Hannah can protect him while they’re both still standing on the airport tarmac. By the time she’s finished answering, only one of them is still standing. Director Elizabeth Allen Rosenbaum told Swooon she hadn’t read Katherine Center’s book when the screenplay came her way, but she knew she wanted the job the moment Hannah tossed Jack over her shoulder. “I mean, how often does the romantic heroine get to throw her leading man over her shoulder? I was in.” Rosenbaum had directed Meester on Gossip Girl, where Blair Waldorf could do considerable damage to a man without having to lay a hand on him. For Guarding Stars, Meester learned how to flip a stunt performer, ride a horse, and jump clear of an explosion.

Padalecki, meanwhile, gets to put a considerably less lethal skill to use: he sings with country artist Walker Hayes on a Christmas parade float. Hayes originally auditioned to play Jack’s older brother, and when the filmmakers decided to make the brother younger, Rosenbaum rewrote the part of the town sheriff to keep him in the cast. Giving the sheriff a duet with Padalecki was also her idea.

Guarding Stars premieres November 18 on Netflix.

#3399. All 7 Episodes Of Netflix's 10/10 Western Are Perfect From Start To Finish

While the small-screen Westerns of the 2010s might be hit-and-miss, Netflix’s seven-episode masterpiece hasn’t got a single weak episode in its entire run. Hard as it might be to believe in 2026, there was a time when Westerns were the biggest genre on TV. Admittedly, this was back in the days of Gunsmoke and Rawhide, when shows set in the Wild West produced record numbers of live-action episodes and set early TV ratings records.

However, as the decades went on, cop shows gradually replaced Westerns as the most-watched genre on TV, and the genre wouldn’t regain its mainstream popularity until the rise of the Yellowstone franchise. While the Yellowstone spinoff Marshals is CBS’s biggest show of 2026, it is important to note that the spinoff is part Western and part police procedural. Sharing many building blocks in common with cop show franchises like CSI, NCIS, FBI, and Law & Order accounts for a lot of the show’s mainstream popularity.

Even Yellowstone itself and its sequel Dutton Ranch are contemporary crime dramas as much as they are Westerns, since Sheridan’s greatest trick was selling a modern-day spin on Dynasty and Dallas as a “Neo-Western” rather than the trashy, soapy family saga that the original series really was. To find a traditional historical Western, viewers need to look to Yellowstone’s prequels 1883 and 1923, or Netflix originals like American Primeval, The Abandons, and the underrated seven-episode masterpiece Godless.

Released in 2017, Godless was inexcusably missed by many viewers upon its original release. Set in 1884 New Mexico, Godless stars Sinners supporting star Jack O’Connell as the outlaw Roy Goode, who hides out in the New Mexico town of La Belle as he attempts to avoid a murderous mob boss, his former employer Frank Griffin. In an unsettling subversion of his usual genial screen presence, The Newsroom star Jeff Daniels wows as the icy, terrifying Griffin.

However, the story of Godless isn’t defined by male characters like O’Connell’s Goode, Daniels’ Griffin, or even Scoot McNairy’s local sheriff, Bill McNue. Thanks to a mining disaster, McNue is one of the only male citizens left living in La Belle, a town that is populated almost exclusively by women. These women include Michelle Dockery’s steely wealthy widow Alice Fletcher, Merrit Weaver’s more welcoming Mary Agnes, and a host of other well-sketched heroines with complex motivations and backstories.

Thus, Godless sets up a story that functions as both a tense, gripping self-contained small town siege Western and also a daring subversion of the genre at the same time. While most traditional historical Westerns sideline their female characters in favor of stories focused on sheriffs and outlaws, Godless forces viewers to think about the women left on the margins of these old-fashioned stories.

However, no one should mistake the Netflix show for a dry, academic deconstruction of the genre. Even compared to Sheridan’s more famous Yellowstone, Godless is a dark, daring, and thoroughly enthralling Western through and through. Unpredictable and inventive, Godless is as satisfying as any earlier Western show like Deadwood or AMC’s underrated drama Hell on Wheels.

Sadly, this didn’t do anything to help the show’s performance. While Godless was a big, well-deserved hit with reviewers, the show seemingly failed to find a major mainstream audience as the series arrived shortly before the modern Western revival was kickstarted by the success of Yellowstone in 2018. As noted above, Yellowstone’s success spawned the spinoffs 1883, 1923, Marshals, and Dutton Ranch.

However, the show also helped get the green light for further Neo-Westerns from Sheridan, such as Landman, Lawmen: Bass Reeves, and arguably even the crime drama The Mayor of Kingstown. Outside of Sheridan’s work, Netflix’s Ransom Canyon proved that Godless might be better known if the iconic show had just debuted a decade later.

The Samsung S90H OLED TV is a winning 2026 release from Samsung, delivering impressively vibrant yet natural colors and striking contrast. Right now, a 55-inch Samsung S90H OLED TV is  $400 off on Amazon at a record low price of $1,197.99 (originally $1,597.99) in an early Black Friday deal. It’s worth noting that the other sizes are also discounted, with the 77-inch model 29% off.

While it has identical pixel-level contrast and wide viewing angles compared to the S90F, the major upgrade here is a matte-like screen, previously only seen on Samsung’s pricier models like the S95 series, bringing an extra perk and better reflection control for those with sunny media rooms. Contrast and color accuracy are highlights on this model, as is shadow detail.

#3397. How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles

Editor’s Note: The following story contains spoilers for “Paper Tiger.”

James Gray never hid that Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway were playing fictional versions of his real-life parents in his 2022 drama “Armageddon Time,” based on the writer/director’s experience as a sixth grader growing up in Queens in the 1980s.

“Jeremy is doing my father to such a degree that it is disturbing.  He sounds exactly like him, looks exactly like him; it’s bizarre. Annie, too, is uncanny about [playing my mother],” said Gray while a guest on this week’s episode of IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast. “So I had had such a great time with them shooting ‘Armageddon Time,’ I said, ‘Well, why don’t we do this again?’” Related Stories Sean Connery Wasn’t the First James Bond: Meet Barry Nelson in the ‘Casino Royale’ You’ve Never Seen ‘Madden’ Review: David O. Russell Fumbles Again with an Unfunny and Purposeless Football Biopic

Gray knew his next film (what would become “Paper Tiger”) would be set in 1986 and once again focus on a Jewish family of four, with two sons, in Queens. In the project’s early stages, Hathaway and Strong were up for reprising their roles, but it soon became clear Gray would have to wait 18 months — after both “The Odyssey” (Hathaway) and “The Social Reckoning” (Strong) finished filming — to start production.

“You can’t wait a year and a half,” said Gray. “And then I started thinking, ‘Well, maybe this is a blessing in disguise.’ That the [film] could start to take on a new style, and so then I started to pursue it in a different way. So in the beginning, in its origin stages, it was [a sequel of sorts], but like any movie, it’s like a wild horse that’s going to get away from you.”

While Scarlett Johansson and Miles Teller’s characters in “Paper Tiger” are inspired by Gray’s parents, they are not as deeply grounded as Hathaway and Strong were in “Armageddon Time” as facsimiles of Gray’s parents in how they talked, looked, dressed, and behaved. Through this lens, Gray began to see the film as less of a straight memoir, freeing him to embrace elements of the crime genre in his storytelling.

Explained Gray, “What I tried to do was to make a film more in — for lack of a better way of really explaining — a bit more Hitchcockian in certain places. Almost — again, ‘pulpy’ is not quite the right word — a little bit more, how do I put this — more of an engagement directly with a tense idea of narrative, that it would be a driving, tense story.”

What also changed is the sympathetic lens through which Gray now saw his father. In “Paper Tiger,” Irwin (Teller) puts his family in danger when he unwittingly gets entangled (pursuing environmental consulting work for businesses along the polluted Gowanus Canal) with the Russian mob. While Irwin is guilty of pride and naivety, it is (especially compared to Gray’s previous films) a positive portrayal of a hard-working and earnest father pursuing the American dream.

In this sense, the shift from Strong to Teller was fortuitous. Strong had painted an unforgiving portrait of a miserable, strict father — tortured by generational trauma and unbending with his sons striving for upward mobility — whereas Gray saw something in Teller he could lean into for a different portrayal of his father.

“Miles has a kind of — I can’t believe I’m going to say this, he might even resist this— a softness to him, which would probably offend him, but I think that’s a great thing,” said Gray. “He doesn’t have a softness in his persona. He doesn’t have it in physical terms. It’s actually a tenderness inside. You have to embrace [that] beauty in him and hope it works for the film.”

When it came to recasting Hathaway, Gray was more practical, saying he needed three characteristics: another bankable star, who was also Jewish, and a real New Yorker. He believed the way the city seeps itself into a person’s bones is not something that even the best actors can learn to portray. Those three unnotiables made Scarlett Johansson the clear number one choice.

“I had met [Scarlett] years before on a project that never wound up happening, and quite liked her. She’s a total New Yorker through and through. Then when I found out that Annie [Hathaway] was going off to do Chris [Nolan’s] movie [‘The Odyssey’] for a thousand years, she was the first choice because you’re talking about one of the biggest stars in the world, and she’s also a Jewish woman from New York,  checks the boxes,” said Gray. “When I sent [the script] to her, I sent her a note, ‘There’s probably no chance in hell you’re going to do this, but I love you, can you read this?’ And then she texted me back very, very quickly and was like, ‘Let’s go.’”

While Hathaway’s portrayal of Gray’s mother was more open and loving than Strong’s version of his father — and therefore didn’t require as sharp a contrast in how the role was recast — Gray believed Johansson’s approach better fit the needs of “Paper Tiger.”

“It’s a more operatic idea of character than Annie’s was in ‘Armageddon Time,’” said Gray. “It’s much more a kind of high emotion. And of course, because the situation is much more tragic, and she embraced it completely.”

“Paper Tiger” opened last weekend in New York and Los Angeles, and expands on November 20.

#3395. ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Throws Netflix’s Oscar Campaign a Curveball

From a purely awards-hunting perspective, there’s a great argument to be made that Netflix could have pushed back its late November release “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” until next year. Historically, the perception of the embattled studio is that its had issues being distracted by too big an awards slate to pin down its Best Picture frontrunner. Remember in 2023 when it seemed like the streamer did not realize until the Oscar shortlists (in mid-December!) that “All Quiet on the Western Front” was its best bet at Best Picture? The Edward Berger film went on to win four Oscars, including Best International Feature. Related Stories How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles Sean Connery Wasn’t the First James Bond: Meet Barry Nelson in the ‘Casino Royale’ You’ve Never Seen

This year, Netflix is running their best awards campaign yet with “La Bola Negra,” which the studio acquired out of Cannes, where its helmers, Los Javis, won the jury prize for Best Director. Come the fall festivals, it became the first Netflix film to win the People’s Choice Award at TIFF. Since then, it has fronted Netflix’s experiment in expanding the theatrical distribution of its awards slate, doing admirable business in key markets. The consensus among prognosticators is that the film is not only a lock to receive a Best Picture nomination, but is also sure to win the Oscar for Best International Feature on behalf of Spain.

If Netflix wanted to secure a second Best Picture nomination, with “Cliff Booth” out of the picture, the team could put all its energy into Lee Chang-dong’s “Possible Love.” Not only is the near-three hour film, which won the Grand Jury Prize at Venice, another Best International Feature contender (on behalf of South Korea), but it is one of this season’s most critically lauded films. If enough critics’ groups get behind it in the coming weeks, a la “The Secret Agent” last year, then a second Best Picture nomination for Netflix at the 2027 Oscars becomes highly plausible.

Somewhere along the way, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” became something of a puzzle for Netflix. The streamer had no choice but to follow through with putting it out around Thanksgiving, because it was already set to replace the IMAX screens that had initially been secured for Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia” film. So how does a company not run an awards campaign for the sequel to a recent Best Picture nominee, directed by a three-time Oscar nominee, written by a two-time Oscar winner, and starring Brad Pitt in the role he just won a Best Supporting Actor Oscar for?

What reads as a home run on paper is more of a double or triple in execution. “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is made by people who know what they are doing, and that expands past director David Fincher, screenwriter Quentin Tarantino, and star Pitt.

Cinematographer Erik Messerschmidt, editor Kirk Baxter, production designer Donald Graham Burt, set decorator Jan Pascale, and composers Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross have all won at least one Academy Award. Costume designer Trish Summerville was nominated for an Oscar for her work on “Mank.” Even if there is a low bar for getting the Academy excited about a late-’70s period piece set in Hollywood, “Cliff Booth” easily clears it.

But we are in a spectacle-heavy year, with “The Odyssey” and “Project Hail Mary” in the awards conversation, and “Dune: Part Three” and “Werwulf” on the horizon. Even “Digger” is a formidable contender in the craft races. So if the feeling is that “Cliff Booth” is more of a hangout movie than a cinematic event, then the focus of its awards campaign should be on categories that are more willing to embrace that, like Best Production Design or Best Costume Design. (Not so much Best Sound, which “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” did actually receive nominations for.)

In terms of the acting performances, again, Pitt is great as Cliff Booth, but there is no rush to nominate him for a performance he already won for. And there are plenty of other Best Actor contenders, like Matt Damon and John Malkovich (who have never won) and John Turturro and Andrew Scott (who have never even been nominated for an Oscar before).

The top performance of the film is with Cliff’s love interest, played by Emmy winner Elizabeth Debicki, who actually does have a shot at her first Oscar nomination, given the love for her performance in “Wicker” as well, and the lack of current consensus in the Best Supporting Actress race.

Everyone else in the film, from Scott Caan to Yahya Abdul-Mateen II to Carla Gugino, is very additive to the project but does not necessarily cross the threshold into Oscar-contender territory. In that way, it is similar to Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!,” another awards hopeful from this season.

Ultimately, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is entertaining enough to garner support from certain branches of the Academy, but falls too late in the year, in too few theaters, to truly become the last-minute surprise blockbuster that would get as many as 10 Oscar nominations, something its predecessor “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” did handily.

#3394. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

#3393. Sony Fans Debate Major Game Awards Snub

Sony titles and The Game Awards often go hand-in-hand, as plenty of PlayStation exclusives feel tailor-made for the kind of mainstream critical appeal that makes winning awards a cinch. From The Last of Us to the modern God of War games, the company's emphasis on cinematic storytelling has resulted in plenty of nominations and wins over the years.

Of course, that's no guarantee of victory. Sony's 2024 win for Astro Bot was bookended by Marvel's Spider-Man 2 losing to Baldur's Gate 3 in 2023 and Death Stranding 2: On the Beach falling before the unstoppable Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 wave in 2025. 2026 has shaken things up to a significantly greater degree, though, leaving plenty of PlayStation fans conflicted about the nominations.

As Andy Robinson of VGC pointed out on X, 2026 marks the "first time in 11 years" that a title published by Sony hasn't landed among the Game of the Year nominations at The Game Awards. While Marvel's Wolverine followed the critically successful Marvel's Spider-Man games from developer Insomniac Games, it failed to make the same splash, instead earning nominations for Best Performance and Innovations in Accessibility.

Plenty of players seem to be perfectly fine with this snub, at least if the responses to Robinson's post are anything to go by. Jakeinvades argues that Marvel's Wolverine "absolutely did not deserve to be nominated," and FOX suggests that the publisher simply "hasn't produced a GOTY quality IP this year."

There's still some room for debate, however. Some Marvel's Wolverine fans would certainly argue for its inclusion, but the more prevelant argument seems to be in favor of SAROS, which was also released under the Sony umbrella. While X user simon agrees that the Marvel's Wolverine snub is correct, they suggest that SAROS "could've been in the conversation."

I have less affection for games like Marvel's Spider-Man and the 2018 God of War than most, so Sony breaking its nomination streak is no particular skin off my back. ScreenRant's Austin King, who provided our review of Marvel's Wolverine, also wasn't an advocate of any Game of the Year potential, awarding it a respectable but unexceptional 7/10 score.

Sadly, the absence of Marvel's Wolverine in the Game of the Year pool didn't seem to open the way for any particularly intriguing dark horse candidates, as this is a year of fairly predictable AAA inclusions. Games like Control Resonant and Phantom Blade Zero are certainly less omnipresent than Grand Theft Auto 6, but there's no upstart indie darling like 2024's Balatro in the mix.

As to whether Sony can still take home any awards, the company may not go home empty-handed. Marvel's Wolverine might not take either of its categories — Wolverine actor Liam McIntyre could have an uphill battle to take Best Performance over standouts like Resident Evil Requiem's Angela Sant'Albano, and its laudable accessibility options might be too heavily associated with its heavy hand-holding to secure a win for Innovations in Accessibility. MARVEL Tōkon: Fighting Souls in the Fighting Game category at The Game Awards 2026, though? That one could work out.

#3392. 8 Years Later, George R. R. Martin’s ‘Fire & Blood’ Still Has No Sequel

Being a George R.R. Martin fan requires a level of patience that would make even the most dedicated Maester of the Citadel proud. It's been 15 years since A Dance with Dragons arrived in bookstores, and readers are still waiting for The Winds of Winter to continue the main A Song of Ice and Fire series. In the meantime, Martin has kept himself busy expanding the history of Westeros, particularly the rather complicated family tree of House Targaryen. Unfortunately, one of those other books has now developed a lengthy wait of its own.

Martin's Fire & Blood will officially celebrate its eighth anniversary on November 20, 2026, without the publication of its promised second volume. The book was released on November 20, 2018, with publishers announcing from the beginning that it would be the first of two volumes chronicling the history of House Targaryen. Well, it looks like the television series that's based on Martin's work is going to end up concluding before Martin manages to get the words on the page because, eight years later, its follow-up still has no confirmed publication date.

Set roughly 300 years before A Game of Thrones, Fire & Blood begins with Aegon the Conqueror's invasion of Westeros and follows generations of Targaryen rulers. It also covers the Dance of the Dragons, the brutal civil war that forms the basis of HBO's House of the Dragon.

There's a big one coming up, alongside the final season of House of the Dragon and the next seasons of A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms. Earlier this year, Warner Bros. Discovery officially confirmed that Aegon’s Conquest will be released as a theatrical event movie, marking the first feature film set in the Game of Thrones universe.

“Beyond 2027, the slate will continue to leverage iconic intellectual property, including the theatrical event film Aegon’s Conquest from the Game of Thrones universe, the next installment of The Matrix, the next Batman film, and a live-action Jetsons film starring Jim Carrey.”

Aegon’s Conquest tells one of the most pivotal stories in George R.R. Martin’s mythology. It's also probably the coolest, because it's set 300 years before the events of Thrones and follows Aegon Targaryen alongside his sisters Visenya and Rhaenys, as they invade Westeros with their dragons Balerion, Vhagar, and Meraxes.

#3391. A24’s TV Division Is Quietly Having as Strong a Year as Its Film Team

Maybe it’s just because we can’t get enough headlines and discussion about “Backrooms” and “You Can See Everything,” but despite the banner year A24 has had at the box office, its TV division has quietly had nearly as strong of a year.

The indie label has produced more shows in 2026 than in any year in its history, including sleeper commercial and critical hits across the board, and even managed to land shows on virtually every streamer in town.

Led by Sam French, the U.S. head of TV at A24, the studio this year has cranked out the third season of “Euphoria” on HBO Max, the second season of “Beef” and the third season of “Survival of the Thickest” both on Netflix, “Margo’s Got Money Troubles” on Apple TV, the “Friday the 13th” prequel series “Crystal Lake” on Peacock, and most recently the British sitcom “It Gets Worse” on Paramount+ led by the UK Heads Piers Wenger and Rose Garnett. Its unscripted division, led by Johnny Hausfater, has also ramped up aggressively, with shows like “Neighbors,” “Born to Bowl,” and “Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow” all on HBO Max. Related Stories Sean Connery Wasn’t the First James Bond: Meet Barry Nelson in the ‘Casino Royale’ You’ve Never Seen ‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Christmas Special Trailer: Can Mary Bennet Still Be Herself and ‘the Perfect Wife’?

Not unlike its film slate, its series have been a blend of auteur-driven prestige and genre shows with a twist. The David E. Kelley series “Margo’s Got Money Troubles” is a tongue-in-cheek, real-world satire on motherhood and the modern economy about a young single mom played by Elle Fanning who needs to turn to OnlyFans for extra cash. On the other side of the coin, “Crystal Lake” follows masked killer Jason Voorhees’ mom and stands out from other modern horror TV shows by, as our critic wrote, not trying to secretly be a family drama or a slapstick comedy or some other genre or metaphor, but it just amplifies the grisly kills in the best way it can.

The recurring theme between these shows isn’t genre but the stamp of quality that A24 lends.

While something like “Beef” saw a steep drop in viewership of a reported 60 percent between its first and second seasons, “Euphoria” in its return was up 17 percent in its finale ratings compared to Season 2. “Crystal Lake” was also a big hit on Peacock, its top show on the streamer last month, logging 1.3 billion minutes watched over its first 11 days, making it the fourth-highest scripted original series ever on Peacock. A24 now has roughly 30 to 40 shows in various stages of development, pre-production, or active production, with its executive team expanding from about 15 from just 3 people in its early days.

It’s been able to ramp up firstly because of its partnership with numerous TV buyers across the major streamers, but also because of working with largely first-time creators and showrunners. While “Crystal Lake” is a notable exception, A24 generally is operating on its TV side the same way it does with its film, leading with the artist and the project they want to pursue rather than the IP.

That has produced some very personal and idiosyncratic projects over the years like “Ramy” and “The Curse,” the latter of which was the kernel of getting Nathan Fielder to working with A24 again on “You Can See Everything.”

The breadth of content A24 has amassed on its TV side and continually making shows that have the same barrier-pushing flavor and stamp of quality that has become known with A24’s brand is what will help make it as essential a part of the company’s overall business and valuation as its film and distribution business. But we’re seeing even its TV division branching out and embracing IP and tentpoles in the same way its film side has.

Coming up for A24 are a Claire Danes and Ewan McGregor drama “The Spot” on Hulu and “The Apology” with Gwyneth Paltrow on Netflix, which already got a two-season order and was an example of a show that grew out of Paltrow being convinced to try TV after already working with A24 on the film side for “Marty Supreme.” The studio is also is working with Ben Stiller on a New York Knicks documentary series for HBO and a competition cooking show based on the video game “Overcooked” for Netflix. A24 could’ve made a Knicks series with anyone, but teaming with a superfan like Stiller was another example of putting the creator above the concept.

Yet, both a strength and weakness of its TV model is that it does not have a distribution mechanism the way it does on the film side. It’s not bogged down with an unprofitable streamer, a dwindling linear cable channel, or a broadcast network, but that makes it reliant on the many partners it has built up across the industry.

Warner Bros. merging with Paramount arguably reduces the buyers in the market, even if there are still two streamers at Skydance. Netflix just had a massive shakeup of its leadership team that could easily have a different attitude toward A24’s series. And the overall industry trends around the end of Peak TV mean it’s always a volatile business for independents in the TV space.

But no one saw “Backrooms” or “You Can See Everything” coming either, and A24 has as good a chance as any to have lightning strike twice with the next “Euphoria” or “Beef.”

However, as PCMag notes in its review, the color display produces more subdued tones than a conventional tablet, so the Paperwhite remains the more economical choice if you primarily read novels.

The Like-New Kindle Scribe (16GB) is down to $284.99 from $359.99, the biggest dollar discount in this roundup. Unlike the other Kindles here, it's built for reading and writing, with a 10.2-inch, 300ppi glare-free display and a Premium Pen with an eraser and shortcut button—making it the most versatile option for readers who want an e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Home security cameras have become ordinary household hardware. SafeHome.org’s 2026 survey of 2,435 US adults found that 61% of households have at least one, up from 52% in 2024 and 42% in 2023, while video doorbells have reached 48% of households. Renters drove much of that growth. Their adoption rate jumped from 42% to 54% between 2024 and 2026, which makes sense given how many battery-powered cameras can be mounted without drilling and moved at the end of a lease.

In other words, when looking for one of the best home security cameras, it makes more sense to start with the features and subscription, rather than the headline numbers on the spec sheet. That, of course, can make finding the right one even harder. Here are some things to keep in mind when looking for a home security camera.

Arlo's Essential Wireless Security Camera helps you keep an eye on all the places that matter most. With Smart Detection for people, pets and packages, along with real-time alerts and color night vision, this high-quality security camera will give you peace of mind. Get two wire-free, rechargeable cameras this Black Friday, and with easy installation, they'll be up and running for the holidays.

The best way to figure out what security camera is right for you is to start with thinking about what you actually need a camera for.

A video doorbell suits packages and callers because its head-to-toe view and two-way talk are built around a front door. A driveway or yard needs a weatherproof outdoor camera, while a floodlight camera covers a broader area and adds deterrence. As a rule, cover each entry point instead of asking one camera to watch the entire property.

Prices generally fall into three useful bands. Budget models can be found for as little as $29, but you can still find features like 2K video and a pan-and-tilt designs that physically turn to cover a room. Mid-range models (around $100) offer good value, with additional features or better designs. Premium hardware reaches the $249 level and beyond, where you'll find such things as 4K video.

The number of megapixels figure on the box matters less than how many pixels land on a face. A 4-megapixel camera with a 2,560-pixel-wide image and an 80-degree lens can, under the older IEC 62676-4 identification guideline, identify someone at roughly 20 feet. A 4K camera captures 3,840 pixels across, but pair it with a wider 100-degree lens and that estimate rises only to about 21 feet. The extra pixels have been spent on width, so with the same lens, 4K gives you roughly twice the identification distance of 1080p, not four times.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Treat these numbers as geometry rather than guarantees, especially since the IEC standard for measuring detail at distance was revised in 2025. It uses 500 pixels per meter of scene width for validating a known person and 1,500 for high-certainty identification, while many spec sheets still rely on the older 250-pixel guideline. For a doorbell, 1080p is generally enough because visitors are close. For outdoor cameras, 2K, usually around 2,560 pixels across, is the sensible default. Pay for 4K when you need more detail at distance rather than simply a wider view, and check that your storage and Wi-Fi can handle it.

That said, two ordinary cameras in the right places will often beat one expensive 4K model covering everything badly.

“Spend less time chasing the highest resolution number in isolation. More detail can be useful, but placement, nighttime visibility, and useful notifications deserve just as much attention,” says Lars Felber, director of PR at Eve Systems. “A camera pointed at the wrong part of the porch can miss what matters regardless of its resolution.”

Judge a camera on its night footage, too. Infrared night vision uses light outside the visible spectrum to produce a black-and-white image in darkness, so it can show details relatively cleanly, but not with any color. Color night vision needs ambient light from a streetlamp or porch, or a built-in light — though often color night vision is a little less detailed, and usually can't see as far.

Watch for smeared movement too, since some battery cameras reduce their frame rate at night. Keep the lens away from glass and nearby eaves, which can bounce infrared light back into it.

Power decides where a camera can go and whether it can record continuously. Battery models are the easiest to install and the most renter-friendly, but they sleep until motion wakes them, so you get event clips rather than a full timeline and may lose the moments just before a trigger. Plug-in models remove charging breaks but leave you with a cable to route. Hardwired doorbells and floodlights can support 24/7 recording.

Power over Ethernet, usually shortened to PoE, carries power and data down one network cable for a more dependable connection. PoE requires cabling and a compatible switch or recorder, which is more work than most people want for a single doorbell. Solar models are the compromise. Solar models still have a battery, but solar panels keep the battery topped up so you don't need to worry about manual charging.

A solar panel is often the more practical upgrade for an awkward outdoor mount. Just about every company that makes one of the best outdoor security cameras offers a compatible panel. You’ll need a position with dependable sun, and short winter days can still leave the camera reliant on its battery, though it still beats climbing a ladder every few weeks.

Outdoor hardware also needs a weather rating. IP65, which means dust-tight and protected against low-pressure water jets, is a common floor for outdoor cameras and suits eave-mounted units, while IP66 is the better target for fully exposed walls. Check the stated operating temperature too. Arlo rates the Pro 6 down to −4°F, while cheaper models don’t always cope as well with freezing conditions. If you live somewhere that gets truly cold, like Canada, many models may not work for you.

Before drilling, test Wi-Fi at the exact mount point with your phone. Exterior walls and foil-backed insulation can badly weaken 5GHz Wi-Fi, which is fast but relatively short-ranged. Many budget cameras use only 2.4GHz, which reaches farther but contends with more household congestion.

Finally, check your upload speed if you plan to run several cloud cameras. Local recording to a memory card or hub doesn’t use that upload link, but continuous cloud video can saturate it surprisingly quickly.

Often, the price you pay for the camera itself is just a starting point. You still have to store video — and unless you can do so locally, you may have to pay for a subscription.

A local hub splits the difference. These live in your house, but are connected to your cameras wirelessly, so footage can survive both a damaged camera and an internet outage. A hybrid setup is generally the better choice, with local recording for continuity and cloud copies for important events.

“One of the most important things to look for in a home security camera is if a subscription is required to set up and use the device,” says Carney. “Going into the purchasing process, consumers should be aware that some security companies tack on a required subscription as a hidden cost without being transparent about it at purchase.”

Without a plan, some company's cameras will only let you view live events, and not save recordings, or access all of a camera's features. Be sure to look at the price of the subscription, and see if what's being offered is worth the long-term investment.

Once footage is being recorded, the next problem is getting alerted only when it matters. A camera that pings every time a car passes will eventually be ignored. Custom motion zones, sensible sensitivity controls and reliable person, vehicle and package detection do more for daily use than another AI label. At a door, two-way audio is worth having too, so you can speak to a courier without opening it.

“A camera can be very advanced and still fail at its only job if notifications are delayed,” says Rod Sides, founder of Loxx Boxx. “Worse, if it displays too many notifications in a way that you haven’t customized, you’re more likely to overlook the one important notification that may pop up.”

And don’t forget the microphone, since many cameras record audio by default. Recording a private conversation without everyone’s consent can break the law in all-party consent states such as California. If you don’t need sound or two-way talk, switching it off is the safer default.

“What consumers can spend less time worrying about is having the highest resolution or every bell and whistle on the market,” says Zavin. “Instead, focus on what the camera can actually do when a potential threat arises.”

For most homes, a well-placed 2K camera with accurate detection and a local fallback is the better buy. Step up to 4K or paid AI search if you have a specific use for them, not just because they're available.

#3388. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.

#3387. Stephen King Praises Hit 4-Part Thriller As "The Best Cop Show On TV"

Stephen King just revealed what he considers to be the best police procedural on TV.

The bestselling horror author is known for publishing such hits as Carrie, The Shining, The Stand, The Dark Tower, Pet Sematary, It, Misery ,and The Green Mile. When he's not writing, King takes to social media to share his views on current events and gives recommendations for the books, TV shows, and movies he believes his fans should consume.

On that latter front, he has done it again. On X, King showered praise on the British series Blue Lights, calling it "the best cop show on TV," and singled out the season 1 episode "Full Moon Fever," which he believes "deserves all the kudos there are." He also acknowledged that a reviewer once compared Blue Lights to The Pitt due to the authentic way it depicts the field of law enforcement, similar to how The Pitt does the same for medicine.

"BLUE LIGHTS (Britbox): The best cop show on TV, and one episode 'Full Moon Fever'--deserves all the kudos there are. Some critic said 'It's THE PITT with police.' Smart critic."

Blue Lights premiered in 2023 and centers on three recruits—Grace, Annie and Tommy—who work for the Police Service of Northern Ireland at Blackthorn Station as they deal with gangs, feuds, and division in the city.

Sian Brooke, Katherine Devlin, Nathan Braniff, Martin McCann, Richard Dormer, Hannah McClean, Andi Osho, Jonathan Harden, and John Lynch star in the series, which was created by Declan Lawn and Adam Patterson.

With a critics' score of 91% and an audience score of 87% on Rotten Tomatoes, Blue Lights has earned positive reviews throughout its run on the air and won Best Drama Series at the BAFTA TV Awards last year.

Blue Lights is available to stream on BritBox and ended its fourth season earlier this month. While BBC One has not renewed Blue Lights for season 5 yet, if it were to come back, Lawn and Patterson won't be there as they recently revealed they've exited the production to work on other projects.

King is no stranger to the world of television, as many of his novels have been adapted for the small screen over the years, including It, 11.22.63, The Mist, Mr. Mercedes, The Outsider, The Stand, Chapelwaite, and The Institute.

His very first book, Carrie, was recently given the TV treatment on Prime Video, courtesy of Mike Flanagan, who previously adapted King's Gerald's Game, Doctor Sleep, and The Life of Chuck.

With Summer H. Howell in the title role, Carrie received positive reviews this fall from critics and audiences alike, and King, who serves as an executive producer, gave it his stamp of approval.

Adaptations of King's books have been hit or miss, according to the author himself. He hasn't been shy about expressing when a film or show hasn't met his expectations. On the flip side, he's always eager to share his recommendations from other creators and storytellers, like he has done with Blue Lights.

As viewers wait to find out whether the series gets renewed, perhaps Stephen King's positive reception will create new fans and help the network with its decision.

Blue Lights (2023) is a police drama set in Belfast, following three new PSNI recruits as they learn how dangerous and complicated frontline policing can be. Their training quickly becomes a test of judgment and survival as they face criminal gangs, divided communities, and the pressures that come with policing a city still shaped by its troubled past.

#3386. ‘Superman’ Star’s New Heist Thriller Is Officially 2026's Latest Box Office Bomb

Nicholas Hoult has enjoyed a pretty remarkable run over the past few years, appearing in everything from The Menu and Nosferatu to James Gunn's Superman, where he stepped into the role of Lex Luthor. With a growing collection of major franchises and acclaimed performances under his belt, the British star has become one of Hollywood's most recognizable leading men. Unfortunately, that hasn't translated to box office success for his newest movie.

How to Rob a Bank has officially opened to just $5.175 million domestically across 2,810 theaters, making it one of Hoult's weakest wide-release debuts. The Amazon MGM Studios thriller also earned approximately $5.1 million internationally, bringing its worldwide total to $10.275 million following its first weekend in US theaters. The movie reportedly cost around $40 million to produce, meaning its opening represents a difficult start for a film that will need considerably more revenue to cover production and marketing expenses.

In How to Rob a Bank, Hoult is The Wolf, an anonymous YouTuber whose merry band of bank robbers — played by Pete Davidson, Anna Sawai, and Rhenzy Feliz — go viral broadcasting their heists on their channel. As they continue to garner more views, an FBI agent (John C. Reilly) enlists the help of a hacker under house arrest (Zoë Kravitz) to help track them down. Director David Leitch spoke to Collider's Steve Weintraub earlier this month about the inspiration behind the film, and how there's more to it than a simple cat-and-mouse thriller.

"It was very, very contemporary. I think these characters, although you don't really find out their motivations until the second act, which I've held off that reveal by choice, they're very relatable. People are dealing with health care debt, people are dealing with homes they can't afford, people are dealing with medical issues, and the system is not necessarily working for them."

Leitch added that he knew he still had to make the movie entertaining as well as informative, however, adding: "That's what art is supposed to do, and that's what this film is supposed to do, outside of it being a big, fun commercial heist movie. I think I set that up in the first act, but then I'm taking you on a journey."

How to Rob a Bank opened in US theaters on November 13, 2026, and is currently playing nationwide. Stay tuned to Collider for all the latest news and updates on the biggest and best movies and shows heading to your favorite streaming platforms soon.
