#3385. 10 Shows Like 'Minimum Wage' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Spinning off of a popular web series, Netflix's Minimum Wage is currently in the middle of a 28-episode first-season run. If that sounds like a lot of episodes for a show in 2026, keep in mind that they're generally less than 15 minutes each, which is perfect for your overloaded to-watch list—especially when they go down so easily. This cringe workplace mockumentary follows the crew of teenagers running a failing pizza place and making (you guessed it) minimum wage; they're under enormous pressure from their boss (Randall Park) to save the business and their one dumb source of income.

The punchy episodes will leave you plenty of time to explore other streaming shows dealing with the utter ridiculousness of the modern workplace. Here are 10 to get you started.

Workplace comedies usually revolve around white-collar office environments (The Mary Tyler Moore Show, 30 Rock, Parks and Recreation, etc.). Like Minimum Wage, Superstore instead follows the staff of Cloud 9, a generic big-box retailer. The show’s deep bench and diverse cast are largely focused on the jokes, but much of that comedy involves the relatable situation of working a job that demands commitment and a smiley attitude in the face of both entitled customers and obnoxious bosses. It's a different venue and age bracket, but a nutty workplace is a nutty workplace. Stream Superstore on Hulu and Peacock.

We're moving away from the workplace and aging things up a bit, but no worries: the name is a little ironic given that the codependent, co-habitating twenty-somethings of the title are hardly mature. Five friends are cohabiting in the childhood home of Samir (Malik Elassal), and dealing with the uniquely Gen-Z humiliations around dating, work, and even health insurance. Only one member of the group has an actual reasonably good job, while career paths for the others include being a temp, waiter, and a part-time ballet instructor. Stream Adults on Hulu.

This offbeat workplace comedy kicks off with a fabulous premise: Jeong Bok-dong (Kim Byung-chul) was a high-level director in a major corporation until one bad meeting saw him demoted. To president! ...of the company's failing Pegasus Mart offshoot. Bok-dong makes it his mission to get revenge by bankrupting the store, hiring eccentrics to execute eccentric, entirely whackadoo plans and accidentally getting Pegasus noticed by customers, who quickly make it more popular than ever. Think The Producers, but in retail. Stream Pegasus Market on Tubi.

It might sound a little (or a lot) niche, but we’ve seen enough headlines about the working conditions at many video game production houses to understand why a workplace comedy set against such a backdrop would make for a dark and juicy comedy. Charlotte Nicdao and Rob McElhenney are the leads, playing a brilliant workaholic and an unsociable egomaniac, respectively, and the chemistry between them gives the show more than enough spark. There's also a four-episode spin-off called Side Quest. Stream Mythic Quest.

A half-hour comedy-drama with an emphasis on the comedy, Gentefied follows three Mexican-American cousins who have built lives in Los Angeles, only to be faced with a new challenge: the looming gentrification of the neighborhood they helped to build via their family's taco shop. Gentefied has a baked-in sense of place and culture and a lot of heart; the second season is even better than the first. Stream Gentefied on Netflix.

Perhaps there's a bit of counter-programming in this dramedy about a couple of scrappy New York City outsiders, but there's a fundamental goofiness to this show about a couple of nice guys who are great at getting themselves into trouble, and equally good at talking themselves out of it. Bryan Greenberg plays Ben Epstein, a quiet guy with any number of big ideas, while Victor Rasuk plays the outgoing, often shameless Cam Calderon; together they manage a startup clothing business with the benefits of neither money nor experience, amiably hustling their way to success, maybe. Stream How to Make It in America on HBO Max and Netflix.

Debuting at the beginning of the Obama administration before getting a surprise revival just a couple of years ago, Party Down is an acclaimed cult sitcom for the ages—lots of laughs, low ratings, and always worth rediscovering. A group of six (or so) struggling LA actors and writers work as cater waiters for a fancy company, with every episode into a new and wildly absurd situation, even as their aspirations far outstrip their actual lives. Stream Party Down on Prime Video and Netflix.

A legitimate sitcom that just happens to be set in Northern Ireland during the violent Troubles of the 1990s, when clashes between nationalists and unionists frequently resulted in violence. It’s a fascinating contrast, brought to life by a writer and creator (Lisa McGee) who lived it. It’s also laugh-out-loud funny—though it doesn’t make any allowances for audiences unaccustomed to Irish accents, so don’t feel bad if you need subtitles until you get the hang of it. Erin, Orla, Clare, and Michelle are joined by James, the only male student at their Catholic girls' school, dealing with normal growing-up stuff in absurd times. This world is a far cry from that of Minimum Wage, but Lisa McGee's sense of the absurd connects both shows—if the setting is a bit more dramatic, the comedy is just as wonderfully silly. Stream Derry Girls on Netflix.

Not a comedy! But about as good an indication of where we are in the modern global workplace as you're likely to find. Hyuk‑jun is a young guy saddled with debt who signs on for some part-time work at a job agency...at 50x the going rate, no less (should've been a red flag). Each new assignment places him in new and increasingly horrific situations, with increasingly arbitrary-seeming rules. But, hey, in 2026, it's a living. Stream Dead-End Job on Netflix.

It's an office (obviously) and not a pizza joint, but the point here is kinda that white-collar jobs in the 21st century can be at least as soul-killing as working customer service. The Office inherited some of the finer tropes of the workplace comedy (mostly involving tossing together a group of weirdos overly invested in their jobs) while also launching a million mockumentary-style shows, running for nine seasons, and becoming one of the most popular shows of its era. Stream The Office on Peacock.

#3383. There’s a Good Reason the NYC Marathon Winners Wore These Watches

Over 60,000 runners crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon last week. When you think of the elites fighting for a spot on the podium, you might expect to see only the priciest, most feature-packed GPS watches money can buy—historically, this meant the most premium Garmin Forerunners. Looking at the wrists of this year's New York City Marathon podium finishers, though,  you’ll see that Garmin—the name most recreational runners reach for by default—was far from the only brand on the course.

Here are the watches I’ve been able to confirm among the top NYC Marathon finishers:

Men's winner, Andreas Almgren: Coros Pace 4 Pro (sponsored)

Men's runner-up, Yemaneberhan Crippa: Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro (sponsored)

Women's runner-up, Jessica McClain: Garmin Forerunner 570 (sponsored)

Women's third place, Hellen Obiri: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Nonbinary winner, Ryan Montgomery: Suunto Race 3S (almost certainly sponsored, since this watch was released last month)

An important disclaimer: I haven't spoken with any of these athletes. What follows is my opinion, based on what I know running watches offer the people who wear them.

"Garmin" has long been the default answer to "what running watch should I buy?" It earned that spot with reliable GPS, excellent software, and a huge ecosystem. And on this podium, it's represented by a Forerunner 570—a great watch, but at a price tag most runners would struggle to justify.

Of course, sponsorships muddy the water, since athletes wear what their sponsors put on their wrists. But that's exactly the point: Other brands are investing in elite runners because they believe their products can stand next to Garmin's, and it looks like they’re making the right bet.

It's fair to ask whether Garmin's grip is loosening. The company has increasingly pushed toward the fanciest watches with the most features at higher and higher price points. The Forerunner 570 starts north of $500. Meanwhile, COROS, Amazfit, and others are proving that a perfectly solid, competitive watch doesn't need to cost that much. Is Garmin still the best running watch overall? For ecosystem, polish, and depth of features, it's still a strong contender. But "best" no longer means "the only serious option," and the gap between Garmin and the field is narrower than it has been in years. Sponsored or not, seeing two Coros Pace 4s and an Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro among the top finishers is worth noting.

You don’t need an expensive watch to be elite—just look at the cheap running watches worn by the men who broke the sub-two-hour barrier at the London Marathon this past spring. Training load scores, recovery metrics, maps, music, and smart notifications are nice, but they're extras. If you're shopping for a watch, spend your money on the basics being done right, and don't feel pressured to pay for features you'll never use. Everything besides your time and pace is icing on the cake.

Whichever brand you choose, focus on these basics in your running watch:

The New York City Marathon podium shows a running-watch market that's a bit more competitive and intriguing than the era of "just buy a Garmin" suggests. Garmin is still excellent, but now we’re seeing proof that Coros, Amazfit, and Suunto are all making watches good enough for the fastest humans on the planet. If they can trust those watches on their biggest days, the rest of us can probably trust them with our Saturday long runs.

#3382. Dragon Ball’s Best Episode In 8 Years Proves Fans Were Wrong About The Series’ New Anime

The Dragon Ball Super: Beerus anime has been doing a great job of removing unnecessary filler and improving on the original Dragon Ball Super series, but changes in the latest episode were so good that they've justified the entire project. While long-time Dragon Ball fans have been anxiously awaiting the continuation of the story in the Galactic Patrol arc, the news that the latest anime project would be devoted to improving Dragon Ball Super's first three arcs felt like a waste of Toei's talents, but the latest episode proves those fears were unfounded.

When the original Dragon Ball Super anime first aired, its extremely rushed and poorly planned production cycle created episodes that were lacking in many ways. With the franchise being one of the world's most beloved, the anime's static battles and mind-numbing filler material deflated the years of hype that had been building for Dragon Ball's anime return.

In 2015, episode #5 of Dragon Ball Super featured Goku's first sparring match against Beerus, the God of Destruction. The battle's flat presentation and underwhelming choreography felt like a mistake that nearly destroyed the hype the Dragon Ball franchise had built for its return. The goal of Dragon Ball Super: Beerus was to fix those mistakes and also make the Destroyer God more intimidating, and after six episodes, it's clear that goal has been accomplished.

It didn't take long for Dragon Ball Super: Beerus to prove that it would be different from the original anime and even the Battle of Gods movie. The first arc of the franchise's big revival introduced the God of Destruction, Beerus, and his Angel attendant Whis. It was an arc that took the first anime series 14 episodes to tell, but the new series was able to condense that all into only six episodes, with the sixth episode being the perfect example of the series' improvements.

Now that the production team was given time and the opportunity to revise previously released content, far more detail, upgraded coloring, and even entirely new animations help fix the series' stalest moments. Those improvements can be noticed in several of episode #6's upgraded scenes. This is especially true during Goku's first battle as a Super Saiyan God, which now includes higher levels of drama and intensity, especially with the changes to Beerus.

After watching from the sidelines for weeks, English dub viewers finally have an official streaming schedule for Dragon Ball Super.

One particular part had Beerus holding Goku underwater, and in the original series, the Saiyan broke out of the hold, violently pushing the God of Destruction back while Beerus made a silly expression of surprise. It was one of the many moments with the Destroyer that was played for comedy. However, the new Dragon Ball anime has removed a lot of those moments, with episode six even replacing Beerus's expression with one of competent curiosity, one that reminds viewers that Beerus was always in control.

Besides the improved artwork, pacing, and music, brand-new sequences have also helped Dragon Ball Super: Beerus feel more than a simple remaster cash grab. Near the end of Goku and Beerus's match at the highest levels of Earth's atmosphere, an added monologue from the Destroyer God to an unconscious Goku saw Beerus explicitly express his respect for the Saiyan. It was an extremely rare peek into an important character's honest thoughts, and it was a moment that added to Beerus's developing humility and Goku's accomplishment of impressing him.

When it was announced that Dragon Ball Super: Beerus would be condensing the original series' first 41 episodes into only 19, it was inevitable that some good material would land on the cutting room floor. Fortunately, the remastered series removed most of the scenes that failed to move the main plot forward, including the Pilaf gang's annoying side-quest to steal the Dragon Balls. Still, there were a few moments that were drastically shortened and some that were completely removed that I wish had stayed.

Dragon Ball Super: Beerus has premiered on Crunchyroll, and the first episode of the anime is so popular that it crashed the streaming service.

Moments that were specifically missing from the part of the story that episode #6 covered were great character moments for Piccolo, Whis, and even Goku. The part where Piccolo grabs Whis's arm, and the Angel's demeanor suddenly shifts into a cold and threatening tone, is gone. Notably, a fan-favorite moment where Goku breaks through several layers of Earth's bedrock while screaming "I won't let you destroy my world!" at the God of Destruction also did not make it into Dragon Ball Super: Beerus. Those scenes add moments of hype and character depth that new audiences will miss if this is all they watch.

One of the most divisive alterations relates to Vegeta', and the depths he was willing to go to protect the new life he's worked so hard to create. In both the Battle of Gods movie and the original Dragon Ball Super anime, Vegeta is willing to embarrass himself in an attempt to entertain Beerus. It showed that the safety of his family now means more to him than his Saiyan pride. That change removed a moment that speaks to Vegeta's character development and ultimately helped improve the overall narrative.

Now that the first Dragon Ball Super arc has concluded in the remastered series, it's safe to say that it's an improvement. Large sections of the original series that focused on unfunny and uninteresting scenes involving characters who have no narrative impact on future events severely dragged the pacing. And when battles did finally happen, the flat animation and repeated sequences felt like another insult that ultimately repelled viewers who'd grown up idolizing Dragon Ball Z. Thankfully, Dragon Ball Super: Beerus has addressed those glaring problems and become the best way to enjoy the beginning of the sequel series.

Even though Goku & Vegeta's strength has become godly, there are still a handful of Dragon Ball characters they can't & may never be able to defeat.

The first arc has been an improvement in almost every way, but there are still scenes that Toei left in that could have been removed. The shapeshifting pig, Oolong, hasn’t provided anything important to the narrative in decades, which is why it was baffling to see his prolonged game of rock-paper-scissors against Beerus remain in the new series. Still, even if a few moments like that stay and reduce the time for beloved scenes, Dragon Ball Super: Beerus has made enough smart and exciting changes to change my mind about it and power up my anticipation for more.

I have this running bit where I call Robert Pattinson my girlfriend. It started sometime after "The Lighthouse" because old men gone bitter with yearning is very much my brand of terminally ill brain worm, and the joke's only gotten funnier with the stellar year the "Twilight" star's had. Yesterday, Amazon MGM Studios announced that Pattinson is taking up the mantle of 007, and I broke the news to the group chat with the following message: "my girlfriend is gonna be James Bond!" No explanation needed.

I've never seen a James Bond movie all the way through, a fact that shocked my (mostly male) coworkers this morning. Now that my favorite weird little guy is in the lead, I'm willing to break that streak. Before you go calling me a rabid fangirl, I have another confession: I first watched "Twilight" all the way through this year. I attempted once in high school but had to bail at the baseball scene where the level of unabashed white corniness on display had my eyes nearly rolling out of my skull.

No, my excitement for Pattinson's 007 reign doesn't stem from nostalgia, but from a quiet fascination that's sparked into an obsession over the past decade. This, the man who insists he's "spiritually Gen Z" despite pushing 40, who lies in interviews for fun, who dragged millions of screaming fans into theaters by being a brooding, sexy vampire for a series he openly despises. And I suspect his casting has activated those same millennial women like sleeper agents who will no doubt propel this latest Bond run into one of the most commercially successful to date. With many, like myself, turning out for their first Bond venture in theaters ever.

Action films are a notable blind spot in my cinema knowledge, one that I've been trying to fill in recent years since writing about streaming for Tom's Guide. It's not that I avoided them, per say, just that they didn't immediately appeal to me in the same way as my favorite genres — horror, art house, and damn near anything animated — did.

All the Jason Bournes, John Wicks, and Ethan Hunts of the world struck me as carbon copies of one another made in a lab to be propelled through one bombastic shoot out after the next. Now that I've caught up on a few of these iconic franchises, that opinion still rings true, though I've gained an appreciation for the kind of high-octane set pieces action fans still talk about to this day.

With Pattinson at the helm of the next Bond film, for the first time in my life, I'm excited to see a 007 movie in theaters. His talent and magnetism, even as some of the most pathetic characters I've ever seen on screen, is something straight out of the golden age of Hollywood.

Today's Bond announcement is the cherry on top of a year that's cemented Pattinson as a once in a generation acting talent. Between making our skin crawl as the charismatically slimy Chris Hansen in "Primetime" to going viral for shouting “somebody get these beggars out of here” in Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster megahit “The Odyssey" and proving once again that no one does pathetic quite as well as he does in "The Drama," it's been a banner year for Pattison.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

The British actor most known for his roles as Edward Cullen in “Twilight,” Cedric Diggory in "Harry Potter," and Bruce Wayne in Matt Reeves’ “The Batman” series will now succeed Daniel Craig as everyone's favorite suave superspy. There's no release date yet for Pattinson's debut as 007, though we do know Denis Villeneuve, who has already worked with Pattinson on the upcoming “Dune Part 3,” will be at the helm with a script by "Peaky Blinders" creator Steven Knight.

It's clear Amazon MGM is trying to appeal to younger viewers with this pick too. After being around for over 70 years, James Bond's built a reputation as your father's (or maybe even grandfather's) favorite spy franchise. As Bruce Wayne in "The Batman," Pattinson proved he can bring a fresh edge to an iconic character without losing the mass appeal that makes a franchise work. With "The Batman" sequel currently in production, he’s also firmly established as a leading man audiences will turn out to see. For a franchise looking to usher in its next era, that's a pretty convincing résumé.

#3380. The 10 Best Alternative Rock Albums of the 21st Century, Ranked

Looking over alternative rock music, most of the greatest of the greats can be found in the final couple of decades of the 20th century. Like, the 1980s and 1990s was the time when alternative rock was at its most classic and dominant, like how classic rock, you know, dominated (and felt “most” classic) in the second half of the 1960s and then throughout the 1970s.

That doesn’t mean you should only look to the 1980s and 1990s, though, if you want to hear great alternative rock. There have been more than enough artists tackling that genre so far throughout the 2000s and a little beyond as well. Case in point, these ones, which can count themselves among the very best alternative rock albums of the 21st century so far (more of them in the 2000s and the first half of the 2010s, sure, but rock – alternative or otherwise – just hasn’t thrived in quite the same way since about the mid-2010s onward).

It’s obvious to point at Interpol and say, “Hey, that band sounds quite a lot like Joy Division,” but maybe that’s okay. After all, there are only a couple of Joy Division albums, so there’s more territory with the whole post-punk sound to mine, but also, Interpol do some interesting things with that sound and aren’t just like a Joy Division cover band. Also, of course there’s going to be similarities, since Interpol are sometimes lumped in with the post-punk revival genre.

That’s what you'd expect it to be: post-punk returning with a bit of a sheen a couple of decades on from its heyday. Turn on the Bright Lights is the sort of definitive album you can listen to not just if you want to work out whether you'll like Interpol, but whether you'll like this whole sub-genre of alternative rock. It’s an album with a ton of hype behind it, but it thankfully lives up to all that.

Listing off highlights in terms of individual tracks feels hardest for Radiohead’s In Rainbows, owing to how well the album flows, and how consistent it is. Once you mention “15 Step,” “Weird Fishes/Arpeggi,” “Jigsaw Falling Into Place,” and “Videotape,” you feel obligated to mention all the other tracks, and that won’t be done. They're all great. They're all worthy of mentioning. That’s the main thing.

In Rainbows is a little more rock-adjacent, definitely came out in the 21st century, and it’s almost as good as Kid A, so it’s going here.

If Kid A counts as a 21st century album, then maybe it’s a little better than In Rainbows, but not by much. But the year 2000 is kind of the end of the 20th century rather than the start of the next one. Oh, and Kid A doesn’t have a lot by way of alternative rock. In Rainbows is a little more rock-adjacent, definitely came out in the 21st century, and it’s almost as good as Kid A, so it’s going here. It feels right.

Tame Impala is easily one of the best rock acts of the century so far, and it’s easier to call Tame Impala an act or a project than a band, since Tame Impala is – as the meme says – just one guy (Kevin Parker). The same can be said for The Cure (Robert Smith), though, so it’s not unheard of. Anyway, Tame Impala is great and/or Kevin Parker is great. Either way, same greatness.

Lonerism is the easiest album to label as “rock,” and probably the strongest overall, too, even if the slightly poppier Currents (2015) does have some undeniable highlights track-wise. Like, “Let It Happen” and “The Less I Know the Better” might be better than the best song on Lonerism, but Lonerism has extra appeal as a coherent album, with all its tracks bleeding into each other so well, making for a seamless listen for the 50-ish minutes it goes on for.

As the title might suggest, Songs for the Deaf is kind of a concept album, but not really the sort that goes far enough to have an in-depth narrative or a particularly notable number of themes it really hones in on. It’s more of an experience kind of thing, designed to replicate the feeling of cycling through a bunch of strange and/or unfamiliar radio stations during a long drive, and hey, it does do that premise/concept pretty well.

You’ve got a few interludes and snippets of audio contributing to this concept, but mostly, Songs for the Deaf stands out for being very generous with a ton of great alternative rock songs. Queens of the Stone Age peaked here, and that’s not so bad when the peak is this high (and, for what it’s worth, there are definitely other albums by the band worth checking out if you got something out of Songs for the Deaf).

You might not like this particular realization dawning on you, but if American Idiot were a person, it would've been able to drink legally for a year, and it’s been able to vote for about four years. It is old. Maybe that makes you feel old, too. But hey, it’s held up well. Maybe you’ve held up well, too. Best to stay positive (maybe not during September, though, if you want to be woken up when it ends).

American Idiot isn't really a positive album, though, for what it’s worth, since it’s an angry album, and one focused on reflecting feelings that were felt during a confusing and politically charged time in history. Time passes, though, and maybe even that simpler kind of anger and passion feels a little nostalgic. Anyway, this album is very much a time capsule for alternative rock in the 2000s, and maybe even the 2000s overall, so it’s well and truly got its place in history, all the while still sounding pretty great when listened to today.

Fever to Tell might be one of the best punk rock albums not released during that genre’s heyday, though it’s got a bit more to it than just punk, and so it fitting within the pantheon of great alternative rock albums also feels fitting. This Yeah Yeah Yeahs album definitely has that punk energy throughout, but its indie/alternative rock elements are implemented flawlessly, and it does indeed feel like rock a good deal of the time.

Counting the hidden track, there are 12 songs here, and the album isn't long, so the average track length is only about three minutes, meaning nothing really risks overstaying its welcome (a couple of songs even clock in at under two minutes in duration). Though it sounds of its time, Fever to Tell has aged surprisingly well and still sounds awesome, all the while also being able to count itself as easily the best album by Yeah Yeah Yeahs to date.

Quite a bit of what could be said about American Idiot can also be said about The Black Parade, with the two being rock operas/concept albums that blended alternative rock, pop, and a bit of punk. With The Black Parade, you can also lump it in with the emo genre, but it’s a cut above a ton of the other stuff associated with that particular genre/movement, all the while being the best and most ambitious of all the My Chemical Romance albums to date.

And then like American Idiot once again, nostalgia could have some impact on The Black Parade feeling as great as it does, but not wholly. The Black Parade is a genuinely great concept album dealing with all sorts of heavy things, and it goes more in-depth on those topics than you might expect, based on the genres it’s associated with. It’s something that was operating on a whole other level compared to all the comparable albums from around this time, and it’s aged exceedingly well all these years later.

The National had a good run throughout much of the first two decades of this current century. Like, there’s Alligator (2005) and Boxer (2007) often being fan favorites, and then the likes of Trouble Will Find Me (2013) and Sleep Well Beast (2017) are also excellent, being close to the standards of those other two albums. Yet you can see The National and their very best right between these two pairs of albums.

It’s High Violet (2010) that makes that halfway point, being a pretty much perfect album that encompasses everything great about The National within a single album. It is a somewhat dreary and downbeat listening experience, but there’s thankfully a lot of passion here alongside all the sadness, so it’s not miserable or too much. For something oftentimes sad, it’s also got a surprisingly high number of earworms and moments of catharsis.

With Arcade Fire, it’s a bit of a Radiohead kind of situation where the album here might not be the band’s very best, but it’s also not far off, and it’s here because it fits within the confines of “alternative rock” to the greatest extent. It’s The Suburbs, which is the band’s third album overall, and one where they really seem to tackle Americana, doing a bit of a Bruce Springsteen thing in parts alongside referencing and paying homage to some other great classic rock acts.

It’s eclectic, though, as can be expected from an Arcade Fire album, with the best song here sounding more like Blondie’s “Heart of Glass” than any classic rock song (the song in question is “Sprawl II (Mountains Beyond Mountains)”). Everything here is pretty great, though, and it could well be the most approachable album of the band’s, too.

If you're into indie/alternative rock, you'll pretty much guaranteed to like Wilco’s Yankee Hotel Foxtrot, but if you also like more old-fashioned sorts of rock, you'll likely also find things to like here. It’s just a great album, right up there with the century’s best so far, and that’s probably the easiest thing to say. It’s a more mellow sort of rock, sure, but rock nonetheless, maybe scratching a similar melancholic itch to some of the best The National albums.

Some sadness is inevitable when the album begins with a song named “I Am Trying to Break Your Heart,” so that one sets the stage quite ideally. Then there are other songs here that lyrically go beyond more personal topics like love, loss, and loneliness, with the variety being appreciated, of course. Some of the songs here are quite long, and Yankee Hotel Foxtrot also clocks in at over 50 minutes all up, but you never really come close to feeling the length here in a detrimental way.

#3379. Kid Rock's Nashville Bar Sued By Woman Who Claims Security Did Nothing After She Was Attacked

Kid Rock's Nashville bar is facing a new lawsuit related to its security guards ... though this time someone is alleging the security wasn't aggressive enough.

A woman named Ava Bozzo is suing Kid Rock's Big Ass Honky Tonk Rock & Roll Steakhouse ... claiming she went to the establishment to dance and drink with friends in November 2024, when an unidentified man allegedly attacked her, picked her up, and threw her down while she was dancing.

Ava claims she "sustained significant injuries," including a broken tooth that required medical attention ... as well as emotional injuries after the alleged incident.

She says security did not rush to her aid ... and she's suing for breach of duty and negligent supervision and training.

While she essentially says security didn't do enough, another man sued the same establishment and alleged the bar's guards did too much ... claiming they badly beat him up for touching a performer's guitar.

He claims one of the men became "disproportionately agitated" ... before slamming him against the wall of an elevator while he was being thrown out of the establishment.

In response to both lawsuits, Kid's Rock Big Ass Honky Tonk Rock & Roll Steakhouse has denied all wrongdoing.

#3378. This Actively Exploited Chrome Vulnerability Is Putting Your Browser at Risk

If you've seen an uptick in security updates as of late, you're not alone. AI models have become very good at finding new security vulnerabilities throughout 2026. Researchers and hackers alike are increasingly relying on these models in their individual pursuits: Hackers want to find these flaws to exploit them, while researchers want to block hackers from doing so. Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday update included more than 1,400 patches; meanwhile, Apple's latest security update fixed two iMessage flaws that let both bad actors and innocent parties alike access texts they shouldn't.

Whether you use a Mac or a PC, you probably browse the web with Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser. As it happens, Google's web browsing platform is the latest to receive an important security update—but it's far from the first important Chrome update of the year.

As reported by The Hacker News, Google released a new update for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws. While all vulnerabilities are important to patch, one in particular is more serious than the rest: CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component.

Use-after-free vulnerabilities happen when the system frees up a memory location, but a program tries to access it anyway. It's a glitch in programming, but it offers bad actors an opportunity to break into your system. At worst, it allows arbitrary code execution, or, in other words, gives hackers the ability to run their own code in the app or system.

That's bad enough on the surface, but, unfortunately, Google confirmed that CVE-2026-125350 has an active exploit in the wild. The company is keeping other details close to the vest, but it's dangerous nonetheless. At least someone, somewhere, has used this flaw against a target, which puts all Chrome users (as well as users of Chromium-based browsers) at risk.

What's more, this isn't Chrome's first active exploit of the year—this is its eighth. The company is playing catch-up with hackers looking to target users of its browser, which makes sense, seeing as Chrome is by far the world's most popular browser.

If you're using Chrome on your computer, you'll want to update it as soon as possible. Make sure you're running at least versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Mac or PC, or 157.0.8103.50 on Linux. To check, click the three dots in the top-right corner of your Chrome window, then go to More > Help > About Google Chrome.

Other Chromium-based browsers may not have the update yet, but they are affected by this flaw. If you use browsers like Microsoft Edge, Opera, or Brave, keep an eye on your updates to install any of the latest patches.

#3377. High-Protein Packaged Foods May Not Be As Healthy As They Look

Of the three major macronutrients—protein, carbs, and fat—protein has the best reputation, and it’s fairly well deserved. We need significant amounts of protein in our diet, and nothing particularly bad happens if we get too much. Dietary protein helps you build muscle, and if you’re trying to lose weight it helps stop you from losing too much muscle along with the fat. It also helps to make meals feel filling. Great! But.

Once the general public gets the idea that something is good for you, the companies that make packaged food start putting it in everything. Or, they make products where the good-for-you thing features prominently on the label, whether or not there is very much inside. So a lot of packaged food now boasts protein on the label. Here’s what you should ask yourself about those foods:

Take a close look here—sometimes a food will boast of a certain amount of protein per package but the package contains two or three servings. Other times, the protein per serving is correct, and we're supposed to be excited to have, say, 7 grams per serving. That's just not very much—and certainly not worth paying extra or choosing a less-delicious food just for those few added grams.

It’s good to know how much protein you need in your diet. If you’re not gaining or losing weight, and not doing very much exercise, a 150-pound person only needs about 54 grams of protein a day. (I've done the math for various body weights here.) If you’re working out a lot, or if you’re trying to gain or lose weight (yep, either way), that same 150-pound person will need more like 81 to 95 grams of protein per day. More is OK, but not necessary.

So if you’re trying to get 90 grams per day, 30 grams per meal is a reasonable amount to shoot for. Coincidentally, 30 grams is the amount of protein that tends to make a meal feel satisfying. You can do the math to figure out whether a protein-added product is going to be helpful in your day’s diet.

I think this is the most important question about protein-added foods. It’s not hard to get protein in a meal; meats, dairy, tofu, beans, and grains all tend to supply plenty. So what is this protein-added thing you’re considering, and are you eating it instead of a traditional meal?

Here’s an example. If I’m heading straight from the gym to run some errands, and I need something to substitute for a meal—yeah, this isn’t great planning, but sometimes it happens—a protein bar with 20 grams of protein is a step in the right direction. Much better than a candy bar, anyway.

But then there are things like this "protein mix" trail mix: 7 grams of protein with 200 calories. A double serving would be 400 calories and only 14 grams of protein. Hardly a great choice if your goal is just to add to your protein intake for the day.

And then there are the chips that my kid, for a time, couldn't stop eating. He loves Doritos and such; on a whim, we bought him some protein chips (yes, these are a real thing). Are they better for him than the equivalent amount of Doritos? Arguably, sort of yes. But then he started arguing that since they have protein, he should be able to eat them in place of dinner. We nixed that, but admit it: Are you having that same argument with yourself, feeling better about a snack food because it contains extra protein? If so, the marketing is working—you’re feeling good about your supposedly healthy choices, even though you’re just eating a bag of chips.

#3375. Elden Ring: Become Lord Officially Releases January 2027

Elden Ring will be nearing its fifth anniversary next January, and it's become increasingly clear in the time since release that the game won't be going away any time soon. The open-world Soulslike has proven to be one of the defining games of its generation, and its longevity has been helped along by the release of the massive Shadow of the Erdtree expansion and the standalone multiplayer title Elden Ring Nightreign.

It doesn't look like another game is set to arrive any time soon — developer FromSoftware has The Duskbloods up next instead — but that doesn't mean that Elden Ring will be leaving the spotlight. Elden Ring: Become Lord takes a new look at the Shardbearers in a manga format, and the English translation of its first volume is almost here.

Per the official Yen Press website, Elden Ring: Become Lord, Vol. 1 will release on January 26, 2027, in both paperback and digital formats. As a paperback volume, the manga will retail for $20.00, while the digital version will slash the price to $9.99. Along with direct pre-orders from the Yen Store, the volume is also available for pre-order from major booksellers like Amazon, Barnes & Noble, Books-A-Million, and Kinokuniya.

Like the game, Elden Ring: Become Lord follows a Tarnished protagonist, using the character as a tool to chronicle the stories of various Shardbearers. In true FromSoft fashion, the official description promises that "the path ahead is perilous indeed, for the shardbearers will not relinquish their power without a fight." The manga art comes from Tegekiken, with the script credited to 21g and original story to FromSoftware via the game.

If you're wondering why there's such a price discrepancy between digital and physical versions of Elden Ring: Become Lord, Vol. 1, it's presumably due to the format. Unlike the typical black-and-white approach for most manga, Become Lord advertises itself as a "beautiful full-color retelling," inherently driving up the production cost of a physical copy, and it features a larger trim size of 7"x10" that's more comparable to trade paperbacks for western comics than to typical manga publication. It's a fairly standard length, however, with a listed count of 176 pages.

This isn't the first Elden Ring manga to be published, but it should offer a very different experience from its predecessor. Yen Press also released Elden Ring: The Road to the Erdtree, a comedic, gag-focused retelling of the game. Nine volumes of The Road to the Erdtree are currently available in English, with the tenth set to arrive on February 23, 2027, one day before Elden Ring's fifth anniversary. There's also Elden Ring: Distant Tales Between, which focuses on the side stories of various characters.

If you're curious to find out more about Elden Ring: Become Lord, the contents of the first volume have been officially available in Japanese for a while, so there are already plenty of opinions out there. If you'd rather just go in relatively blind for another Elden Ring adventure, thoguh, the remaining wait won't be too long now.

A combination of tech and practical steps can keep your property safe

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As we head into the winter (at least in the Northern hemisphere), it's getting darker, earlier. That means that by the time you get home from work, it might already be dark. Some police departments have noticed the same shift and are already planning around it. For example, as daylight saving time ended, the Palos Verdes Estates Police Department in California warned residents that an early sunset gives burglars more chances to spot homes that look unoccupied, and urged people to leave a few interior lights on or use timers, and to keep entryways lit. It's a useful starting point, and a fairly simple one.

But the risk is actually more complicated than the old image of a burglar creeping around at midnight, and so is the defense. Good locks, lighting and habits do a lot of the work, and many of those checks cost almost nothing. A camera or alarm then adds a layer on top, since it shows you what's happening and lets you act on it.

The darker months have arrived, and Arlo's Essential Outdoor Pan Tilt Zoom Security Camera's 360-degree pan and 180-degree tilt capabilities keep an eye on every corner of your property with an integrated spotlight and color night vision. Automatic motion tracking follows activity so you can stay aware of what's happening, and Smart Detection for people, vehicles, pets and packages helps you distinguish between a cat passing through your backyard and a potential security threat.

Thankfully, burglaries are on the decline. The FBI's 2024 burglary rate of 229.2 per 100,000 people was about 69% below the 2005 rate, and the FBI's 2025 data show burglary falling roughly another 16% in 2025.

But falling crime doesn't make prevention optional, because the FBI's 2024 data show that just 15.9% of property crimes were cleared by arrest or exceptional means, and burglary has run a bit lower, at 14.1% in 2019. Getting property back is, realistically, a much weaker plan than keeping someone out.

Package theft is harder to pin down. In Security.org's 2026 survey, 30% of American adults said they'd had a package stolen at some point, up from 24% a year earlier, though the survey wasn't weighted and the increase alone doesn't prove the rate has risen. It does put the exposed parts of a property, including porches, driveways, yards and garages, at the center of a winter plan, since long nights make an approach much easier.

Winter doesn't turn burglars into night owls, but it does change when your home is most exposed. In the Bureau of Justice Statistics' analysis of household burglary, which covers 2003 to 2007, 43% of burglaries of empty homes happened between 6 a.m. and 6 p.m., compared with 26% overnight. In winter, though, sunset moves into the commute window, so a house that's empty and unlit at 5:30 p.m. can look as unoccupied as one at midnight. And the evening stakes are higher, since someone was home in 61% of nighttime burglaries versus 33% of daytime ones.

A sizable share of break-ins also don't need force. The FBI's 2019 breakdown classed 37.8% of burglaries as unlawful entry with no force used. In the dark, an unlocked back door or ground-floor window is easier to try without anyone noticing, which is why the winter checklist starts with locks.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Lock everything, even when you're home, and that includes first-floor windows and any upstairs window reachable from a flat roof or ladder.

On main doors, a deadbolt offers far more resistance than a simple spring latch. Fit it with long screws that anchor the strike plate, the metal plate around the lock bolt, into the frame rather than just the decorative trim. Look for a deadbolt certified to the ANSI/BHMA A156.40 residential standard, ideally with an A grade for security. One of the best smart locks can help too — most offer an auto-lock setting (make sure it's switched on), so even if you forget to lock the door, it won't remain unlocked.

Windows need more than a handle pulled shut. Fit a working lock to every accessible window, and add stops that limit how far it can open. A wooden or metal bar in a patio door's track stops it from sliding, even when the latch is easily broken.

A peephole or door chain gives you a way to check a caller before opening up. Check ID from anyone claiming to be from a utility company, and be especially skeptical of urgent repair offers after bad weather. The FTC warns that scammers often turn up after severe weather, pushing homeowners to sign a contract right away or pay up front, and advises confirming a contractor's license and insurance before agreeing to anything.

Outside, lock the side gate, shed and garage, since long winter nights make outbuildings an easier target. Put ladders and tools away, since they can also help someone reach or force the house. Frost or obscure garage windows too, so nobody can casually browse your belongings from the street.

The boundary of the property matters too. Low front hedges preserve visibility, while gravel makes a quiet approach considerably harder. Anti-climb paint can make fences difficult to grip and marks anyone who touches it, but pair it with warning signs and follow the product's reapplication instructions closely.

Finally, photograph valuables and record serial numbers in an inventory stored somewhere secure. An ultraviolet pen can add ownership details that aren't normally visible, while a forensic marking kit links items to a unique registered code. Neither will stop a theft, but both can help police identify recovered property and make an insurance claim less painful.

One way to help prevent break-ins is to make your home look occupied even when it's not. Start outside with motion-activated lights at entrances, along driveways and on paths. For a side passage or secluded corner, a dusk-to-dawn light switches on automatically when daylight fades, while a solar model avoids running a cable. Smart bulbs and floodlights can go a step further, with schedules tied to local sunset so they shift automatically as the days get shorter, or by switching on when a camera or sensor detects motion.

Aim the light at the approach rather than into a camera lens or a neighbor's window. The goal is to expose movement and give any camera a usable image, not to turn the whole yard into a stadium.

Inside, put a few lamps on timers or smart plugs that switch on around dusk, and vary the schedule if you're away. A smart plug also lets you adjust the lights from your phone if you're delayed getting home or traveling, so the house doesn't sit dark on the one night it matters. Leaving one light on all day can have the opposite effect, because a lamp burning at midday suggests that nobody is there to turn it off.

It's also worth closing curtains or blinds in the evening so screens and valuables aren't visible, and asking a neighbor to collect mail and deliveries.

Then there's the use of other smart security devices. The best home security cameras, of course, are a major one. Place cameras around the routes someone would actually use. The front step matters, but so do the side gate and rear entrance. Good lighting on those approaches will usually do more for night footage than a bigger night-vision range claim, because you need enough detail to identify a face at the gate rather than simply spot a shape. Many smart cameras also let you draw activity zones, so you're alerted to someone at the gate but not to every passing car or neighbor, and models with a built-in spotlight or two-way audio let you light up the area or speak to a visitor from your phone.

The evidence broadly supports that layered approach. A 2019 systematic review of 40 years of research, led by Eric Piza, found that closed-circuit television systems were associated with a significant and modest decrease in crime, with better results when cameras were combined with other measures, so a camera on its own isn't really a perimeter.

Visible alarms still have real value, and in a UNC Charlotte study of 422 convicted burglars, 60% said an alarm would make them choose another target. Monitoring is the part that turns a notification into action. A monitored service watches alerts constantly and can escalate them when you don't respond.

It's also worth making sure your cameras are charged up properly. The usual advice for battery cameras is to keep a second charged pack to swap in, or add a compatible solar panel or USB-C charger where conditions allow. A solar panel won't perform miracles on a shaded wall in December, of course, so keep in mind where the sun will hit when it is out.

Apart from standard cameras, a smart video doorbell can help too. The front door, of course, is where deliveries and visitors arrive. With a smart doorbell, you can see and talk to them straight from your phone, even when you're not there.

The cheapest useful check is to simply walk around your property at dusk and look at it as a stranger would. Can someone reach the back gate unseen? Are ladders out, valuables visible through a window, or packages sitting on the step?

Start with those basics. Good locks, sensible lighting and a routine for looking occupied come first. Then add monitoring that fits your home, whether that's a visible alarm or a well-placed camera, and extend the same attention to sheds, cars and parcels.

Before you travel, test the alarm sensors, clean the cameras, charge or replace batteries in cameras and smart locks, confirm that auto-lock and your lighting schedules are working, confirm that alerts reach someone who can act on them, and check the policy's unoccupied limit.

You don't need to overhaul everything at once to improve the odds. A locked door, a lit approach and a delivery that isn't sitting outside for six hours go a long way, and a camera or alarm that alerts you when something does happen makes those habits more effective.

#3373. Everything You Should Know About Black Friday 2026 Sales: Early Deals, Dates, and Retailers

As is often the case with major sales these days, retailers are increasingly blurring the lines between early deals and the official start of a sale. Black Friday sales appear to be becoming a month-long event, with early deals appearing in the first week of the month. If you haven't been paying attention, major retailers have already put out their plans and even started churning out deals. But you're still in time to make this upcoming Black Friday sale a great one. Here is everything you need to know to prepare you for the big sale.

Black Friday is always the day after Thanksgiving. This year, Black Friday starts at midnight on Nov. 27. Cyber Monday is the Monday following Black Friday, which starts at midnight on Nov. 30.

The major retailers doing sales are the usual: Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Home Depot, and many others. Currently, Walmart has publicized its plans already and has early deals available. Best Buy is offering one of the largest Black Friday and Cyber Week sales, with multiple events and early deals. Target has a three-day event. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

Unlike Spring or Summer sales, Black Friday doesn't focus on specific categories, which means everything is fair game for discounts. In previous years, we've seen tech, tools, fitness equipment, outdoor supplies and furniture, bedding, video games, kitchen appliances, and more. This is one of the best times to make a list of what you need. You're likely to find what you're looking for discounted, and probably at its lowest price it has ever been. If you'd like to avoid having to do all that work, we always vet all of our deals for you. Just follow our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Prime Day and Black Friday are the two best times of the year to get the best deals on most purchases. Of course, depending on what you're shopping for, you might find other opportunities throughout the year, but in general, Prime Day and Black Friday have the best sales.

#3371. Netflix’s ‘Black Doves’ Has the Perfect Solution for James Bond’s Biggest Problem

There are more than a few shows about espionage and spycraft on television right now, and the genre is about to get a major shot of adrenaline on the big screen with the confirmation that Robert Pattinson has been cast as the newest James Bond. Black Doves stands out among other secret agent shows because it portrays more of the characters than just their relationship to government conspiracies and world-ending threats. Being an assassin is a dangerous line of work, but it's also a profession both Helen (Keira Knightley) and Sam (Ben Whishaw) have fallen into and now have no way to escape. Although there are certainly threats that could potentially thrust all of Great Britain — and potentially the entire world — into chaos, the emphasis on grounded characterization is what makes Black Doves such an exhilarating series.

The titular “Black Doves” is an organization of high-ranking assassins who perform covert missions with global implications, and one that Helen is still working for while her husband, Wallace Webb (Andrew Buchan), becomes the Secretary of State for Defense. While Helen struggles to be more open with her loved ones, Sam has the opposite problem; he has never been able to find someone he can have a permanent relationship with, and often chooses isolation to avoid being further devastated. Black Doves shows how spies’ advanced training and perceptiveness come at the cost of other aspects of life, making “normalcy” a foreign concept. It’s among the most action-packed and twisty shows on television right now, but the solid writing provides just as much reason to care for the characters on screen.

Helen is an atypical protagonist for an action show because Black Doves highlights a mother in the middle of a struggling marriage that does not provide an easy solution to her problems. Although she was initially assigned to seduce Wallace and gain information through him for the Black Doves, she develops a genuine attraction to him that ultimately turns into love. The guardedness that Helen shows, leading to her affair with Jason (Andrew Koji) in Season 1, isn't a sign that she is unhappy with Wallace, but that she can't fully open up to someone she can't be honest with. This makes for a fascinating character arc, as Helen is clearly an expert in her field but is made to feel guilty about what she is best at.

Espionage meets the unground world of crime.

Whishaw gives Sam a gritty, worn-down persona that reflects his efforts to bury his emotions and avoid any commitment. Although, in theory, not being tied down to a single person would make Sam less vulnerable to threats, Whishaw is able to show the draining impact this has as his character is forced to give up time with those who might make him happy; Season 2 even introduces a heartbreaking twist when Sam’s duties get in the way of his burgeoning romance with Jerry (Samuel Barnett). This leads to one of the show's most powerful moments, where Sam admits his vulnerabilities to Helen, revealing the strong connection between them, forged by the shared secrets they are forced to keep.

Black Doves goes beyond the clichés of a typical spy story because it provides context and depth to one of its most mysterious characters. Season 1 introduces Elizabeth Reed (Sarah Lancashire) as the most ruthless, brilliant mastermind in the Black Doves organization who serves as a handler for Helen, positioning her in a way similar to Bond's MI6 chief M. Season 2 complicates the character by examining her backstory through an undercover operation in East Berlin that went south. It’s a reminder that there are no clean getaways for those involved in espionage who think they can make a clean break, and the complex dynamic that emerges between Reed and her daughter Vita (Bailey Fines) in the aftermath explores the generational cost of giving up one’s life to duty. Black Doves is able to expose the faults in even its heroic characters; all of them have committed terrible acts in their line of work, and it is up to the audience to determine whether the ends justify the means.

Although its trio of stars makes Black Doves one of the best-acted shows on the air, the ensemble cast is full of great performances that offer more depth to the characters. Season 2 develops an earnest and emotional bond between the assassins Williams (Ella Lily Hyland) and Eleanor (Gabrielle Creevy); while they easily could have been used for little more than comic relief, Black Doves makes a thoughtful point about generations' different priorities by showing how sharply this pair contrasts with Helen and Sam. Just because someone possesses incredible skills doesn’t mean that they aren't also human. Not only is the ability to graft emotional honesty within a series that is so frequently absurd (in the best way) one of Black Doves' biggest achievements, but it's also a storytelling strength that the upcoming James Bond reboot should take a page from.

#3370. Why Websites Show the Wrong Server Location When You Use a VPN

There are many reasons why someone might use a VPN, but most often, it’s to conceal your real geographic location or prevent websites from tracking your online activity. It can also be a way to get around location-based restrictions that stop you from accessing certain websites or platforms.

When you connect to a VPN server in the United States, websites are supposed to detect that your online traffic is originating from the U.S. That way, you can access online platforms that use IP filters to block non-U.S. traffic or circumvent regional censorship when travelling outside the U.S. But if you connect to a VPN server in the United States while you’re vacationing in Mexico, and a website thinks your IP address is from Brazil, that might not solve your problem and may even add unnecessary complications.

If you’ve encountered something similar with your VPN provider, there are several fixes you can try. Depending on why your IP location is being misinterpreted, one of these should help you access the internet from the server location of your choice.

IP geolocation isn’t infallible. Websites rely on third-party IP databases to look up your location based on your current IP address. Maxmind, which has one of the largest such databases in existence, claims that its GeoIP products have a 99.8% accuracy. Lesser-known providers with smaller IP databases may be far less accurate.

Websites can also use more than just your IP address to estimate your location. For example, they can send WebRTC requests to your browser or directly query your device’s GPS. Moreover, VPN providers often have physical servers in one country while their IP addresses are registered to another country, and this discrepancy can also create issues. Let’s take a closer look at each of these problems individually, so you can find the fix that works best for you.

WebRTC is an open-source technology that lets your browser reduce latency when engaged in high-bandwidth tasks like streaming or video calls. Based on the IETF standard RFC 8828, it lets a website choose between your VPN server and your real IP address so it can establish the quickest path to transmit large amounts of data and reduce wait times or buffering.

But the catch with WebRTC is that it exposes both your VPN server and ISP-assigned addresses to websites, which can reveal your real IP location and cause websites to reject your VPN server country. Firefox now comes with built-in protections to prevent WebRTC leaks, while Chrome and Edge support third-party extensions like WebRTC Control that you can use to eliminate these issues. To check if your browser is leaking your real IP address during WebRTC requests, you can use a free tool like BrowserLeaks.

Even when a browser isn’t leaking your real IP address, DNS resolvers may fetch inaccurate location information if their nearest servers are too far from your current location. For example, a user in São Paulo may be geolocated to Chile when using Google Public DNS because that’s where Google’s nearest resolvers are located.

If you toggle on DNS leak protection in your VPN app, this will force websites to use your VPN’s resolver to perform DNS lookups. That often solves the problem, but, again, you can confirm the fix worked through a service like BrowserLeaks or IPLeaks.

Websites rely on IP databases like Maxmind, IP2Location, IPinfo, etc. to look up your exact location, but these databases get outdated quickly and need constant updating. Most of these databases also correct errors on request, but that takes some time. Also, each website has its own rules for how often it queries IP databases for updates.

Even when locations are updated in the actual database, a website may be sitting with outdated information unless it actively has refreshed it recently. MaxMind recommends doing this at least twice a week, but that’s ultimately up to the specific website.

VPN providers often rely on virtual servers that use IP addresses registered in a different region than the server’s physical location. For example, ExpressVPN notes that it serves IP addresses in Bolivia, Ecuador, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela through servers located physically in Brazil.

While this is usually to help with the lack of local infrastructure or strict surveillance laws in the region, many databases and analytics tools will flag the discrepancy for websites, leading to confusion and inconsistency regarding your actual server location. In these cases, your best bet is to switch your VPN server or use a dedicated IP address by signing up for a paid add-on for your VPN.

Before investing in a specific solution, it’s better to do a thorough lookup to make sure why your IP address is pointing to the wrong location and whether a WebRTC or DNS issue, virtual servers, or something else is the cause. Here’s how I’d go about it, step by step:

We’ll start by recording your baseline IP address, country, city, and ASN. With your VPN disconnected, navigate to IPConfig.co on your browser to grab your default IP details. I like this tool because it’s free and uses echoip to pull your location data straight from Maxmind. If you prefer using Terminal instead of your browser, you can also run curl ifconfig.co/json to grab these details in plain text format.

Now connect your VPN server. Then visit IPConfig.co again to note down the changed details.

Make sure the Country and Timezone fields match your current VPN server location. Also make sure the ASN (organization) field does not list your home ISP.

In case these details do not match your VPN server, run a WebRTC leak test and a DNS leak test using BrowserLeaks. If either of these tests doesn’t return your VPN server’s IP address, you’ve found your culprit.

If both the leak tests come back clean but a specific site still gets your location wrong, the issue is likely originating from an outdated database or virtual server.

There’s no surefire way to solve IP location mismatches for good. But if it happens often enough to disrupt your internet use, you can consider switching to a different VPN server and getting a browser add-on that prevents WebRTC leaks. If that doesn’t work, I’d consider buying a dedicated IP address that isn’t based on a virtual server. While many IP databases like MaxMind or IP2Location also have ways to request a location correction, that takes a while to go through and isn’t worth the effort unless it’s a permanent IP address registered through your ISP.

#3369. Hackers Now Want Your Browser Sessions More Than Your Passwords, but You Can Stop Them

There’s a very organized dark web supply chain that attackers use to trade in stealer logs. Russian Market has effectively replaced Genesis Market as the new storefront for black hat cybercriminals, although much of the market has also shifted to private channels on Telegram.

According to threat analysts at DarkOwl, approximately 180,000 stealer logs were sold on Russian Market in just the first half of 2025. What's more, Russian Market is a well-designed storefront that users can access even without Onion links or the Tor browser. That means anyone could go there and buy a bunch of stealer logs to start attempting account takeovers at scale.

Meanwhile, Flare Research estimates that this isn’t even close to the actual scale of the threat, because 90% of stealer logs now surface privately on Telegram. There, automated chatbots let scammers shop for stealer logs like it’s Amazon, with options to filter by country, app, and account privilege. Logs sell for anywhere between $5 and $500 a piece, depending on the estimated value of the target accounts.

The easiest way to go about this is to take a look through all your active devices and their locations in your account settings on most websites. If you see a device or location you don’t recognize, you are likely the subject of an ongoing breach. However, keep in mind that this may not always be a reliable method if you use iCloud Private Relay or a VPN. Still, it's generally best practice to log out of all active sessions every once in a while and perform a fresh login to invalidate any unauthorized sessions.

Reset the passwords on your email account, enable two-factor authentication for added protection, and sign out of all sessions before doing a fresh login. Your email inbox is the single point of entry for most attacks because that’s where most websites send their verification codes or magic links.

Sign out of all active sessions on every account that you suspect is compromised. This will log out any attackers who are currently on a hijacked browsing session.

Change your passwords on every platform in order of priority. Start with banking websites, cloud storage providers, and password managers first.

Look through each compromised account’s third-party integrations and app permissions. Revoke access if you can’t recognize an app, or it looks suspicious. Also make sure to rotate any API keys that you’re currently using, since those may have been compromised as well.

But while the initiative has already been open-sourced, no other major online provider has begun offering native support for it as of this article. That means DBSC’s security benefits are limited to Google services like Gmail and Docs, Chrome for Windows, and third-party websites that offer single sign-on (SSO) options for your Google account. We might see a wider rollout in the near future, though.

#3368. 4 Years After The Series' End, Disney's Amphibia Returns With Strange Voyage

Disney’s Amphibia is returning more than four years after its animated finale, although not with a new season. Creator Matt Braly is bringing the story back through Amphibia: Strange Voyage, a serialized comic published by TOKYOPOP and Disney Manga. Its first installment is scheduled to reach comic shops on January 13, 2027.

The announcement gives fans a reason to revisit Wartwood and the Plantars, while also setting up an adventure that moves beyond the television series’ final battle. Amphibia ran for three seasons on Disney Channel and ended on May 14, 2022, with “The Hardest Thing.” Strange Voyage picks up after that conclusion rather than retelling Anne Boonchuy’s original arrival.

The opening premise begins months after Anne saves Amphibia from the Core and returns to Earth. With that crisis behind them, the Plantars embark on a voyage to find a new continent. Their expedition does not go according to plan: a dangerous turn leaves the crew stranded on an unfamiliar island, where unexpected secrets await.

That setup gives the comic room to explore a part of Amphibia that the television series did not have time to map out. The animated show balanced its fantasy setting with comedy, friendship, and a coming-of-age story, but Strange Voyage introduces new territory and a fresh mystery. The island may prove as important as the destination.

Matt Braly is writing the new series, keeping its storytelling in the hands of the person who created Amphibia and guided its three-season run. Beatrice Bovo is providing the artwork, including the cover designs. Their collaboration gives the project a direct creative link to the original series while allowing a different artist to interpret its familiar characters.

Fans should not expect a handful of disconnected comic strips. Braly has described Strange Voyage as one continuous narrative planned across ten issues, with a new installment arriving every three weeks. He has also characterized it as an important canon miniseries, showing that the journey is intended to matter to the larger Amphibia story.

That distinction is worth paying attention to, especially for viewers who want the comic to build on the series rather than simply recreate its episodic humor. A serialized format gives the writers space to develop the island’s mysteries, the Plantars’ expedition and the consequences of the choices made along the way. The first three issues establish the opening stretch.

The release schedule starts with Amphibia: Strange Voyage #1 on January 13, 2027. Issue #2 is scheduled for February 3, followed by Issue #3 on February 24. Each issue is listed at $4.99, and the first three installments are 32 pages apiece, giving readers a regular way to follow the story.

Readers who would rather sample the comic series for free will have another opportunity in the spring. Amphibia: Strange Voyage – Issue #1 is among the titles announced for Comics Giveaway Day 2027, Penguin Random House’s branding for the 2027 Free Comic Book Day event. Participating comic shops are scheduled to hand out the giveaway books on Saturday, May 1.

There is an important distinction between that promotion and the regular release schedule: the listed giveaway is Issue #1, not a free collection of the first three installments. The January and February issues are separate $4.99 releases, so readers who want to keep up with the story before May will need to pick them up individually.

Atlantis: The Lost Empire is the most underrated movie in all of Disney, but 25 years later, it's finally getting the epic sequel it deserves.

Comics Giveaway Day could also introduce the series to readers who missed Amphibia during its Disney Channel run. The 2027 lineup includes books from several publishers, making the event a broad entry point for comic newcomers. For returning viewers, the bigger attraction is Braly’s continuation of the Plantars’ story in a planned canon adventure.

Matthew Lillard, who has now worked on more than a few Stephen King adaptations, has spent enough time in haunted houses to know how badly this can go. Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

The fun of casting Lillard in Anything But Ghosts is how much of his career already points to how perfect he is for a scenario like the one Barker and Tomlinson have cooked up. He spent two Scooby-Doo movies as the guy who wanted out of the haunted house before anybody had finished explaining why they were there. In Scream, he got one of the movie’s biggest laughs out of Stu realizing he might actually bleed to death. That timing could do a lot for a comedy about two frauds who have to keep up the act once the ghosts show up. Lillard’s more recent work in Mike Flanagan's Carrie and Daredevil: Born Again shows how much darker he can go, and his William Afton in Five Nights at Freddy’s is a reminder that the same guy who’s great at panicking can be just as good at giving everybody else a reason to panic.

Anything But Ghosts premieres in theaters May 7, 2027.
