#3363. Aura's Second E-Ink Picture Frame Is Much Improved, and Much Cheaper

Last year, Aura released the Aura Ink, its first digital photo frame using an e-ink display rather than the LCD screens common to the other devices that made them the major player in the market (Aura customers have already uploaded more than one billion photos this year alone). When I reviewed the original 13-inch Aura Ink last year, I recommended it, with a few major reservations. Today, Aura announced its second-generation 10-inch Ink frame, and while I wouldn't exactly say they've solved every one of my issues, the new device is significantly improved—and much cheaper.

Most digital photo frames will remind you of an iPad with a decorative border around it. They're great for displaying hundreds of your photos with vibrant color, but not everyone loves the look, or the fact that these frames always need to be plugged in. An e-ink frame, on the other hand, uses a variant of the sort of low-power screen you'd find in a Kindle Colorsoft—less bright, but more paperlike, and much closer to the look of a traditionally printed photo.The Aura Ink is a great choice if you want a digital frame that looks more like a "real" photo and doesn't need to be plugged in and doesn't light up like a tablet (though it does have a light, it's really to make up for the fact that color e-ink screens don't reflect light very well, and thus can make your pictures look way too dark without an additional boost). You'll still get all the benefits of an LCD frame like the Aura Aspen, including the ability to load photos from anywhere using the versatile Aura app (you can now even text them directly to the frame), but you'll only need to charge it once every few months.

Now for the downsides: Where most digital frames allow you to flick between photos with a swipe, the Aura Ink is much more sluggish—switching from one photo to another takes about 45 seconds. While an LCD can match the colors in your photo exactly, e-ink uses a "dithering algorithm" to blend tiny pixels together to create the illusion of different hues ("millions" of them, according to Aura). In practice, this means up close, your pictures will look rather grainy, and the colors won't be nearly as bright as what you see on your phone screen.

All of that said, the Aura Ink is a great product, provided you know what you're buying, and the new 10-inch model offers some big upgrades over the 13-inch original released in 2025:

Resolution has been bumped up from 150 ppi to 200 ppi, so your images look more detailed and less grainy. (Though the difference is hard to capture in a photo, I can definitely see the improvement when comparing them side-by-side.)

Instead of the six base colors available on the older frame, the 10-inch Aura Ink blends nine different hues to approximate the colors in your images, offering greater color accuracy and improved contrast.

The transition effect when you move between photos has been updated to look more intentional—like waves of color moving across the screen versus a series of increasingly intense flashes.

It's a heck of a lot cheaper: $349, versus $499 for the 13-inch model—though that's still significantly pricier than Aura's most popular offering, the 10.1-inch Aura Carver, which starts around $200 less.

I write a lot about e-ink devices, from e-readers to tablets, and my common refrain, especially with color devices, is that they're great at what they do, but you should understand what they do before you plunk down your money. The Aura Ink will never look as bright and colorful as an LCD frame, and if you want a frame that can switch between images every few minutes or even play video, you'll need to look elsewhere (to maximize battery life, Aura recommends swapping photos on the Aura Ink no more than 12 times per day).

But if you want to display photos that look more like the ones that hung on the walls of your childhood home, in a frame that doesn't need to be plugged in all the time, you'll probably dig it, provided you can stomach the $350 price tag.

#3361. Jeff Bezos' Role In Robert Pattinson James Bond Casting Revealed

Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos reveals what role he had in casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond.

After acquiring half of the franchise and its distribution rights when it bought MGM, Amazon coaxed complete creative control of the James Bond franchise from longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. For the next film, Amazon hired Denis Villeneuve as director, with Stephen Knight writing the script, and after a long and exhaustive search, Robert Pattinson beat out several other candidates as James Bond.

Now, at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World conference (via The Hollywood Reporter), Jeff Bezos says he was "heavily involved" in casting Pattinson as Bond, collaborating with Amazon MGM executives, producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman, and Villeneuve:

We ran a really tight process, and we made the final decision on Friday. There were a big group initially, and we selected down to five finalists, and then we did real old-fashioned screen tests of those five finalists.

The shortlist is no secret at this point – Callum Turner, Josh O'Connor, Jack Lowden, Nicholas Hoult and, ultimately, Pattinson, who landed the coveted role. Bezos says the team conducted extensive screen tests, having each actor perform three scenes in full costume on constructed sets. They initially had reservations about Pattinson before coming around to the idea that he was the right fit:

They were all amazing, but there was something special about Rob and his performances, and it was kind of immediately un-debated. Denis, the director was, we all sort of gravitated to him. By the way, initially, I would say we were slightly biased a little against him just because he’s already so famous. We sort of thought, maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown. But in the screening tests, it was so obvious: He is James Bond.

Robert Pattinson's casting marks Amazon's most significant move yet since its acquisition of MGM and its subsequent buyout of the Broccoli family's stake, giving the company control of the franchise.

There's a certain irony in the shift, given that the James Bond movies have long featured tech billionaires and media moguls as villains, from Hugo Drax (Michael Lonsdale) in Moonraker (1979), Max Zorin (Christopher Walken) in A View to a Kill (1985), and Elliot Carver (Jonathan Pryce) in Tomorrow Never Dies (1997).

Now, the James Bond franchise is in the hands of one of the world's wealthiest men – whose business empire stretches across technology, media, entertainment, and even space exploration. And this time, the mogul is on the other side of the table, helping make the decisions.

Since Bezos was "heavily involved" in selecting the new 007, it stands to reason he will continue to be involved in casting the next Bond villain, too. In turn, it's unlikely the next Bond film will continue the tradition of tech billionaires as villains, since the Amazon CEO likely won't want to risk lampooning or villainizing himself. For now, it looks like the biggest Bond villain might be Bezos himself.

There are a few things you can do to make sure your packages don’t get stolen

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Porch piracy is still a major problem. 30% of American adults have had a package stolen at some point in their lives, and 49% worry more about package theft during the holidays than at other times of year, according to Security.org’s 2026 Package Theft Report. The report estimates that 47.7 million people had a package stolen in the past year, and that the stolen packages were worth $7.7 billion. And with the average adult expecting 28 deliveries between October and December, there’s simply plenty more opportunity for boxes to sit unattended.

Of course, there are things you can and should do to keep your packages safe. The best protections stop a theft before the package lands, either by arranging a verified hand-off, shortening the time a box spends outside, or sending it somewhere secure. Here are some practical ways to protect your packages from porch pirates this holiday season.

If you're looking for a deal on a video doorbell this Black Friday, the crystal-clear 2K video on Arlo's option helps you keep an eye out for holiday deliveries and feel connected to your home, even when you're away. Arlo Chime 2 offers convenient in-home audio notifications, while the Arlo Secure App provides real-time, personalized notifications and the ability to see and talk with visitors on your doorstep.

The strongest option for an expensive order is probably to require a verified hand-off. UPS Protected Delivery, which launches Nov. 16, requires the recipient to give the driver a PIN, or numeric code, before an eligible package is released. FedEx Authenticated Delivery uses a unique QR code instead. Both of these services are a little limited in how and where you can use them, and they may cost more too. The shipper, not the recipient, has to select either one, so ask the retailer before you order.

For everything else, the carrier’s tracking app is the first line of defense. Turn on notifications from Amazon, UPS, FedEx and USPS, and act on the “out for delivery” message rather than waiting for “delivered.”

Security.org identifies delivery alerts as a popular prevention method, with 39% of shoppers using delivery notifications or tracking apps. An alert alone won’t protect a box, but it at least gives you a notification you can act on relatively quickly.

“The goal shouldn’t be watching your front door all day,” says Ken Sedberry, director of Xfinity Shield. “It should be knowing when a package arrives and having a plan to bring it inside.”

Amazon’s scheduling tools can shorten that exposure further. Map Tracking shows the driver’s live position on eligible deliveries, while estimated two- to four-hour delivery windows give you something more useful than an all-day estimate. Prime members can also use Amazon Day to batch orders onto one day each week when someone is home. Security.org found that 43% of shoppers schedule deliveries for when someone will be there.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Photo on Delivery adds a record of where the driver left the package, which is especially helpful if it ended up behind a planter or at a side entrance. It doesn’t prove the package stayed there, though.

For valuable shipments, a traditional signature requirement is still worth requesting if the newer verification services aren’t available. The sender usually has to add it, and fees vary by carrier and service.

The best way to secure where packages are left is to not leave them there in the first place. That may sound silly, but there are actually a few different ways you can prevent packages from being left alone on your doorstep. Amazon Locker and Counter are free alternatives, and they’re part of a network of more than 25,000 pickup locations across the country.

“For those receiving a high volume of deliveries, especially during the holidays, giving carriers a secure place to leave packages is much more effective than simply hoping a camera discourages someone from taking them,” says Rod Sides, founder of Loxx Boxx, which makes package lockboxes.

Lockers give you three calendar days to collect a package, and size or item restrictions mean not every order qualifies. Staffed Counters at retailers offer another option if you’d rather collect from a person.

Carriers like UPS and FedEx have their own pickup locations too. UPS Access Point locations hold packages for up to seven days at no charge, although redirecting an in-flight package costs $5.99 for free Basic My Choice members. Premium, at $19.99 a year, includes it. FedEx Hold at Location keeps packages for up to seven days at FedEx Office and FedEx facilities, but FedEx says to pick up within five business days at participating retailers such as Walgreens and Dollar General. Redirecting to a retail location is free.

USPS offers free Hold for Pickup through Delivery Instructions, along with free Hold Mail for three to 30 days when you’re away. Its Smart Lockers in Post Office lobbies provide another free option with a five-day collection window. Hold windows and redirect fees change periodically, so confirm them in the carrier’s app before rerouting a valuable order.

Home parcel boxes are more convenient, but they depend on driver cooperation. Some allow you to lock packages behind a four-digit PIN — but a driver rushing through deliveries in a busy season may not take the time to do that, or may not see the request in the first place.

If you do go the route of using a drop box, it's worth anchoring it properly. An empty, lightweight lockbox can be carried away and opened elsewhere, so bolt it down or weight it properly. Then make it as hidden from the street as you can. Delivery instructions should name an exact hiding place rather than simply saying “front door.” Something like “inside the parcel box behind the side gate” gives the driver a workable instruction. It still isn’t a guarantee, and some carrier menus offer limited space for custom directions.

Some of the best home security cameras and video doorbells can help deter porch pirates as well. A battery-powered video doorbell is a pretty reasonable entry-level option. Look for higher-resolution 2K video, a wide-angle view, person and package alerts, and a choice of battery or wired power.

Prices tend to drop during holiday sales, but keep in mind that the hardware price is only part of the cost. Cloud recording, which saves clips to the manufacturer’s servers rather than in your home, typically requires a subscription.

Person and package detection makes these devices much easier to live with. AI, in this context, mostly means pattern-recognition software that distinguishes people and packages from other movement. It reduces alerts caused by passing cars, animals or swaying branches. It can make a pretty big difference.

“Delivery drivers often drop a package without ringing the bell, but a motion alert lets you know the moment someone is at your door, often before the carrier’s delivery email arrives, so you don’t have to keep watching the front door,” says Veronica Moturi, senior vice president and chief customer officer at Brinks Home.

It's worth keeping in mind the fact that cameras don't always deter theft and often document it more than prevent it. Pairing one with motion-activated lighting and a camera monitoring sign can help with the deterrence, though.

Lighting deserves special attention during the winter, when many deliveries arrive after dark. A lit entrance helps drivers find the right drop spot and removes some of the cover a thief would prefer.

“Look for a camera with clear night vision, since shorter days mean more deliveries and holiday visits happen after dark,” says Moturi.

Apartment residents have a lot more reason to plan ahead. Security.org found that 10% of apartment dwellers had a package stolen in the previous three months, compared with 3% of single-family home residents. That’s more than three times as likely. Shared lobbies, dense delivery traffic and long periods with nobody watching the entrance all create opportunities.

If your apartment building offers some kind of locked package room or front desk, it may be worth having packages left there rather than in front of your door. If you don't, there's no harm in requesting one from building management — and if there have been thefts, a request from multiple tenants could carry more weight.

Renting also makes it harder to mount security cameras and smart doorbells. Thankfully, there are plenty of battery-operated ones that don't require drilling or changing wiring, so if you are renting and want something like that, they are available.

If you do fall victim to a porch pirate, there are a few things to do. Start by verifying that the package is actually missing. Check the tracking status and delivery photo, then ask household members, neighbors or the doorman whether they collected it. Look around side entrances and other plausible drop spots. Sometimes, you might find that it wasn't stolen at all.

If you still can't find it, it's worth contacting the retailer promptly with the order number, tracking details, delivery date and any photos or footage you have. That’s usually the fastest route to a replacement before a holiday.

Amazon often asks customers to wait about 48 hours after a package is marked delivered and to file a missing-package claim within 30 days of the delivery date, but policies differ for third-party sellers and other retailers. Refunds and replacements are common, not guaranteed.

File a police report even if the retailer refunds you or sends a replacement. Only 23% of recent victims in Security.org’s survey reported their most recent theft to police. Those reports really help departments identify repeat locations, spot organized activity and decide where to assign patrols.

Purchase protection through a card such as American Express may cover eligible items for 90 days after purchase, and Amex asks for notice of a claim within 30 days of the loss or as soon as reasonably possible. Terms vary, so you’ll want to check your benefits before relying on them.

Gene Petrino, a former SWAT commander and police sergeant, offers the simplest summary of the whole problem. “Thieves can’t steal what they can’t see.”

Concealment matters, but removing the package from public view altogether is better. No single gadget covers every delivery, and paid verification won’t be available for every order. The best plan to protect your packages is to combine methods. Do what you can to prevent them from being left alone in the first place, use carrier alerts to get your packages to safety quickly, and use security cameras as a deterrent or to monitor anything that does get stolen.

Christian de Looper is a freelance writer who has covered every facet of consumer tech, including mobile, audio, home theater, computing, gaming, and even car tech. #3359. Kim Zolciak's Son KJ Biermann Faced 16 Alleged Sex Offenses in Prior Case

Kim Zolciak's son KJ Biermann's previous run-in with the law was far more serious than previously known ... with prosecutors now detailing 16 alleged sexual offenses stemming from an incest allegation.

According to Page Six, prosecutors laid out the allegations in new court documents filed Monday ... listing one count of incest, eight counts of child molestation, one count of sexual battery, one count of statutory rape and five counts of sexual exploitation of children.

The filing says probable cause was found for the alleged offenses ... though that doesn't mean KJ was convicted of all 16 charges.

Prosecutors revealed the details while fighting to keep the 15-year-old's current sexual assault case in adult court ... arguing he already had a chance at rehabilitation through the juvenile justice system.

KJ is currently facing seven felony charges stemming from an alleged April sexual assault involving a female classmate inside a Georgia gym's changing room. He has pleaded not guilty.

As we reported, KJ was released from jail on $200,000 bond and is living under his mother's care ... with restrictions preventing him from contacting anyone under 16, including his younger siblings.

#3357. HBO's 5-Part Haunting Historical Miniseries Is a True Streaming Masterpiece

There are few miniseries that can actually be considered masterpieces. Some shows are popular at the time they air, but don't hold up once a few years have passed. Of course, there are some limited series that manage to be extraordinary whenever they're viewed. Adolescence, Band of Brothers, Angels in America, and the classic Roots are still every bit as powerful as when they aired. There's one other HBO miniseries that is truly brilliant and can definitely be considered one of the best among these fantastic shows.

Chernobyl is a five-episode limited series that aired in 2019. It is a dramatized version of one of the most significant historical events in recent memory. In 1986, a disaster occurred at the Chernobyl nuclear plant in the town of Pripyat in the Soviet Union, which is now considered Ukraine. In a chilling, heart-racing narrative, the series depicts the events that led up to the meltdown, as well as the harrowing aftermath. Two engineers were killed in the initial explosion, and many others were badly burned. But it became apparent that the dangers Chernobyl exposed were actually much more far-reaching. Many of the plant workers and emergency response team began dying of acute radiation syndrome. Their deaths are portrayed in several excruciating scenes in the series.

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

The most devastating aspect is that the disaster continued to cause deaths even years later, with one study estimating that a total of nearly 4,000 deaths can now be linked to the meltdown (many from cancer-related illnesses). Chernobyl depicts not only the immediate fallout from the explosion, but also the major cover-up that took place following the event. A brave scientist named Valery Legasov (Jared Harris) tries to share his knowledge of the true breadth of the disaster with the Kremlin, but he is silenced. Because of this denial of the facts, the Soviet Union's choices led to many more deaths. The actual environmental effects from the Chernobyl disaster are still being felt even 40 years later.

Chernobyl, created by Craig Mazin (The Last of Us), is a completely compelling piece of art because it feels easy to get sucked into the haunting storytelling. Every emotion, whether it's bloodcurdling terror or heartbreaking grief, is conveyed effortlessly through the writing, so that you'll feel as though you're a part of the action yourself. Mazin ensures that every decision made by the characters (and their real-life counterparts in turn), whether heroic or calculated, creates a world in which things can never go back to the way they were. The heart-wrenching realism of the narrative makes some of the scenes difficult to watch, especially in their graphic gruesomeness, but this only adds to the authentic nature of the series.

Chernobyl thrives because Mazin is able to showcase so many different perspectives within the framework. One of the most captivating POVs is that of Lyudmilla (Jessie Buckley), the loving wife of one of the brave firefighters who is called to the scene. The range of emotions she experiences during her journey are masterfully displayed, and Buckley ensures that we see the tragic, complex nature of her story. Stellan Skarsgård is fascinating as Boris Scherbina, a chairman of the Kremlin, and Harris is equally transfixing as Valery. Emily Watson portrays Ulana Khomyuk, one of the few characters in the series who is actually fictional. Her fierce devotion to the truth makes her an essential part of the narrative. Harris, Skarsgård, and Watson all received Emmy nominations for their incredible work here, and it's no surprise that viewers were deeply affected by their performances.

History's most exceptional television miniseries.

Chernobyl received plenty of acclaim from critics when it premiered, and managed to take home 10 Emmy wins, including Outstanding Limited Series, and a total of 19 nominations. The series consistently lands on lists of the best miniseries ever made, and upon viewing, it's easy to see why. The realistic depiction of such a world-changing event is handled with historical accuracy and attention to detail, but the humans who were deeply affected by the events that day remain the heart of the storytelling. Whether you're watching Chernobyl for the first time, or are planning a re-watch, you'll have to agree that it has certainly earned its title of masterpiece.

Chernobyl is available to stream on HBO Max in the U.S.

#3355. 'GTA 6' Runs Best on This Console

Grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time. It's been 13 years since Rockstar dropped GTA 5, and after years of rumors, leaks, and official announcements, the sixth mainstream installment in the series is nearly here. In fact, anyone who pre-ordered the game digitally can now pre-load it onto their console, if you want to ensure you're ready to play the second the game comes out.

Now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox. (The PC version of the game isn't expected until at least early 2027.) But, as it turns out, there's one specific console that can run GTA 6 better than the rest.

Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game. But, interestingly, it spurred a discussion about the performance of the game itself, as well as which consoles are best to run it.

No matter which console you play GTA 6 on, Rockstar says that the game will only target 30 fps (frames per second). That's decided slow for a mainstream game in 2026. GTA 5 also shipped at 30 fps in 2013, but newer consoles can run it at higher frame rates. In fact, most games that launch on the latest generation of consoles can run at 60 fps, if not higher. While it's certainly not a dealbreaker, it is interesting that Rockstar's latest game can't run at a faster frame rate even on the PS5 Pro or the Xbox Series X.

To that point, Rockstar called out the PS5 Pro specifically in its post, announcing, "The PlayStation 5 Pro offers breathtaking visuals, with improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro."

PSSR is Sony's AI upscaler, similar to options like DLSS from Nvidia, which uses AI to add extra graphical information to games in real time. That allows developers like Rockstar to run the game at a lower resolution to save on processing power, but still boost the visuals to reach a higher perceived resolution. As such, it's not as ideal as running the game at a higher resolution natively, but it can help improve the visuals without pushing the hardware beyond its limits. Meanwhile, ray-tracing offers realistic lighting effects and can also be graphically intense.

While PlayStation and Xbox players alike will be stuck at 30 fps, it seems only PS5 Pro gamers will be able to play the game with ray-tracing effects and AI upscaling. It's surprising that Xbox Series X players don't have similar benefits, as the hardware is more powerful than Xbox Series S. Rockstar didn't specify why only the PS5 Pro gets these upgrades.

In the post, Rockstar also announced that the PS5 version of GTA 6 takes advantage of other PlayStation-exclusive perks, like high-fidelity haptic feedback in the DualSense controller, spatial audio rendering using the PlayStation's Tempest 3D audio, as well as improved load times—though Rockstar didn't specify what those load times would be. These perks apply to all PS5 consoles, not just PS5 Pros. Rockstar goes so far as to say that GTA 6 plays best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

That's not to say that Microsoft's consoles are totally left out of the perks. Rockstar says that GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both Xbox Series X and S, as well as Xbox One. In addition, both PlayStation and Xbox gamers can play GTA 6 using Remote Play, so no one has to physically play on their console if they want to game on the go.

Again, there's no reason to go out and buy a specific console for GTA 6, so long as you have something that can run the game. After all, PS5 Pros are difficult to find, especially without wildly overpaying. But it's interesting that Rockstar has managed to give Sony's consoles the extra perks here, particularly since the company hasn't explained why that is.

#3352. Lifehacker's Pick for the Best TV to Gift in 2026 Isn't Actually a TV

Welcome to Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, a collaborative multimedia project in which Lifehacker, CNET, ZDNET, and Mashable harness the power of our product testing laboratory and our editors' expertise to offer the best gift-buying recommendations possible. In this episode, we're talking televisions.

I recently did a deep dive into TV development history, checked out what was on shelves for 2026, and I concluded that the best gift TV you can give this year is, actually, a pair of sunglasses. The XBX by XReal video display glasses are basically a TV you can shove in your pocket. Check them out:

I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? More importantly, there's the nature of television itself. Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

Then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a big screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.

While the first HomeView units won’t reach customers until tomorrow, Apple today released a software update addressing nine security vulnerabilities. Here are the details.

Apple today released HomeView Software Version 27.2 (build 24V526), which contains some of the security fixes the company included in recent updates to its other operating systems, including iOS 27.2, macOS 27.2 Golden Gate, and iPadOS 27.2.

These include a vulnerability that could allow a remote attacker to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages, as well as another that could allow a malicious Bluetooth device to pair without user interaction.

In practice, this means that users who get the device starting tomorrow are advised to update it as soon as possible, since the vulnerabilities have been publicly disclosed.

Here’s the full security content of HomeView Software Version 27.2

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts

Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management.

Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data

Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management.

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory

Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management.

Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption

Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation.

Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction

Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks.

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction

Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management.

Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages

Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation.

Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined

Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code.

Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts

Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management.

HBO's Harry Potter hasn't made a magical first impression

HBO Max has released a first look at its upcoming ‘Harry Potter’ TV show, and it’s fair to say the online reaction has been mixed. And by mixed, I mean mostly extremely negative.

The 90-second clip is presumably from an early episode (I would guess episode 2). It offers a first look at Hogwarts’ start-of-term feast, alongside a brief conversation between headmaster Albus Dumbledore (John Lithgow) and professor of Transfiguration Minerva McGonagall (Janet McTeer).

The show, which will be called “Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone” for its first season (no, Sorcerer’s Stone this time), will adapt J.K. Rowling’s 1997 book of the same name across a reported eight episodes. Dominic McLaughlin will play the boy wizard, with Alastair Stout and Arabella Stanton playing his schoolmates Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger, respectively.

The first episode is due to premiere on HBO in the U.S. and HBO Max internationally on December 25, and it’s already been earmarked as one of the most anticipated (and most expensive) television projects in history. I suspect HBO was hoping this clip would be well-received…

HBO’s “Harry Potter” has faced backlash since its initial announcement in 2023. The necessity of adapting Rowling’s best-selling books a second time has been questioned, as the movie versions, released between 2001 and 2011, remain extremely popular to this day. And are seasonal staples for many.

Also, you can’t talk about Harry Potter in the current climate without acknowledging the controversy surrounding its creator, J.K. Rowling. Rowling has become an extremely divisive public figure due to her outspoken views, particularly in relation to the transgender community, which makes anything related to the Harry Potter brand controversial.

One look at my feeds, and the initial reactions to this short teaser clip haven’t exactly been magical. Over on X, the clip has been labeled “lifeless in all aspects,” and comparisons to the same scene in the 2001 movie starring Daniel Radcliffe, which is noticeably more colorful, have done few favors.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

This new Harry Potter looks so lifeless man in all aspects. https://t.co/NeLhmHNTpWNovember 15, 2026

One post from X user Matt del Rio, which has amassed more than 35,000 likes as of writing, reads, “As a millennial who spent hours upon hours reading Harry Potter growing up, I’m insulted by this,” suggesting that even viewers who haven’t turned their back on the series in the wake of Rowling’s incendiary comments are unimpressed with HBO’s first look.

As a millennial who spent hours upon hours reading Harry Potter growing up, I’m insulted by thisNovember 15, 2026

And as far as cutting remarks go, one X account states, “It’s actually so funny they spent millions of dollars to make Temu Harry Potter.” Ouch! Probably not the reaction HBO would be hoping for, considering the show reportedly cost roughly $25 million per episode to produce.

it’s actually so funny they spent millions of dollars to make Temu Harry PotterNovember 15, 2026

As one of the biggest Harry Potter fans on staff at Tom’s Guide — a label that comes with an uncomfortable degree of shame these days — my feelings on this first clip are decidedly more muted. Overall, I think, judging solely on this new 90-second clip, the show looks generally fine.

The problem is that for millions of us, myself included, we literally grew up on the Potter movies, so there is an inherent disconnect when watching a new production of “The Philosopher’s Stone.”

It’s hard to see anybody as Harry Potter but a young Daniel Radcliffe. Getting past the nostalgic fondness so many have for the movies will be tough.

I do agree with the criticism of the lack of color, but this seems to be a trend across modern TV shows and movies. The art of color grading seems to be a dying one.

Not to mention the lack of floating candles to light the Hogwarts Great Hall is a curious production design decision, considering the justification for the show’s existence has largely been that it will be more book-accurate than the movies, which jettisoned many narrative elements and characters to squeeze the increasingly lengthy novels into two-hour movies. What's up with that?

Nevertheless, there are some nice flourishes here, like the way food literally pops into existence on the tables, and the musical score from Hans Zimmer does indeed scream Potter.

Will the HBO “Harry Potter” series be any good? Will it feel completely unnecessary? Will movie nostalgia sour it with viewers? Only time will tell, but I’ll be reserving making any definitive judgements until I’ve seen the full season. Fortunately, we don’t have much longer to wait before its premiere.

#3347. HBO’s ‘Harry Potter’ Reboot Is About To Take One Iconic Scene Much Further

Next month will more than likely see HBO ramping up the promotion for its upcoming Harry Potter series, which is looking to bring the Boy Who Lived to life for a new generation. The series is facing an uphill battle, thanks to major comparisons with the Harry Potter movies and behind-the-scenes drama surrounding the casting and the involvement of J.K. Rowling. However, one star has revealed that the upcoming Season 2 will feature a key moment from the books that never made it into the movies — and it's bound to make fans of one character very happy.

While speaking to Deadline, Rafe Spall, who's set to play Arthur Weasley in Harry Potter and the Philospher's Stone (aka Season 1), confirmed that he has a key scene with Johnny Flynn's Lucius Malfoy in Season 2. While Spall was coy about the details of said scene, he did note that it was ironic that he was starring in a new version of Harry Potter while his father Timothy starred in the Potter movies as Voldemort's right-hand man Peter Pettigrew, who disguised himself as Ron's rat Scabbers:

"It’s funny that my dad played Ron’s rat and now I’m playing Arthur Weasley. The other day I was on set and Ron’s rat was there. I took a photograph next to it. If I had social media, I would post it."

Eagle-eyed Potter fans have probably guessed that the scene Spall mentions centers on a conflict between Arthur and Lucius when the two take their respective families to a bookstore where Gilderoy Lockhart (Kit Harington) is doing a signing. Lucius winds up insulting the Weasleys' lack of wealth, causing Arthur to get into a fight with him; the struggle serves as a cover for Lucius to plant Tom Riddle's diary on Ginny Weasley, kicking off the plot of Harry Poter and the Chamber of Secrets. Yet that one scene also highlights a key conflict that was rarely touched upon in the movies, namely the Weasleys' status in the Wizarding World.

Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets dives further into the Wizarding World, as Ron and his brothers Fred and George wind up busting Harry out of imprisonment at the Dursleys. But it's also Harry's first encounter into how lucky he truly is; when the Weasleys take him shopping for school supplies, he witnesses that they don't have much to spare while his parents left him a sizeable fortune. Contrast that with Draco Malfoy; his father can not only afford to buy him the finest robes and books, but even gets his son onto Slytherin's Quidditch team by gifting each member a top of the line broomstick. This gets touched upon in further books, where Ron outright expresses he hates being poor in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire upon learning that a handful of gold he picked up is cursed to disappear.

This class conflict is one of many underlying factors of the Harry Potter books, and it takes on an even greater scope in Goblet of Fire and Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix. Goblet reveals that Lucius Malfoy is secretly a member of Voldemort's Death Eaters, while Order of the Phoenix centers on the titular organization led by Albus Dumbledore, which counts Arthur and his wife Molly among its members. By showcasing the pivotal conflict between Arthur and Lucius, HBO's Harry Potter could lay the groundwork for future seasons to come.

The fact that Harry Potter is set to actually build on the Weasleys' place in the Wizarding World makes it stand out, as it's a chance for Ron to fully shine. Despite Rupert Grint turning in a great performance, most of Ron's appearances in the Harry Potter movies boil him down to being merely comic relief or Harry's sidekick. The HBO series has a chance to dig deeper into the insecurities that are born out of being the best friend of the most famous wizard in the world, and his family's financial status — not to mention being part of a large family. One single scene might help give HBO's take on Harry Potter the depth it needs to succeed.

Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone premieres on HBO Max on December 25, 2026.

#3345. 10 Google Privacy Hacks Everyone Should Know

Your Gmail account doesn't just have one email address. In fact, it has unlimited addresses, but you need a hack to utilize them. When you're signing up for a new service, you can add another word to your email address, as well as the "+" symbol, to create an alias. For example, if your email is "[email protected]," and you're signing up for an Amazon account, you can use "[email protected]" as your email address. The email will still end up in your main inbox, as if you simply used [email protected]. Not only can this trick turn one Gmail address into an unlimited number of addresses, but it also helps you identify who sold your email address to spammers, because those emails will have the alias in the "To" field.

Gmail's web view has a crucial security feature that lets you view session logs. This feature is inexplicably buried at the bottom of the inbox, and the font size is tiny, so it's easy to miss. To find it, log in to Gmail on the web, and scroll to the bottom of your inbox. Click the Details button in the bottom-right corner, below "Last account activity." This will show you a pop-up that lists the devices, apps, and locations you've recently logged in from. This makes it easy to see if there's been any suspicious activity in your Google account, and you can click the Security Checkup link in the pop-up to review this data. Just note that if you use a VPN or a service like iCloud Private Relay, you might not recognize your own device's location. To check if unwanted apps have access to your Google account, you can visit this settings page.

Google wants to show you personalized search results, which initially feels very helpful, but it also ends up trapping you in an algorithmic bubble. The best way to break out of your search bubble is to periodically use other search engines, but if you wish to stick to Google, you can disable personalized search recommendations in Google Search and the Play Store on Android. Go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized Recommendations and Play Personalization.

Google tracks your web and app activity by default, which includes your search history, voice data (if you use the speak-to-search feature), and activity from sites, apps, and devices that use Google services. However, associated information, such as your location data, is also saved to your Google profile, which you might not assume gets included in "Web & app activity." Fortunately, you can disable this tracking by going to this settings page, scrolling down to "Web & App Activity," and turning off all options in this section.

Google's Timeline feature saves your location in Google Maps to create a map of places you've visited. This is useful if you want to keep track of your recent stops; however, Google can use Timeline data to help businesses see how effective their ads were, or how likely you are to visit nearby stores. Its confirmation page confirms this: "Depending on your settings, activity saved as history in your Google Account, including ad interactions, may also be connected to Timeline data to help nearby businesses estimate the likelihood that people will visit their stores. No personal information is shared with businesses."

Timeline isn't enabled by default, but in case you enabled it a while ago, and are no longer using it, you can turn it off by going to this settings page. Click Turn off, and delete your activity to remove Timeline data from your Google account.

You can't fully escape Google's ads or tracking, but you can disable personalized ads to stop the company from using your account data to show ads. To do this, go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized ads.

While Google claims that it isn't using your emails to train AI, the company does offer AI features that make your emails feel more robotic than human. One of these is "Smart Reply," which offers email reply suggestions such as "Got it. See you soon." I can type that on my own, and I feel uncomfortable with Gmail analyzing the contents of my emails and replies to offer suggestions that I wouldn't use anyway. You can disable this by going to Gmail Settings > General, or by visiting this settings page. Scroll down to "Smart features," and turn off the checkbox next to it. This will disable Smart Compose, Smart Reply, suggestions for pending replies and follow-ups, spelling, grammar, and autocorrect.

A physical security key is a great security upgrade. It's a physical barrier that prevents most ways to hack into your account remotely. Even if someone discovers your email ID and password, and has access to your two-factor authentication code, they won't get in without physical access to that key. You can check out Google's support page for physical security keys for more information on compatibility and setting up your security keys.

Google uses data from Gmail and Google Drive to target ads, which means that your emails, files, and photos could be used for monetization. To stop this, you'll need to disable Personal Intelligence. To turn it off, visit this settings page, and click Turn off Personal Intelligence.

#3343. Garmin Cyclists Can Now Make Themselves Appear on Waze in Real Time

Cyclists who ride with Garmin gear can now appear as live, moving icons on the Waze driving app, and nearby drivers will receive an alert to slow down and watch for them on the road.

For riders already using Garmin devices, opting in costs nothing and adds a new layer of safety, particularly on roads where drivers may not expect cyclists. The feature is rolling out now, but you should be aware of its limitations.

Riders can simply opt in once through Garmin Connect. After that, sharing starts automatically when an outdoor cycling activity begins and stops when the ride ends. While a ride is underway, Waze users near the cyclist see a cyclist icon move along the road and receive a Live Cycling Alert reminding them to slow down and stay aware.

The feature runs on LiveTrack, Garmin's existing live location-sharing tool, which lets friends and family follow a rider's real-time location, speed, course, and more. Garmin says this collaboration extends that peace of mind to motorists, giving them greater awareness of their surroundings.

Garmin notes its location sharing is temporary and session-based. The rider's name, identity, and route are hidden, and no personal information is shared or displayed in Waze. Drivers see only an anonymous icon and the alert.

You'll need a few things to get this feature up and running:

A compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin watch

A phone running Garmin Connect with a data connection

An outdoor cycling activity (the feature doesn't apply to indoor rides)

The good news is using the feature is free: LiveTrack costs nothing on compatible Garmin bike computers and watches, and Waze is free for drivers.

This new feature is a great safety perk, but there are real-world caveats worth considering:

This feature is for Waze only. Alerts reach drivers only when Waze is open on their phone. Google Maps, which has far more users, is excluded, so a large portion of the drivers you share the road with won't see you this way.

It depends on your phone's signal. Your position travels from the Garmin to your phone, then to Garmin's servers, then to Waze, and finally to the driver's phone. On a patchy rural signal, a few seconds of lag could put the icon on the wrong side of a bend from where you actually are. A rider who leaves their phone at home or whose phone loses signal simply won't show up on a Waze map, as a ride without a data connection is invisible to Waze.

Finally, remember to treat this safety feature as an extra perk, not a guarantee. At the end of the day, it isn't a replacement for bike lights, bright clothing, and defensive riding.

The 2027 Audi S6 Sportback e-tron pairs its luxury aesthetics with a sporty drive that makes it fun on the road, all while remaining whisper-quiet on the inside thanks to its air-suspension ride and solid soundproofing. While its nearly $95,000 as-tested price tag is a hefty amount, it’s accompanied by premium features and surprisingly efficient for drivers who want sports-sedan thrills without sacrificing everyday versatility.

Hefty cost puts it out of the budget of most people

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

When I got into the driver's seat of the Audi A6 Sportback e-tron last year, my expectations weren’t all that high. But it ended up impressing me so much that it quickly became one of the best electric cars I’ve tested. With the 2027 Audi S6 Sportback e-tron, it’s pretty evident that Audi has dialed up the aggression and sportier flair.

While there are similarities between the two, the S6 Sportback e-tron differentiates itself with standard dual-motor quattro all-wheel drive, sport-tuned adaptive air suspension, and up to 543 horsepower. Quite simply, it’s a mid-size luxury sedan that trades some range for extra muscle.

I tested the 2027 Audi S6 Sportback e-tron Prestige for a week, which carries a $94,490 as-tested price — putting it squarely in the crosshairs of similar models I’ve tested, like the BMW i5 and Lucid Air Touring. And after seven days behind the wheel, I discovered this pricier performance variant still holds a few surprises up its sleeve.

Dual Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motors (AWD)

I drove the 2027 Audi S6 Sportback e-tron Prestige for a total of 152.4 miles and recorded an overall average efficiency of 3.6 mi/kWh. While that overall figure trails slightly behind the results I got out of the BMW i5 and Lucid Air Touring, it’s well within striking range of its main rivals.

Personally, I think it’s a valiant result given how the A6 Sportback e-tron yielded 3.7 mi/kWh in my previous test. On longer highway stretches, I’ve recorded a best mark of 3.9 mi/kWh with the A6 Sportback — while short trip efficiency reached 3.6 mi/kWh.

When plugged into a standard household outlet for Level 1 charging, the S6 Sportback e-tron added range at a rate of 4.05 miles per hour. That places it squarely in the middle of its rivals, beating the Lucid Air Touring while trailing the BMW i5 xDrive40.

I’ve always been a fan of Audi’s signature design philosophy, and the 2027 S6 Sportback e-tron takes that familiar luxury aesthetic and injects it with an aggressive, sporty edge. Between its low-slung fastback silhouette, razor-sharp LED lighting, and glossy front grille, it strikes an athletic stance that never feels overdone — and makes me feel young at heart.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Behind the wheel, the 2027 Audi S6 Sportback e-tron delivers a refined, whisper-quiet ride that glides effortlessly over rough pavement thanks to its standard sport adaptive air suspension. Yet the moment I bury my foot in the accelerator, it pins me back in the seat with blistering off-the-line speed.

That effortless torque makes overtaking slower traffic on the highway feel almost instantaneous, giving me serious passing power without ever sacrificing its composed demeanor. It actually offers a better ride than the Lucid Air and matches the BMW i5 on open roads.

One of the standout tech features on the S6 Sportback e-tron is Audi's augmented reality head-up display, which projects crisp visuals directly into my line of sight on the windshield. Beyond showing me all the usual stats — like my current speed, turn-by-turn navigation arrows, and speed limit signs — it also visualizes adaptive cruise assist and following distance in real time.

It’s one of the most comprehensive and advanced HUDs out there, even turning red when the gap to the vehicle ahead gets too short.

In 2026, it’s still very rare for any vehicle to come with an integrated dashcam, but the S6 Sportback e-tron is one of them. Ingeniously, it’s built into the auto-dimming rearview mirror — keeping the windshield free of clutter, unlike third-party camera solutions with dangling power cables. Not only does it offer automatic loop recording for convenience, but it also doesn’t require an extra fee or subscription just to work.

Another practical advantage of the S6 Sportback e-tron is its rear liftback design, which opens up a massive cargo hold that puts conventional sedans to shame. Unlike the traditional, narrower trunk openings I dealt with on the BMW i5 and Lucid Air Touring, the Audi’s entire rear glass lifts with the power tailgate — making it far easier to load bulky gear, luggage, or larger items that simply wouldn’t clear a standard trunk lid.

With roughly 26 cubic feet of space behind the second row (and even more when you fold the rear seats flat), it gives you crossover-like versatility wrapped in a sleek sport-sedan profile.

I’ll be the first to admit that its $95,000 as-tested price is hefty, but Audi compensates for it with a serious tech suite of luxury features you don’t traditionally find. Overhead, the panoramic glass roof features variable light control that electronically lets me switch between transparent and opaque at the touch of a button, while LED interior ambient lighting wraps across the dashboard and brings the cabin to life at night.

On the outside, I love small details like the animations of the LED headlights and OLED taillights, which give it a slick look when turning the vehicle on and off. There are also dual charging ports on either side of the vehicle, giving me the convenience of parking however I want for Level 1 and 2 charging — albeit with Level 3 DC fast charging only supported on the driver’s side.

Entertainment and audio get just as much attention, thanks to a crisp 10.9-inch front passenger display and a booming Bang & Olufsen 3D sound system that even builds speakers directly into the front headrests.

While the S6 Sportback e-tron’s sleek, low-slung roofline looks fantastic from the outside, it comes at the expense of a narrower rear windshield compared to its rivals. As a result, it creates a somewhat letterbox-like view.

Between the low roofline, chunky A-pillars, and the large sensor housing behind the rearview mirror, spotting overhead traffic lights can be challenging when pulling up close to an intersection.

I’m the kind of driver who religiously activates adaptive cruise control, and while I appreciate how the S6 Sportback e-tron keeps steady in its lane, it lacks automatic lane-change assist. That means I’m still forced to manually take over whenever I want to pass slower traffic on the highway — a glaring omission for a pricey $95K luxury vehicle.

Compounding that frustration is how Audi continues to put all of the adaptive cruise control functions on a dedicated stalk tucked behind the lower left side of the steering wheel, which forces me to move my hand slightly away from the wheel. I’d much rather have them integrated into one of the control pads on the steering wheel itself.

There’s a lot to love about the 2027 Audi S6 Sportback e-tron, starting with its sharp and sporty design, all the way to its genuinely practical hatchback-like utility. Add in a rich roster of high-end comfort tech — from its augmented reality HUD to its built-in dashcam — it delivers an upscale daily driving experience.

Still, at nearly $95,000 as tested, that steep price tag makes it a tough pill to swallow for most buyers, especially when smaller quirks like a narrow windshield and inconveniently placed cruise-control stalk hold it back from perfection. If you don't need the extra cargo space or blistering acceleration and are willing to go a little smaller, the 2027 Mercedes-Benz CLA 250+ delivers exceptional luxury EV value at a dramatically lower price.

#3338. 10 Movies Like ‘Interstellar’ You Should Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Christopher Nolan’s 2014 megahit Interstellar has it all: big sci-fi ideas, cool robots, ugly crying, and a Matt Damon character in need of rescuing. Grounded in the intensity of the human experience, this story of humanity’s potential extinction and the sacrifice of one man to save it doesn’t just deliver exotic planets and thrilling spaceship maneuvers; it also provides all the feels as Joseph Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) sacrifices everything he has in an effort to save the entire human race. It’s one of the best science fiction films ever made, with Nolan’s signature complexity, time manipulations, and emotional wallop. If you love this movie, here are ten more that offer a similar viewing experience.

If you loved both the special effects in Interstellar that make space travel feel viscerally thrilling (and terrifying) and the mind-blowing concepts, this is the film for you. Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 epic (written by sci-fi master Arthur C. Clarke) traces humanity’s development from mildly smart apes to spacefaring capitalists who discover a mysterious obelisk on the Moon that sparks a mission to Jupiter. While it operates in a colder emotional key than Nolan’s film, 2001: A Space Odyssey absolutely delivers on the epic side of things (and the cool—if slightly deranged and deadly—artificial intelligences). Stream 2001: A Space Odyssey on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for more existential missions with somewhat reluctant heroes in space, Project Hail Mary is your next stop. When the Sun begins to dim due to the interference of an alien entity, scientists identify the one nearby star that isn’t being similarly affected. Brilliant molecular biologist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) winds up forced to go on what is assumed to be a fatal, one-way mission into deep space to try to find a way to save humanity, unexpectedly assisted by a charming alien he names Rocky. It’s got the same emotional volume and big ideas as Interstellar, and fans of Nolan’s film will love it. Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+ or Philo, or rent it on Prime Video.

Part of what makes Interstellar so compelling is the stakes: The human race is slowly dying, and a handful of people must make incredible sacrifices to save it. That’s the vibe of Sunshine, set in a future where the Sun is dimming and a spacecraft is dispatched to deliver an enormous bomb designed to reignite the Sun’s fusion cycle. But the mission is the second attempt after the first ship vanished mysteriously seven years earlier, and when the new crew stumbles on the derelict wreck of the first mission, things quickly descend into violence and madness—but the crew remains determined to save the world, no matter the cost. Rent Sunshine on Prime Video.

Interstellar works in large part because of the emotional dynamics at play. McConaughey’s character leaves his children behind and is forced to witness them growing up without him, missing out on their lives and saddled with the knowledge that they resent him despite the necessity of his mission. Arrival is a First Contact story focused on language—linguist Louise Banks (Amy Adams) is drafted into an effort to understand the strange, complex language of the aliens. As she slowly builds to an understanding of how the aliens communicate and perceive time itself, her own heartbreak and loss come into play, giving this film a similarly devastating emotional punch. Stream Arrival on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Family dynamics and the toll of lonely space missions fuel Ad Astra, a film with the same emotional core as Interstellar. Twenty-nine years ago, famed astronaut Clifford McBride (Tommy Lee Jones) led the Lima Project, a space station around Neptune searching for intelligent life. Thirteen years ago, Earth lost contact with him. When bursts of energy emanating from Neptune threaten to end life on Earth, his son, Roy (Brad Pitt), is dispatched to try to make contact with his father. It’s an epic journey with a powerful climax that will satisfy fans of Interstellar in every way. Stream Ad Astra on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

Ridley Scott’s prequel to Alien has its flaws, but if you’re looking for a sense of epic spacefaring adventure in the same key as Interstellar, it’s perfect. When two scientists discover a star map apparently left behind by ancient aliens, they secure funding from the Wayland Corporation to organize a space expedition to the indicated planet. Accompanied by a colorful crew and the android David, they discover an apparently abandoned outpost of the species dubbed the Engineers. The story wrestles with questions about humanity’s origins, purpose, and potential—but this being an Alien film, things quickly turn horrifying. Rent Prometheus on Prime Video.

Adapted from Carl Sagan’s 1985 novel, Contact follows astronomer Dr. Ellie Arroway (Jodie Foster), who becomes involved with an effort to decipher a signal originating from the star Vega. The signal turns out to be a set of instructions for constructing a one-person spacecraft of some kind, and Arroway is eventually selected as the candidate to take the journey. There’s a sense of courage in the face of the unknown that’s similar to Interstellar, as well as the thrill of strapping into a spaceship and pressing the ignition. Plus, there’s the added bonus of seeing one of the greatest trick shots in cinematic history. Rent Contact on Prime Video.

Stanislaw Lem’s 1961 novel Solaris explores what Lem saw as the impossibility of ever understanding a truly alien life. The two major adaptations—Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 version and Steven Soderbergh’s 2002 take starring George Clooney—are both worth watching, but Tarkovsky’s film is a masterpiece of psychological horror. The story is set mainly aboard a space station orbiting a planet covered in what appears to be a sentient "ocean" and chronicles the strange haunting and inexplicable experiences of the humans living on the station. If your favorite part of Interstellar is the ending when things get trippy and weird, you’ll probably love Solaris. Stream Solaris on HBO Max, Plex, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

The story of a mission to Jupiter’s moon Europa to search for intelligent life, Europa Report has the same sense of terrifying excitement that accompanies Interstellar’s missions to the different candidate planets. Leaning into the fragility of life in an environment not designed to support it, the mission crew face a steady stream of loss and danger as they work to catch sight of alien life on the frozen, deadly moon, ultimately faced with making terrifying sacrifices in order to provide humanity with the answers that it seeks. Stream Europa Report on Netflix, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

A film based on a 1956 epic science fiction poem written by a Swedish Nobel Laureate might seem like an unlikely match for fans of Interstellar, but it’s actually perfect. As the Earth becomes uninhabitable, humanity begins launching ships to colonize Mars. When one such ship, the Aniara, is damaged and veers irreversibly off course, the passengers and crew are faced with the knowledge that they will sail off into the void without hope of rescue. Within a few years, despair has driven some to suicide and madness, while others cling to the possibility that they might yet find a way back. The film offers a different perspective on the existential crisis of humanity’s extinction, exploring the worst-case scenario to its bitter, bleak end. Stream Aniara on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3337. New Apple TV 4K and HomeView now available: Here’s everything you need to know

The new Apple TV 4K and HomeView smart display are officially available. The first pre-orders have arrived for eager shoppers, and you can now also head to your local Apple Store to buy select configurations.

The new HomeView smart display gives you a way to interact with Siri AI, your HomeKit accessories, and more in a 7-inch square display form factor. It’s available in two versions. There’s one with a built-in base, and another that’s designed to be mounted on your wall.

HomeView is powered by an A18 chip and has a built-in 12MP Center Stage camera for FaceTime calls. It’s available in silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray. You can read my full review for all the HomeView details you need.

When buying from Apple for delivery, HomeView in all four colors is backordered to the first week of December. Most Apple Stores, however, seem to have same-day pickup availability today, especially in silver and starlight. It costs $299.

#3336. The Apple Watch's New 'Siri Recap' Feature Is Even Creepier Than I Expected

The “Siri Recap” feature that Apple announced in September is finally available in a developer beta, and I’ve spent the last 24 hours with the feature turned on. It’s even more unsettling than the “Live Rewind” feature that launched at the same time. It listens to all my conversations, and produces summaries that are both helpful and deeply creepy.

I have a button in the watch’s Control Center that can turn the recapping abilities off, but if I forget to do so, Siri listens to everything. I’ll get a recap of my entire evening, presented in roughly hour-long chunks, including things I would have completely forgotten I had even heard about.

The recaps somberly mention silly memes my kids were laughing about, and make major bullet points out of offhand remarks from brief conversations. If a conversation sticks to a single topic, I’ll often get a reasonably good summary of it, with specific facts and numbers highlighted; but just as often, Siri will get confused and mix up several topics or completely mishear a name or phrase.

Apple has four features that it considers part of “audio intelligence":

Music recognition, better known as Shazam. We’ve had a version of this on the Apple Watch for a long time now, although it has some improvements and now identifies music automatically.

Sound recognition, which can notify you about doorbells and babies crying. A version of this launched in 2020 as an accessibility feature.

Live Rewind, which gives you an on-wrist transcript of the last 15 seconds of detected speech.

Siri Recaps, which summarizes entire conversations for you to read on your phone.

Live Rewind had the flashiest demo from the Apple event: A server rattled off the day’s specials at a restaurant, and then the Apple Watch-wearing diner checked his watch to see a readout of exactly which dishes had just been mentioned. The utility is both obvious and kind of unnecessary: Why wouldn’t you just ask the server to repeat the list while they’re standing right there?

I haven’t found myself using Live Rewind, except out of curiosity about how the feature works. I discovered that it doesn’t pick up song lyrics very well, and also that by the time I think to check what was just said in a conversation, more than 15 seconds has passed since the part I was unsure about. I haven’t yet found a reason to use it for real.

But Siri Recaps? Those are both useful and unsettling. I enabled the feature, and decided to test it out later. But since it was on, it dutifully listened in as I picked up my son from school and gave him an update on an ailing family member’s health. We stopped by the library, and along the way we chatted about a variety of things: holiday travel plans, library policies, and the possibility of humans living in space in the future. Siri was listening to it all.

At least for now, the feature is only available in a developer beta, so sign up for that now if you want to try it. You'll need an Apple Watch Series 12 (or Ultra 4) and an iPhone 16 or better, excluding the 16e. (I have a 16 Pro, so I'm good.)

After you're updated to 27.3, go into the Watch app, tap Siri, and turn on Siri Recap. You can set a schedule for when it should listen (for example, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., if you want it on for the work day but off for the evening). You'll need to set a passcode on your watch, and you'll be guided through a step to upgrade your audio connection. The control center on the watch will have a button you can use to turn Siri recaps on and off at will. To read your recaps, go to the Siri app on your phone.

But still: I feel weird publishing the contents of these recaps, because they do contain things that people said to me in what they assumed was a private setting. I had the feature on when I attended a choir practice, and Siri recapped the brief chats I had with other choir members before and after practice. (Interestingly, it did not recap any of the quiet conversations I had with fellow sopranos while the tenors were rehearsing their part. I’m not sure if the watch was unable to hear us over the music, or if Siri is programmed not to listen when music is being played.)

Because speakers aren’t identified, it seems Siri doesn’t know what to do when there is a disagreement. A human note-taker would jot down that Person A made a point in favor of something, and person B made a point against. But when my son and I disagreed about how likely space colonization might be in the future, the recap didn’t reflect the separate positions that were put forth. It summarized the conversation as including “debating the feasibility and timeline of human space colonization and asteroid mining,” which isn’t exactly accurate, but close enough.

When it comes to the content of the discussion, the recap notes a bullet point of “skepticism regarding permanent space colonies within the next 100 years.” It didn’t include my reasons for being skeptical, and didn’t mention my son’s opposing viewpoint at all. If I were using this recap to jog my memory of the conversation, it wouldn’t be all that helpful.

Details are sometimes egregiously incorrect. After a discussion about a family member’s health, the recap had notes on the prognosis of “father.” The family member we discussed is not anybody’s father. Names in general seem to be a problem; I recommended a book to my son, and the recap includes notes about the content of the book, but not its title. The book’s author appears in the introduction to the recap (sort of a summary of a summary), but not in the content of the recap itself where the book is mentioned.

I should probably turn Siri recaps off. It seems wrong to let people chat with me without letting them know that their conversation is being ... well, not technically recorded, but basically recorded.

But it’s so tempting to leave it on so that I can review my day. Some of the details in the recaps are useful, like the dates that were discussed as options for a holiday party. The recaps will be deleted in about a week (unless I save them to the notes app), so if I want to remind myself of a conversation a few days ago, I should be able to scroll back through my recaps and find it.

I would be a fool to rely on the recaps, though. The most important points of a conversation are often left out; Siri doesn’t know what’s actually important, and there’s no way to guide it as to what to pay attention to. Specific details can be wrong, as I mentioned. There’s also no way to control when a “conversation” starts or stops, unless you are turning the recap feature on and off from the watch.

And there’s more: Not only are names usually omitted (wait, who did she say I should ask about that project?), the few identifiers that make it into the recap, like names of events, are often wrong. Subjects of discussion are often conflated in really unhelpful ways: My husband mentioned paying for certain course registrations for one of our children, and later I talked to that child about an unrelated exam. The recap got all of these things mixed up with each other and was wrong about pretty much every detail. About all the recap could usefully do is to remind me that something about AP U.S. History was discussed. Reading the recaps can be like reliving your day entirely in the passive voice.

#3335. Faizon Love Sued Over Alleged Comedy Show No-Show Amid Child Support Drama

Faizon Love is being sued for allegedly skipping out on a $12,500 comedy show ... and the promoter claims his child support troubles were already raising red flags before the gig.

According to new legal documents obtained by TMZ, event promoter Inga Harden says she booked Love for a July 17 benefit supporting local businesses in Florence, Alabama and claims she shelled out $6,250 upfront for the comedian to perform for at least an hour.

But, according to the complaint, weeks before the show, Love's child support drama in Florida had her worried he might not show up ... so Harden says her attorney reached out to Love's agent, Eric Young, to make sure everything was still on.

She claims Young called back and questioned why everyone was "panicking."

According to the suit, things got even messier 11 days before showtime ... when Harden claims an attorney representing a woman seeking child support from Love contacted her, demanding she withhold a portion of any money owed to him and warning she could face sanctions.

Ultimately, Harden claims Love never showed up ... and she says nobody from his team gave her a heads-up that he wasn't coming.

As we previously reported, Love was arrested in Florida in June on contempt of court charges tied to his case with Tiffany Lee, who claims he owes around $250K in child support.

Harden says she demanded her deposit back, but never got a refund. Instead, she received a mysterious $1 Cash App notification days later, followed by a text allegedly from Young asking her to verify her account. The suit doesn't say who exactly sent the dollar.

The promoter is suing Love, Young and Young's company for $6,436.50 in remaining deposit money and fees ... plus additional damages.
