Black Friday isn't until November 27, but Amazon's early Black Friday 2026 sale is already bringing some decent discounts on TP-Link routers, with prices starting at $44.99 and savings of up to $100. The deals cover quite a few different networking needs, from compact travel routers that let you connect multiple devices to hotel wifi to more powerful home routers designed for faster internet plans and households with lots of connected devices.

TP-Link’s Roam routers are compact enough to travel with and let you share a hotel or public internet connection across your devices through a private Wi-Fi network—and right now, Amazon has three models on sale: the Roam 6 AX1500 for $44.99 (was $59.99), the Roam 6 AX3000 for $55.98 (was $79.99), and the Roam 7 BE3600 for $87.99 (was $119.99). All three support VPN connections and multiple operating modes, with the main differences coming down to speed. The AX1500 offers up to 1.5Gbps, the AX3000 doubles that and adds a 2.5Gbps WAN port, while the Wi-Fi 7-enabled Roam 7 reaches up to 3.6Gbps.

The TP-Link Archer AX21 V5 AX1800 is down to $54.99 from $89.99, saving you $35 on an affordable Wi-Fi 6 router for everyday home use. Its dual-band connection offers combined theoretical speeds of up to 1.8Gbps, which should be sufficient for typical activities like streaming, video calls, and browsing across several devices.

For homes with faster internet plans, multiple gamers, or lots of connected devices, TP-Link's Archer BE700 and BE770 offer tri-band Wi-Fi 7, including access to the 6GHz band for compatible devices. Both support EasyMesh for extended coverage and have 10Gbps WAN ports, although the BE770 provides faster wireless speeds and more wired connectivity. As for pricing, the TP-Link Archer BE700 is down to $248 from $349.99, saving you just over $100. It offers theoretical speeds of up to 15Gbps, a 2.5Gbps LAN port, and three Gigabit LAN ports. For just $52 more, the Archer BE770 (now $299.99, was $369.99) bumps speeds up to 18Gbps and adds a dedicated 10Gbps LAN port, making it better suited to high-speed network storage and large file transfers.

The TP-Link Deco BE25 is down to $99.98 from $129.99, saving you $30 on a Wi-Fi 7 router designed to work as part of a mesh network. It offers dual-band wireless speeds of up to 5Gbps, two 2.5Gbps Ethernet ports, and AI-driven roaming that helps connected devices switch between Deco units as you move around your home.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Almost a year after Below Deck star Nathan Gallagher was arrested for domestic abuse in Australia — and 12 weeks after the news went public — Gallagher’s former partner and cast member Gael Cameron is finally speaking out about their relationship.

Cameron broke her silence on an episode of the podcast We Need to Talk, hosted by Paul C. Brunson, where she publicly accused Gallagher of abuse for the first time and described a toxic relationship that’s left her in fear to this day.

“I know that he is not afraid to do anything to throw me under. He’s not afraid to lie.… He’s always had this idea that he has ownership or control over me,” Cameron said tearfully. “I still feel that. And I am still scared of him. And that’s why I’ve not said anything, even though he’s thrown all these accusations out there.”

Gallagher and Cameron met while filming Season Nine of Below Deck: Mediterranean in 2023, both working on the superyacht’s deck team. Over three seasons, their relationship evolved from flirty co-workers to welcoming a son together last June. But this August — halfway through a season where Gallagher struggled to juggle his bosun duties and be a present father — news broke of Gallagher’s December 2025 arrest on domestic-violence charges. According to Australian police, Gallagher attacked Cameron at her apartment in Sydney, resulting in his arrest on Dec. 27, 2025. During the physical altercation, Gallagher “placed both of his hands around the victim’s neck, applying enough pressure which made her unable to breathe,” according to police records. He was charged with assault occasioning actual bodily harm, common assault, and intentionally choking a person without consent.

Although Gallagher previously told Rolling Stone he had proof that would clear his name, he failed to appear at a mandated court hearing in September. As a result, he was convicted by default on charges of assault. Australian authorities issued a warrant for his arrest, noting Gallagher was suspected to have fled the country. #3290. Perplexity brings AI agents feature called Teammates to the Mac

This week, Perplexity has deployed its new proactive agentic AI feature called Teammates to the Mac. Perplexity Teammates were previously limited to iOS and the web.

Similar to Grok Bot, Perplexity Teammates are task-oriented proactive agentic AI threads that work for you without constantly being prompted. Meta Muse and ChatGPT Dots are similar, but use a single chat model rather than supporting multiple instances.

Teammates are a team of AI agents that own ongoing work. Give a teammate a responsibility, such as managing a growth campaign, triaging incoming bug reports, tracking your metrics, or researching a new market, and it owns that work around the clock. It plans the tasks, brings in more agents when the work grows, and follows through until the result is ready for your review.

Access to Teammates currently requires a paid Perplexity Max subscription. The feature builds on top of Perplexity’s existing AI orchestration system.

Test Gemini’s financial know-how with these prompts

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When it's time to do a bit of extra research into your finances, AI tools like ChatGPT’s Finances dashboard exist to help you do just that (as long as you trust it enough to connect your financial accounts to it through Plaid).

It doesn’t come as much of a surprise that Gemini has decided to join in on that trend. Google has already begun rolling out Google Wallet as the last connected app to become integrated into Gemini—US users now have the ability to use this feature to get informed responses on their finances based on the linked credit card and bank accounts attached to their Google Wallet profile via Plaid.

Turning Google Wallet on inside Gemini is as simple as clicking on the “Settings” icon (which is the gear wheel that sits across from your Google account name and photo), selecting “Personal Intelligence,” clicking “Connected Apps” and adding the Google Wallet connector. From that point forward, you can prompt the connector by starting your inquiry with “@Google Wallet.”

Thankfully, Gemini’s Google Wallet powers exist only to give you financial insight—it will never move, manage or invest any of the money attached to your linked accounts. To get the best insights, it’s worth trying out any of the following prompts to see just how helpful it can be.

I decided to ask Gemini itself about the sort of basic questions anyone willing to try its Google Wallet-connected app should ask. Google’s chatbot came back to me with a collection of readily usable prompts—here are 10 that you should keep in your digital back pocket for yourself and anyone else you know who might want to try them out for themselves:

The first prompt gets straight to the point, as it scans your linked transaction history to check for any recurring charges and flag any sudden price increases you might have missed.

The second prompt investigates your cash flow, producing a dynamic spending chart while pointing out which purchasing categories you may need to cut back on. The third prompt examines your holiday spending trends from the year prior to see how much you may need to save for the current year’s holiday expenses.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

The fourth prompt highlights all the frequent tap-to-pay purchases you might have made on eating out compared to your grocery spending, which could compel you to ease up on dining out so much and look for cheaper alternatives while shopping.

The fifth prompt goes the extra mile to see if any of your linked accounts have any active offers that you can take advantage of before you make a purchase. The sixth prompt makes finding your boarding pass while you’re at a check-in counter and looking up your loyalty numbers while booking a flight so much quicker.

The seventh prompt works across Gemini’s Personal Intelligence “Memory Summary” feature, your connected Google Wallet and your Gmail to compare what you bought (via email receipts) with how much you spent (via bank/card account info). That way, you can see if you're close or far away from meeting the financial goals you’ve told Gemini about.

The eighth prompt works great as a visual aid since Gemini can generate dynamic charts for you and give you an easy-to-follow visualization of how your money is distributed across your checking and savings accounts. The ninth prompt is effective for doing a quick sweep of your accounts to see if there are any anomalies or accidental double charges that have popped up across your linked accounts.

The tenth and final prompt is efficient since it can bring up any stored concert tickets on your Google Wallet while instantly accessing your local transit pass before you use any public transportation to get to your destination.

I’m surprised it took this long for Google to connect its Wallet tool to Gemini, especially since its competitor ChatGPT offers a similar financial tool already.

Nevertheless, it has finally arrived and sticks out as another useful way to utilize AI to give you a clearer picture of your spending habits so you can make more informed decisions about how to save & spend your money. And besides that, it can bring up any other information you need about your linked accounts to make subscription cancellations or whatever other actions you may need to take.

For anyone building a premium home theater around a large TV, the Sony Bravia Theater Trio is down to $1,498 from $2,199.99, saving you $701.99, or roughly 32%. Unlike a conventional soundbar, the Trio uses three separate front speakers for the left, center, and right channels, helping spread dialogue and effects across a wider soundstage. You can read PCMag’s “excellent” review for more details.

The Sony Bravia Theater Bar 7 is down to $718 from $869 for anyone who wants a single soundbar under the TV. Its nine speakers include upward- and side-firing drivers that widen the soundstage and give Dolby Atmos some height, but there’s no subwoofer, so the now $898 Bar 7 with a wireless sub bundle (down from $1,099.99) might be the better pick for deeper bass.

Moving down Sony's lineup, the Bravia Theater Bar 6 is $548, down from $699.99, and pairs a 3.1.2-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer and upward-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos height effects. Spending $100 more gets you the Bravia Theater System 6, now $648 from $799.99, which adds rear speakers in a 5.1-channel setup for movies and games where sound moves behind you.

For a more affordable upgrade, the Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is down to $278 from $349.99, saving you nearly $72. It's a 3.1-channel system with a dedicated center speaker and wireless subwoofer, so dialogue should come through more clearly while music and movie effects get some additional low-end presence.

Sony’s older systems are discounted too, including the HT-S400 at $258, down from $299, which pairs a 2.1-channel soundbar and wireless subwoofer with S-Force Pro Front Surround to widen the sound for everyday TV, sports, and casual movies. The HT-S40R is arguably the better deal at the same $258, down from $329.99, since it adds two rear speakers for a full 5.1-channel setup, though neither model supports Dolby Atmos.

For smaller rooms or for anyone who mainly wants dialogue to come across more clearly, Bose has two compact soundbars on sale: The newer Bose TV Speaker (2nd Gen) is down to $239 from $299, with an updated acoustic design that Bose says improves clarity and overall sound performance. Meanwhile, the original Bose TV Speaker is $199, down from $279, and offers a similarly compact design with a dedicated dialogue mode and adjustable bass.

Samsung’s HW-Q800H is down to $697.99 from $1,097.99, a $400 cut on a 5.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos soundbar with a wireless subwoofer. Its side- and upward-firing speakers help place effects around and above you, while a dedicated center channel keeps dialogue clear during busy action scenes.

For something that takes up less space, the Samsung HW-S60D is $277.99, down from $399.99, and fits seven speakers, including side-firing drivers, into a compact 5.0-channel soundbar. It also supports Dolby Atmos, Adaptive Sound, and a voice enhancement mode, along with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, AirPlay, and Chromecast for music streaming. That said, it has no upward-firing speakers or subwoofer, so its height effects and bass won’t match that of the Q800H.

If you're looking for a complete surround sound system without spending several hundred dollars, the LG S6FTR is down to $249.99 from $399.99, saving you $150, or roughly 38%. It's a 5.1-channel home theater package with a soundbar, subwoofer, and dedicated rear speakers. That makes it particularly appealing for action movies and games, where directional sound adds to the experience.

The LG S40TR is another affordable option for anyone who wants rear speakers included in the box. It's currently $199.99, down from $279.99, and offers a 4.1-channel arrangement with a wireless subwoofer and two rear speakers. This should give movie soundtracks a greater sense of direction than a basic soundbar, while the subwoofer handles the lower frequencies that smaller TV speakers often struggle to reproduce.

At just under $187, the S60T is the least expensive system in this roundup, pairing a 3.1-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer for clearer dialogue and fuller sound than your TV’s speakers. That said, it lacks rear speakers and Dolby Atmos height channels, so it’s better suited to someone who wants a simple, affordable upgrade without filling the room with additional hardware.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

#3286. Fingers Point to RFK Jr. as U.S. Loses Measles Elimination Status

On Tuesday, the Pan American Health Organization announced that the United States, as well as Bolivia and Mexico, had lost their measles elimination status, a situation that requires “urgent attention,” said Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, at a press conference. “Elimination must be continuously protected.”

Calling measles “probably the most contagious virus,” he said that vaccination is “the main measure to protect” against it, and that vaccination coverage must remain “very high, above 95 percent” in every community.

Amid sinking vaccination rates, the same strain of the virus has now circulated unabated in the U.S. for a year, meaning that the virus is now endemic. This determination ends America’s hard-earned measles elimination status, achieved in 2000, which had been unequivocal proof that the country was doing something right in its effort to thwart spread of the disease.

The statistics are stunning. As of November 12, according to records maintained by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, there were 5,412 cases of measles reported in 2026, spread across 46 states and the District of Columbia, and 10 deaths.

Contrast that with 2024, the final year of the Biden administration, which saw a total of 285 cases.

The U.S. is not alone in seeing a rise in cases.  As The Atlantic pointed out, “In January, six other countries — including Austria, Spain, and the United Kingdom — lost their elimination status. Measles was declared endemic in Canada again last year.”

But, despite a worldwide decline in vaccinations attributed to the lost momentum of the Covid-19 pandemic and rising public-health mistrust, it’s not impossible to earn or maintain the measles elimination status conferred by regional commissions of the World Health Organization.

Cabo Verde, Mauritius, and the Seychelles did it last year, eliminating measles and rubella and becoming the “first sub-Saharan countries to attain this milestone,” according to a November 2025 WHO press release. The method was not rocket science, but increased vaccination and improved disease surveillance. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

However, when the wealthiest country on Earth, once a public-health powerhouse that deployed disease detectives and other experts around the world to help control outbreaks, loses its measles elimination status, it is likely proof that the country is doing something wrong.

And that wrong thing is having Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary, Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) tells Rolling Stone, calling his tenure “an utter disgrace” that has “rolled back 30 years of progress.” She adds, “Our health is now held hostage by the lies of a conspiracy theorist. Countless American lives will continue to be lost because of RFK Jr.’s disastrous tenure.”

In a statement, CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz downplayed the significance of the change in status: “The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does. We know where transmission is occurring and we’ve invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities. Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks.”

In an X post on Tuesday, Kennedy pledged to “stop measles outbreaks,” work to “regain U.S. measles elimination status” and continue to recommend measles vaccination as “the most effective way” to prevent measles.

A Health and Human Services spokesperson shared a quote from Dr. Barbosa of PAHO, commending the United States for strengthening its surveillance and vaccination efforts.  Related Content Hayden Panettiere’s Mother Blames Brian Hickerson For Star’s Death Kid Rock’s Nashville Bar Sued After Bouncers Allegedly Beat Patron Who ‘Tapped’ Guitar Trump Brushes Off FAA, Microsoft, Bank Outages: ‘It’s Life. It’s Fine’ Lawsuit Accusing Selena Gomez and Wondermind Co-Founders of Fraud Is Dismissed

The news first broke last Friday that the U.S. had lost its measles elimination status, the same day that PAHO notified Kennedy of its determination in a letter. It cited a single measles chain of transmission that began on January 20, 2025 — the day that President Trump was sworn in — and persisted for more than 12 months.

While the letter noted “significant efforts undertaken by the United States to manage the measles outbreak” through better surveillance and vaccination, it encouraged the U.S. to “intensify these efforts until transmission is interrupted and the outbreak is fully controlled.”

Even Republican Senator Bill Cassidy (R-La.) repudiated Kennedy, telling Face the Nation host Margaret Brennan on Sunday, “This has been a failure. If I were president, I would choose someone else because there needs to be accountability for higher health care costs, more measles deaths, losing elimination status, and no progress on processed foods.”

As chairman of the U.S. Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, it was Cassidy who provided the final vote to advance Kennedy’s nomination as health secretary, after securing a series of fig-leaf promises from him that he would not alter the CDC’s existing vaccine recommendations.

But from a bully pulpit, a lot of undermining is possible. Even as Kennedy first took office, he downplayed the measles outbreak in West Texas and then recommended vitamin A, instead of a tried-and-true method: vaccination and disease surveillance. That decision led at least one newly appointed HHS official to quit.

All the chin-ups in airports, a laissez-faire swim in a contaminated creek, the podcasts, cooking shows, and cameo appearances with now-adjudicated rapist Russell Brand, cannot substitute for the stark fact that one of the world’s most wildly infectious diseases, ruled eliminated 25 years ago, is back under Kennedy’s watch.

Though the post-Covid decline in vaccinations and the accompanying rise in measles cases began under the Biden administration, the failure to effectively address this explosion in cases undeniably belongs to Kennedy, says Dr. William John Moss, a professor in the departments of epidemiology at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

The blame for the longstanding pockets of low vaccine coverage around the country, and the number of infections in unvaccinated adults cannot be laid at the feet of the current administration, Moss says. But Kennedy is unequivocally to blame for the federal response to the measles outbreak. “We’ve just seen mixed messaging, a focus on treatment rather than vaccination, and an executive order from the president that undermines confidence in the MMR vaccine.” He adds, “The response had to be much stronger. RFK Jr. has worked a long time to undermine public trust in vaccines.”

Even in the run-up to the 2024 election, Donald Trump and Kennedy bonded over vaccine skepticism, as a prelude to their joining forces. In a leaked video of the two men talking, Trump could be heard wooing Kennedy by saying of an allegedly excessive childhood-vaccination shot, “It looks like it’s meant for a horse, not a 10-pound or 20-pound baby.”

However, being chastened by failure is not really a thing in this iteration of the Trump administration. As Kennedy told a recent gathering of his Make America Healthy Again supporters, “The Senate has no leverage over me anymore.” It is not clear what further unfortunate milestones could yet be achieved.

Despite ample evidence that the MAHA coalition is crumbling amid the devastation of midterm Republican losses and a series of unkept promises on banishing ultra-processed food and pesticides, Stephen Miller’s ascent as Trump’s chief of staff — a perceived backer of the MAHA agenda — clearly put a spring in Kennedy’s step.

That defiance will run headlong into a Democratic majority in Congress, come the new year, and losing the measles elimination status will likely top the bill of particulars in any effort to impeach the health secretary.  Trending Stories Watch Buffalo Springfield Come Together for the First Time in Many Years Jennifer Lopez Teases New Music on ‘Fallon’: ‘This Does Feel Like a Happy Era’ Priscilla Presley Scores Partial Win Over Fraud Suit, But Claims About Lisa Marie’s Death Can Stand Cynthia Erivo, Travis Barker Honor Phil Collins With Big Vocals, Big Drums at Rock Hall Ceremony

Incoming U.S. Senator Dr. Annie Andrews (D-S.C.), a pediatrician, pledged repeatedly during her campaign to do just that.

“We are seeing the return of an old killer, not because the science changed, but because our politics did,” she said about Trump and Kennedy’s ascent to power in a statement provided to Rolling Stone. “Secretary Kennedy has been a leading voice in the anti-vaccine movement for decades, undermining trust in lifesaving vaccine and putting our children at risk. Even if leadership at HHS changed tomorrow, rebuilding that trust would take years.”

#3285. Microsoft Officially Apologized for Yesterday's Outages

If you were having trouble accessing certain services like Microsoft Teams or Outlook, you were not alone. Early Thursday afternoon, many of Microsoft's biggest apps and services were experiencing downtime. According to Downdetector, which tracks user reports of issues with websites and platforms, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Teams, and OneDrive were all experiencing issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft has restored service to many users, and has officially apologized for the outages.

When I first published this article on Thursday, I couldn't even load Microsoft 365's status page. (I've reported on many service outages, but I can't recall a time when a service's status page was also down.) Even as of Friday afternoon, the page still says "Service degradation on Microsoft 365 (Business or Enterprise)," and Microsoft says the following services may be affected: Exchange Online, Microsoft 365 admin center, Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center, Microsoft 365 Education, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Defender for Office 365, Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft Graph, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Planner, Microsoft Power Apps, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Teams, Microsoft To Do, Power BI, SharePoint Online, Universal Print, and Windows 365.

Looking specifically at Outlook, Microsoft's email service had hundreds of thousands of user reports Thursday afternoon, signaling a major issue somewhere in Microsoft's pipeline. The reports did "slow down" throughout the day, but Downdetector still showed over 50,000 reports coming in every 15 minutes when I checked Thursday afternoon.

While the root cause of the issue was a mystery throughout Thursday's outage, Microsoft confirmed the problem in an apology on Friday. According to the company, "This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI [or] agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions."

Microsoft says it is "deeply sorry" for the disruption to its customers and partners. The company says the fix rolled out slower than some might expect, since it wanted to restore service gradually to evaluate stability at each stage. It also says it will release a full post-incident report once it completes a review.

During the outage, the company had confirmed that some of its infrastructure was experiencing elevated load, which it said was likely contributing to the issues. Microsoft then said it was pausing all deployments and moving traffic from affected infrastructure, and that it found that a number of its servers were unexpectedly unavailable after failing health checks. The company then thought a specific component responsible for processing server health may be the reason the system is failing health checks. Microsoft said an alternative service health check method successfully restarted some of the affected servers. The company was then actively restarting and validating affected servers to bring them back to service.

#3284. Epic formally asks SCOTUS to uphold contempt ruling against Apple

Epic Games has submitted its official response to Apple’s Supreme Court appeal, urging the justices to uphold the contempt ruling over App Store payment restrictions. Here are the details.

As most 9to5Mac readers probably know, Apple and Epic Games have been engaged in a lengthy legal battle since 2020, when Epic sued Apple after Fortnite was removed from the App Store.

The move came after Epic remotely activated an alternative payment system that bypassed Apple’s In-App Purchase system.

Although the court largely sided with Apple, it did rule that the company could no longer prevent developers from directing users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Apple ultimately allowed those links, but imposed new restrictions, including a 27% commission on external purchases, in addition to new rules limiting how developers could display buttons and links to alternative payment methods.

Epic challenged those restrictions, and the court agreed that Apple had violated the original injunction, holding the company in civil contempt.

Apple has since attempted multiple times to overturn that ruling, arguing that the original injunction contained no explicit prohibition on imposing those restrictions.

Epic, on the other hand, argues that Apple deliberately circumvented the court order by introducing new rules designed to achieve the same result as those originally prohibited.

In May, Apple appealed to the Supreme Court, which agreed in June to hear the case. Apple submitted its opening brief in September, followed by supporting briefs from the U.S. government and several legal and business groups.

Those included the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, Chamber of Progress, and several former federal antitrust enforcers. In a nutshell, the U.S. government argued that the original injunction did not clearly prohibit Apple’s 27% commission on external purchases, but maintained that the company was correctly held in contempt for restricting how developers could display external payment buttons.

In its opening brief, Apple argues, citing multiple legal precedents, that courts must enforce the letter of an injunction rather than its broader spirit.

According to the company, there was nothing in the original injunction explicitly prohibiting it from charging commissions on external purchases or imposing additional restrictions on payment links, so it should not be held in contempt for conduct that the court order did not clearly prohibit.

In its response filed today, Epic disputes Apple’s interpretation of the injunction, arguing that the company “attempts to avoid contempt by proposing an extreme legal standard.”

[Apple] argues that a court can find contempt only if an injunction spells out the exact practice at issue–so an injunction barring Apple’s then-existing anti-steering rules left it free to implement new ones that prevent steering just as effectively. Nothing in this Court’s precedents supports that approach, which would reduce injunctions to a never-ending game of whack-a-mole.

Epic argues that “Apple devised a plan to circumvent the injunction,” claiming that “Apple chose a rate of 27% for the commission, knowing that, when combined with the developers’ payment-handling costs (more than 3%), the rate for linked-out purchases would be higher than the rate for purchases using Apple’s payment system.”

As an Apple executive admitted, every “linked-out transaction is going to be more expensive to any developer * * * than an IAP transaction at 30 percent.” Apple simultaneously commissioned a “sham” report to try to provide an economic justification for the commission; the report contained an “entirely manufactured” rationale for the 27% rate.

The company also argues that “Apple tried to cover up its scheme to circumvent the injunction” by asserting privilege over more than 57,000 documents, and points to Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers’ finding that “its Vice President of Finance ‘outright lied under oath’ when he testified about when Apple decided to impose the new commission.”

Finally, Epic asks the Supreme Court to uphold the contempt ruling against Apple or, if the justices decide to clarify the legal standard for contempt, to send the case back to the lower courts for reconsideration under that standard.

With Epic’s response now filed, Apple has until December 14 to submit its final brief before oral arguments take place on January 11, 2027.

‘The Odyssey,’ ‘Madden’ and more are streaming

First up, if you don’t mind forking over a rental/purchase fee, then the biggest arrival is unquestionably the streaming debut of Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey.” After a lengthy theatrical run, this $1.8 billion-grossing epic is finally swapping the big screen for at-home streaming. Below I’ve collected together all the new movies on streaming this week, along with some insights into my top picks. Plus, be sure to check out our companion guide covering all the top TV shows you binge-watch this week.

“The Odyssey” finally heads to streaming this week after a four-month run in theaters. In an era where some movies swap the big screen for streaming weeks after release, Christopher Nolan’s acclaimed adaptation of Homer’s timeless poem has bucked the trend. This epic blockbuster deserved to be seen on the biggest screen possible (IMAX preferable), but I’ve no doubt it’ll still be satisfying even when watched on a much smaller television display.

For this fantasy epic, Nolan assembled an all-star cast including Matt Damon, Tom Holland, Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson, Zendaya, Jon Bernthal, Charlize Theron, Elliot Page and more. The flick follows Odysseus (Damon), a hero of the Trojan War, who endures a multi-year odyssey to return home to his native land of Ithaca and reunite with his beloved wife, Penelope (Hathaway), and son, Telemachus (Holland). Nolan’s “The Odyssey” is an epic in every sense of the word, and one of 2026’s very best movies, period.

Watch on Prime Video (buy/rent) starting November 18

Netflix’s holiday movie slate is underway, and the next seasonal original under the tree is “Guarding Stars.” This wintry romantic comedy is based on the novel “The Bodyguard” by Katherine Center. It focuses on a fake relationship that, to the surprise of literally nobody, quickly blossoms into the real thing. This one definitely doesn't have future Christmas classic written all over it based on the trailer, but it might be good for two hours of festive fun.

Jack Stapleton (Jared Padalecki) is an A-lister action star heading home for the holidays while also trying to dodge the unwanted advances of a very committed stalker. In steps no-nonsense bodyguard Hannah Brooks (Leighton Meester), and because this is a rom-com, the two pretend to be a couple so the actor’s family doesn’t worry about his safety. What starts as a fake relationship heats up over the holidays and becomes a real romance.

Thanksgiving is synonymous with watching football, so in the run-up to Turkey Day, Prime Video is debuting its new biographical sports movie, “Madden.” You probably don’t need any clues to know which football icon this David O. Russell film revolves around. That would be John Madden (duh!), the Super Bowl-winning coach, beloved commentator, and the man who lent his name to the best-selling EA Sports video game series Madden.

Nicolas Cage plays Madden, with Christian Bale (a frequent collaborator with O. Russell) playing his best friend and Oakland Raiders owner Al Davis. Kathryn Hahn features as John’s wife, Virginia Fields. This biopic chronicles Madden’s incredible career in the game, as he became the sport's most recognizable voice, and worked with EA Sports to build a video game dynasty. It’s a celebration of spirit, friendship, and a love of the game that made Madden an enduring American icon.

Watch on Prime Video starting November 18

Speaking of biopics that offer insight into an American icon, “Tony” is heading to HBO Max this week. This coming-of-age comedy-drama chronicles a defining summer in the life of celebrity chef Anthony Bourdain (played here by Dominic Sessa). Rather than trying to cover Bourdain’s entire life or career, “Tony” is a slice-of-life picture set over a single transformative summer. This narrative decision adds intimacy and a delightful richness.

Set in 1975, Anthony Bourdain, going by Tony, is an arrogant student at Vassar College. By his own admission, he's "badly in need of a good ass-kicking." Dreaming of becoming a writer, he follows his high school crush (Emilia Jones) to Provincetown, Massachusetts. In need of a place to stay, he finds himself working in a Cape Cod kitchen under the watch of head chef José Vatel (Antonio Banderas), and develops a passion for the culinary arts that would shape the course of his life. Sessa is excellent, as is Banderas, and best of all, “Tony” is an incredibly warm movie, perfect for cold winter nights.

Disney is gearing up for the release of its tentpole animated movie for the Thanksgiving season, “Hexed.” But if the eye-watering cost of taking a whole family to the theater is already making your wallet shed tears, “Steps” on Netflix might be a suitable lower-cost alternative. This animated fantasy musical looks like a whimsical adventure for all ages, and because it puts a new twist on a well-known fairy tale, it definitely has a Disney-ish quality.

Like many modern animated movies, “Steps” puts a new spin on a timeless tale, in this case, Cinderella. Here, Cinders (voiced by Amanda Seyfried) teams up with Lilith (Ali Wong), one of her misunderstood stepsisters. When Lilith steals the Fairy Godmother’s wand, she accidentally transforms the other stepsister into a frog, and in the chaos, the mean-spirited Priscilla (Nikki Glaser) takes the kingdom’s throne. Now, the unlikely, squabbling pair must team up to save the day and prove that even a "villain" can be a hero.

#3282. Thom Velde Dies: Longtime Head Film Buyer For AMC Theatres Was 83

Thomas “Thom” Velde, a longtime head film buyer for AMC Theatres who also oversaw its Canadian operations, has died. He was 83. His family said he died October 31 of cancer in Rancho Mirage, near Palm Springs.

Velde spent more than a quarter-century at AMC Theatres as head film buyer, negotiating film agreements with domestic and international studios. He also oversaw AMC’s Canadian ops and real estate ventures.

He joined AMC in 1978, rising to become SVP Film Buyer of its Central Division before being promoted to SVP and managing director of AMC international film marketing in 1998. Tasked in that post with handling film buying policies in Canada, Asia, Europe and other regions, he forged relationships with film companies, distributors and government agencies around the world. He also supervised and trained film buyers for the exhibition chain.

After leaving AMC, he launched T Velde Consulting, working independently in motion picture distribution and consulting for clients including Microspace Communications and CJ America.

Velde’s family said was an avid golfer and a devoted college football fan who will remembered for his strength of character, his generosity and the way he made time for the people in his life.

He is survived by his wife, Deborah; daughters Andrea Ter-Velde (John McLoughlin) and Courtney Ter-Velde (Greg Horton); son, Sam Velde; stepsons Matthew Castillo (Crissy Castillo) and Spencer Castillo (Claire Castillo), two grandchildren and five step-grandchildren.

A celebration of life is set for 3 p.m. December 8 at Woodland Hills Community Church, with a reception to follow there. Velde’s family said donations in his memory may be made to to the Will Rogers Motion Picture Pioneers Foundation or the Motion Picture & Television Fund.

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sarah J. Maas’ lush, romance-soaked series A Court of Thorns and Roses has blossomed into a sprawling, complex fantasy series with millions of dedicated fans, and with good reason. A complex heroine who keeps discovering new depths in herself, fascinating supporting characters who shift from antihero to antivillain in unexpected ways, creative and beautifully rendered world-building—the series has it all, while also being unapologetically romantic (and steamy).

The story of a huntress who is kidnapped by a fae prince and brought to the Spring Court as a prisoner, only to become a key player in all that fae drama, ACOTAR is special, but Maas can only write so fast. If you need more books with the same lush feel, here are 10 to get you started.

It’s no shock that one of Sarah J. Maas’ other series would be recommended for fans of A Court of Thorns and Roses, but there’s a specific reason you should jump into her Crescent City series, especially the third book, House of Flame and Shadow. The most recent ACOTAR book, A Court of Splintered Harmony, revealed that the events of House of Flame and Shadow tie directly into the events in Splintered Harmony, particularly with regard to the character of Feyre’s sister, Nesta. In other words, if you read Splintered Harmony and wondered why Nesta was being so weird, there’s a whole other book series you should dig into immediately.

If Feyre’s grit and determination are your favorite aspect of ACOTAR, Julie Kagawa’s Iron Fey series (starting with The Iron King) will be your next obsession. Meghan Chase has never felt ‘normal’ in her life, and she’s been haunted by her father’s disappearance since she was a child. When her brother also vanishes, she goes on a quest for answers, learns that she’s actually the daughter of a faerie king, and finds herself in a magical world that blurs in elements of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Meghan is determined to save her brother (and herself), but a certain ice-cold fae prince captures her attention, even though he’s as dangerous as he is beautiful.

If you’re looking for some serious romance in your fantasy, Jennifer L. Armentrout’s A Blood and Ash series is a must. Poppy was chosen at birth to be the kingdom’s Maiden, isolated and untouched in order to be ready for her Ascension to ensure the land is protected from the evil force that took her family. But it’s a lonely existence—until Hawke is assigned as her sworn protector. Golden-eyed and beautiful, Hawke offers Poppy the connection she’s craved. When chaos erupts around her, Hawke takes the opportunity to spirit Poppy away. But Hawke has a secret, and Poppy is soon in danger of losing both her heart and the favor of the gods themselves.

If you love how A Court of Thorns and Roses takes the “enemies-to-lovers” trope and builds it into a deep, complex mesh of emotions and plot twists, you’ll love Shelby Mahurin’s Serpent & Dove series. When witch Louise le Blanc flees her coven, she takes shelter in the city of Cesarine, where magic is forbidden, and witches are unceremoniously hunted and burned. Louise’s life gets infinitely more complicated, dangerous, and steamy when she’s trapped into an unwanted marriage with Reid Diggory—who happens to be a huntsman of the Church, charged with tracking down and eliminating witches. And then Louise starts to realize that Reid is actually pretty darn hot.

If you’re looking for a romantasy that’s broadly similar to ACOTAR while being its own thing, read A.K. Mulford’s The Five Crowns of Okrith series, starting with The High Mountain Court. Remy is a red witch, which means she’s in hiding and ready to make a run for it if the fae get near. So when a group of fae shows up at her tavern, she makes for the exit—only to be captured by Prince Hale of the Eastern Court. Instead of striking her down, however, Hale asks Remy for help—he needs to locate two ancient magical artifacts created by red witches, and he needs her red magic to find them. Hale promises to set her free and even reunite her with the red witches still living. More importantly, Remy finds Hale irresistible and has a primal urge to stay with him, no matter what the cost.

Looking for a romantasy with a slightly different vibe from ACOTAR? Variety is the spice of life, after all—and The Fourth Wing delivers. Rebecca Yarros’ Empyrean Series made a huge splash when it debuted, and for good reason—it has everything, from a capable, intelligent heroine thrust into a dangerous scenario (in this case, a dragon rider academy where failure can be deadly) and forced to navigate alliances, conspiracies, and her own heart, which is pushing her towards a romance that might be as dangerous as the dragons themselves.

Love the moral complexity of ACOTAR, where everyone has at least a touch of darkness? Check out The Folk of the Air series by Holly Black. When Jude was a child, the father of her half-sister, the faerie Madoc, murdered her parents and took her back to the Faerie world with him. Raised as part of the gentry, Jude lives in a world where her mortal nature is hated and despised, but she battles for her place at court anyway while struggling with her love-hate relationship with her adoptive father and a growing bond with the titular prince, a relationship that is strictly forbidden. Jude is a fierce and extremely morally gray character, and one that fans of Feyre will adore.

Looking for more smart women at the center of beautifully-rendered fantasy stories? You’ll love Princess Lucero-Elisa de Riqueza of Orovalle, star of this series-starter by Rae Carson. Elisa was chosen for “Service” as a baby, when a godstone was placed in her navel by the gods, signaling that she was destined for greatness. But as a young woman, Elisa is self-hating and miserable. She’s never done anything even remotely great, and spends her time isolated, overweight, and reading military strategy books. One day she’s shocked to discover she’s been married off to the king of a distant land on the brink of war—and suddenly all that rage and book learning becomes invaluable as she struggles to survive an unfamiliar court and help her new homeland survive a dangerous onslaught.

If you loved Feyre’s journey as she discovered unknown reservoirs of power and courage inside herself, you should read Leigh Bardugo’s Grishaverse novels, starting with Shadow and Bone. As a child, Alina was tested by the Grisha and found to possess no magical ability. As an adult, she serves as a cartographer in the army. Charged with guiding the Darkling—the most powerful of the Grisha—across the dangerous and terrifying Shadow Fold, Alina is unexpectedly revealed to have incredible powers and is packed off to train with the Grisha. There, she must determine who her friends and enemies are, even while falling under the spell of the charismatic Darkling.

Emilia di Carlo and her sister Vittoria are very different—Emilia is bookish and shy, Vittoria outgoing and brash—but they share a secret: They’re both streghe, and have spent their lives learning to use magic. In this version of Italy, the Malvagi (the seven princes of Hell) haven’t been seen in a long time, but a terrifying accident summons the Prince of Wrath and leaves three witches dead, including Vittoria. Emilia swears to use her power to avenge her sister, but when her revenge is delayed and she’s forced to work with Wrath, unwanted feelings begin to tick up the spice level to an uncomfortable degree.

To celebrate 25 years of Xbox, Microsoft has rolled out Xbox Playback. Similar to Spotify Wrapped, the feature pulls together a highlight reel of your gaming history, including your very first game, total hours played, top years, and longest play streak.

Whether you have been playing since the original Xbox era or jumped in more recently, checking your stats only takes a minute on either your console or a web browser, provided you know where to look and meet a few quick eligibility rules before the feature disappears at the end of the year.

Before checking your stats, keep a few rules in mind. To unlock a recap, your profile needs at least 1 Gamerscore, 1 achievement, and 1 minute of qualifying gameplay — plus at least 1 minute of gameplay on that console if you want to watch it directly on your Xbox dashboard.

It is a bit disappointing that Microsoft has limited the rollout to just 15 countries, especially for longtime players outside those regions hoping to celebrate the 25-year milestone.

Xbox Playback is only live through December 31, 2026, across Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, Colombia, France, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Mexico, Poland, South Africa, Spain, the UK, and the US.

To launch the recap from your console, power on your Xbox, select your profile, and look for the Xbox Playback tile directly on your main home dashboard.

If it does not appear immediately at the top, return to the home screen and scroll down to the Xbox 25 Years section to select Playback from there. You can also press the Xbox button on your controller, head down to the Store, and search for Xbox to find and launch the Playback tab.

If you are away from your console, you can watch your recap on a phone or computer by heading to the Official Xbox Playback Page.

Simply sign in with the Microsoft account linked to your Xbox profile, then press Play to watch your personalized 25-year gaming story, complete with your first game, total hours played, top years, and longest streak.

#3278. The Apple Watch Series 11 Is $100 Off in Walmart's Early Black Friday Sale

If you’ve been counting down to Black Friday and hoping for a deal on an Apple Watch, there’s no time like the present: Walmart recently launched its early Black Friday tech deals, and the rarely discounted Apple Watch Series 11 is currently $100 off, bringing the 42mm GPS model down to $299 (originally $399). The 46mm GPS model is $329 (originally $429), while the GPS + Cellular versions start at $399 and are also $100 off.

Though it has been supplanted by the Series 12, released earlier this fall, the Series 11 is still a great buy. It lasts up to 24 hours, making it a great option for everyday use and sleep tracking, and a 15-minute charge provides around eight hours of use. It has a strong selection of health features, including wrist temperature sensing, sleep score, ECG, heart-rate monitoring, and hypertension notifications, as well as detailed workout tracking. Compared with the Series 10, this aluminum model’s Ion-X display is twice as scratch-resistant. It’s also water-resistant to 50 meters.

While it doesn’t have the Series 12’s new processor or updated health-tracking features, the Apple Watch Series 11 is a great pick for your first Apple Watch or as an upgrade from an older model, such as the Series 8. Its large display, durability, and versatile staple features deliver the core Apple Watch experience at a more affordable price, especially if you don’t want Apple’s latest Audio Intelligence features.

Prime Day and Black Friday are the two best times of the year to get the best deals on most purchases. Of course, depending on what you're shopping for, you might find other opportunities throughout the year, but in general, Prime Day and Black Friday have the best sales.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

#3275. Scammers Tried to Trick Noah Kahan Fans With a Fake Show Outside an L.L. Bean Store

Two New England icons will definitely not be teaming up this summer, with the clothing company L.L. Bean recently warning fans that a purported Noah Kahan concert outside its flagship store is a scam.

Last week, word started spreading online that Kahan was set to play a special pop-up gig outside the L.L. Bean flagship in Freeport, Maine on June 12, 2027. Tickets were even being sold on an Eventbrite page, which (per screenshots) billed the show as “Summer Camp Featuring Noah Kahan.”

A description read. “Summer Camp is here. Explore the pop-up, and when the sun goes down, the lawn opens for an evening concert with Noah Kahan.”

On Saturday, L.L Bean warned fans about the scam, writing on Facebook, “The listing has no affiliation with L.L. Bean and no such event is occurring at our Flagship campus. Once it was discovered we immediately notified Eventbrite and they have disabled the listing.”

It’s unclear how tickets were sold to the fake show, or how refunds would be handled. Eventbrite did not immediately return a request for comment. Kahan hasn’t spoken on the scam attempt either, and his reps did not immediately return a request for comment.

The concert industry has, unfortunately, long been rife with outright scams and sketchy practices. Typically problems arise around ticketing, especially on the secondary market, where phony tickets are often advertised on social media and sold through bogus websites. But fully making up a show appears to be a relatively new, if unfortunately inevitable, scammer escalation. Earlier this year, the Swedish guitarist Yngwie Malmsteen had to warn fans after someone started advertising and selling tickets to a bunch of fake gigs.  Trending Stories Watch Buffalo Springfield Come Together for the First Time in Many Years Jennifer Lopez Teases New Music on ‘Fallon’: ‘This Does Feel Like a Happy Era’ Priscilla Presley Scores Partial Win Over Fraud Suit, But Claims About Lisa Marie’s Death Can Stand Cynthia Erivo, Travis Barker Honor Phil Collins With Big Vocals, Big Drums at Rock Hall Ceremony

That someone would try the same scam with Kahan, one of the biggest artists around, feels especially bold. That said, this particular scam seems to have been kinda well thought out. The L.L. Bean flagship in Freeport does host an outdoor concert series during the summer, and Kahan has collaborated with the brand in the past. And while the flagship, as many Kahan fans noted online, is not as big as the stadiums Kahan is used to playing these days, the singer-songwriter has been known to do an underplay on special occasions.

So while the scammer may have been shrewd in concocting this part of their plan, there was one particularly glaring flaw: Kahan already has a real show scheduled on the same day.

#3274. These Are the Best Ways to Encrypt Your Email

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

As this in-depth explainer from Adaptive Security describes, most emails are encrypted in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS), which prevents anyone from reading your message as it travels from server to server. However, encryption is temporarily stripped at each server: content is received and processed in plaintext and then re-encrypted when it leaves, meaning it could be read, logged, and distributed by the server provider.

Emails are also typically encrypted at rest—for example, while sitting on Google's servers and in a Gmail recipient's inbox. But this only prevents someone with physical access to the server hardware from reading messages, as Google still holds the encryption key and can access stored data. And, as PCMag points out, Google is scanning your messages to a degree, and it (along with other email providers) can and will hand emails over to law enforcement and government agencies in some cases.

If you have an account with a major email provider like Gmail, Outlook, or Apple Mail, you can add a third-party tool that layers an encryption protocol like OpenPGP on top of your existing account. PCMag recommends PreVeil, SecureMyEmail, and Virtru (which is limited to Gmail users in Chrome) for those who want to keep their current emails. Mailvelope is a browser add-on (and therefore a desktop-only tool) available in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, though it can also be installed on other browsers, like Brave, that are built on the same architecture. FlowCrypt integrates with Gmail and Google Workspace on desktop and mobile.

Note that enterprise users of Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 have access to true end-to-end encryption without third-party add-ons. Gmail's Confidential mode and Outlook's Encrypt feature, available to all users, are not E2EE equivalents, as Google and Microsoft, respectively, still manage the keys.

For those who are willing to start fresh with a new email address (or who have a custom domain), providers like Proton Mail or Tuta offer native end-to-end encryption. The caveat: by default, this is only between users on the same service, so from one Proton user to another. If you want to send an end-to-end encrypted email from Proton to a Gmail user, for example, you have to set up password protection (and share the password via another secure channel) or use a PGP-compatible tool like those listed above. You can also Proton's Gmail integration does allow for end-to-end encryption, but only if both Gmail parties are using the Proton integration.

AI data centers are using a shocking amount of electricity

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every time you ask ChatGPT a question, generate an image with Gemini, or have Claude help write an email, a data center somewhere is doing the work. Most of us never think about what it takes to keep those servers running, but new research suggests America's AI infrastructure already has an enormous environmental cost.

A new Harvard-led study published in Nature Sustainability finds that 403 of the largest U.S. data centers consumed about 1.8% of the country's total electricity between May 2024 and April 2025.

That's an estimated 82 terawatt-hours of electricity in a single year, enough to power nearly 7 million American homes for a year, according to an Associated Press report.

And electricity consumption is only part of the problem. Researchers estimate the facilities produced 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions, roughly equivalent to Denmark's annual emissions.

Companies are racing to build more infrastructure to support increasingly powerful AI models, but questions remain over what the technology's rapid growth means for the environment and the people living near the facilities powering it.

Using satellite imagery, facility information and federal electricity-generation data, the team estimated how much power each location consumed and the resulting carbon emissions.

Approximately 54% of the electricity attributed to the data centers came from fossil-fuel generation, including 38% from natural gas and 15% from coal.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

The estimated emissions were also two to three times higher than an earlier assessment of hyperscale data-center emissions in 2018. The study's measurements ended in April 2025, which means they don't even account for the additional data centers built or expanded over the past year and a half.

As AI companies release more capable models and add features such as image generation, video creation and autonomous agents, demand for computing infrastructure continues to grow.

However, the study doesn't tell us exactly how much electricity one ChatGPT conversation consumes, or whether Gemini uses more power than Claude.

The researchers couldn't distinguish between electricity used for AI-specific workloads and traditional cloud-computing operations. That means the findings shouldn't be interpreted as emissions caused exclusively by generative AI.

Still, they provide a revealing look at the infrastructure supporting the AI services millions of people are adopting. And unlike the electricity consumed by a household appliance, the environmental impact of an AI request isn't necessarily visible to the person using the technology.

Power plants that burn fossil fuels release pollutants that can affect air quality and human health.

The Harvard researchers pointed to fine particulate matter, nitrogen oxides and sulfur dioxide as pollutants associated with fossil-fuel generation. Exposure to these pollutants is linked to respiratory and cardiovascular problems.

That means communities located near power plants could experience environmental consequences from data centers operating miles away.

The researchers did not directly measure those health effects, but they identified the issue as an important area for future investigation.

Location also makes a difference. The study found that Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa accounted for more than half of the electricity consumption across the facilities examined.

Some data centers also operate in regions where electricity generation is substantially more carbon-intensive than the national average.

Using cleaner electricity, improving hardware efficiency and making data-center energy consumption more transparent could all help reduce the industry's environmental footprint.

But there's a fundamental challenge. As AI becomes faster, cheaper and more widely available, more people and businesses are finding reasons to use it.

For consumers, the takeaway is that AI may feel effortless, but the infrastructure behind it is anything but. And as the technology becomes part of everyday life, the question is how much energy we're willing to use to make it happen.

#3269. 10 Privacy Hacks Every Mac User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device. Turning on Stealth Mode prevents your Mac from even responding to these requests, essentially making it invisible to anything that's scanning a network you're connected to. This makes it more difficult for hackers and malware to know your device exists, much less attack it. This can interfere with certain essential activity when you're on your home network, but it's a valuable security setting when on public wifi. You can leave Firewall on all the time and enable Stealth Mode only as needed. Go to Settings > Network > Firewall, flip the toggle, then hit Options to manage Stealth Mode.

Images and screenshots contain metadata, such as timestamps, device and hardware details, and, in the case of photos, physical location. Much of this information is stripped automatically when you share files to social media or via encrypted messaging apps, but if you're sending them via text or email, posting to forums, or sharing over AirDrop, metadata remains intact. You can easily remove metadata from your images right on your desktop. Select the file and hit control + click to bring up an options menu, then go to Quick Actions > Convert Image. Uncheck the box next to Preserve Metadata, then hit Convert. (This is also useful for quickly converting HEIC to JPEG without opening a separate app.)

If you're using iCloud to store photos, files, and device backups, your data is encrypted on Apple's servers and in transit. Apple still holds the decryption key, which is useful if you somehow get locked out of your account and need help recovering it, but for sensitive data—including device backups—end-to-end encryption is the most secure way to ensure no one but you can gain access. Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in setting for iCloud that encrypts your information end to end. You'll need to set up an alternative recovery method, such as your device passcode with two-factor authentication, a recovery contact, or a recovery key. Be careful, though: If you lose access to this recovery method, you will lose your data. You can enable Advanced Data Protection on your Mac under System Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Advanced Data Protection > Turn On. Note that some iCloud data, including passwords and payment methods, are already end-to-end encrypted by default.

If there’s one upgrade I’m looking forward to seeing most on the iPhone 20 Pro, it’s the camera. The latest rumor has me excited because Apple is reportedly introducing a far more advanced imaging sensor, which could deliver dramatic improvements.

Although the iPhone 18 Pro Max is still one of the best camera phones around today, I was somewhat disappointed to find minimal upgrades in my iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max face-off. In almost every snapshot, the differences between them were nearly indistinguishable.

That’s why all eyes will be on Apple’s next flagship release. According to Weibo leaker Ice Universe, the iPhone 20 Pro could feature a main camera sensor with logic circuitry manufactured on a new 17-nanometer process. Even though this doesn’t directly mean the sensor itself will be physically larger, a more advanced logic layer gives the camera the capacity to deliver faster readout speeds, handle more complex image processing, and consume less power.

Here’s what I think that could mean in practice:

Most people don’t realize all the complex actions that go on behind the scenes the moment they tap the shutter button. The phone isn’t just capturing a single frame — it’s taking a rapid series of shots and processing them together to deliver one final image.

By introducing a more advanced image sensor that processes data faster, Apple could dramatically improve the iPhone 20 Pro’s dynamic range performance. Think about tricky, high-contrast lighting scenes where bright highlights compete with deep shadows. With a faster readout speed, the sensor could capture and merge exposures more effectively to balance those challenging areas.

Instead of leaving hotspots blown out by harsh light, the iPhone 20 Pro could better preserve detail in the highlights — all while lifting the shadows. You can see some of examples I'm referring to in the gallery above.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

Apple has already made strides in this next area, but a more advanced image sensor could push things even further. I’m referring to zero shutter lag and reduced rolling shutter distortion when capturing fast-moving subjects. If you’ve ever tried photographing someone playing sports, you’re probably familiar with how easily those frames can come out blurry or out of focus.

Frenetic movement can make it tough to freeze a moment cleanly, so an image sensor with faster readout speeds would be much better equipped to handle the action. Just look at the side-by-side shots above of someone riding an electric scooter.

I shoot a ton of videos and know firsthand how quickly a phone can feel toasty whenever I record for more than a couple of minutes. If you really want to see how warm it gets, try shooting continuously for 10 minutes or longer.

Sustained capture like that demands serious processing power, which quickly leads to heat buildup. With a more power-efficient sensor, the iPhone 20 Pro could be better equipped to handle longer ProRes recording sessions without pausing due to overheating.

The iPhone 20 Pro is still a long way away, but this 17nm sensor rumor could become much more exciting if the sensor size itself increases. Apple certainly delighted us with a mechanical variable aperture main camera on the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, yet a physically larger sensor would be a compelling reason to upgrade to the iPhone 20 Pro.

This wouldn’t just improve its light-gathering abilities, but would also help boost detail, sharpness, and definition. If these leaks pan out, next year's anniversary iPhone could deliver the biggest leap in iPhone photography we've seen in years.

#3265. If Your Google Pixel's Camera Is Suddenly Broken, Here's the Fix

Updates are generally good for your devices. The latest Chrome update, for example, patches an actively exploited security vulnerability, while Apple's latest updates stop people from seeing iMessages they shouldn't have access to. In most cases, it's beneficial to update your tech to the latest software version whenever possible.

Sadly, updates aren't all perfect, as Google Pixel users are discovering this week. As reported by Android Authority, Google's November update apparently shipped with a bug that breaks some Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 cameras. Seeing as Pixels are rather famous for their shooters, this is a decidedly unfortunate glitch.

Here's the situation: Following the November update, some users are opening their Pixel Camera apps to find an error that reads, "Something went wrong. Close and open the Camera app again," with a "Learn More" link to, well, learn more. Others aren't receiving the error, but are instead running into a blank Camera viewfinder, as if the lens is totally covered. What's more, some users are reportedly saying that the issue is present on third-party camera apps, not just the Pixel Camera app. That would imply this is an issue with the camera system-wide, not just the Pixel Camera app itself.

To be clear, it doesn't seem like this is a universal issue. It's not like all Pixel users are now running with broken cameras. But based on the forum complaints Android Authority discovered, it seems reasonable to assume that this glitch isn't limited to just a handful of unlucky Pixel owners.

Luckily, there is an apparent workaround here, though it's not totally obvious. Some users are having no luck restarting their Pixels, while others report that a factory reset wasn't enough to restore camera functionality.

What does appear to work, however, is shutting your Pixel down and waiting five minutes or so. It's not clear why, but giving your Pixel a chance to "breathe" seems to shake the glitch and bring back your camera. As Android Authority reports, that fix comes from "Diamond and Gold product experts" on Google's Support forum.

If your Pixel's camera is giving you grief following the November update, this workaround is definitely worth a try—especially since more drastic measures don't actually seem to do anything. As the issue does seem to be rather widespread, I wouldn't be surprised to see Google issue a patch in the coming days. But until then, turning your phone off for five minutes may be a decent compromise.

#3264. Apple @ Work: The spiritual successor to the Xserve is here, thanks to Apple silicon and MLX

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

I’ve spent the past few weeks thinking about how Apple built up the best deal in enterprise AI. Two things happened that make me think Apple knew that all along (or maybe they didn’t and got lucky). Meta released its most capable open-weight model yet and optimized it to run on a Mac Studio. I also spent time with Osaurus, an app that runs a usable local AI model on something as small as a 16 GB Apple silicon laptop without needing a network connection. They even have two models that will run on 8 GB.

The Xserve has been dead since 2011, but its spiritual successor sits on a desk rather than in a rack.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

For the last few years, the narrative has been that Apple fell behind in AI because it didn’t have a frontier model. Siri AI got delayed, and the Apple Intelligence rollout was not great. In hindsight, I think Apple was right not to run that race, as the frontier-model business has turned into somewhat of a capital bonfire. Every frontier lab is spending billions on GPUs to be the best for a few months at a time, and the moment a model is good enough, someone else releases an open-weight version that runs on hardware you already own.

Open-weight models prove it: Muse Spark Open has 816 billion parameters, 42 billion active parameters, and a million-token context window, and Meta is giving it away. Apple didn’t build that LLM. It built the hardware that runs it. With that being said, Siri is still far behind.

Look at what Apple has shipped while everyone was waiting on them to try to compete with Anthropic or OpenAI. With Apple silicon’s unified memory, the GPU can use up to 512 GB of memory on a single Mac Studio, instead of being limited to whatever fits on a graphics card.

MLX is Apple’s machine learning framework, and it’s built specifically for the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon. If you’ve used NumPy, the API will feel familiar right away. On top of that, MLX includes higher-level packages for neural networks and optimizers, along with function transformations for automatic differentiation and graph optimization, so you can build more complex models without giving up efficiency. It also has bindings in Swift, C++, and C, which means it runs on any Apple platform.

Apple’s own Machine Learning Research post shows four M5 Ultra Mac Studios running Muse Spark Open at over 36 tokens per second, which is faster than you can read, while peaking around 300 watts per machine.

Apple’s unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra’s integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip’s 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory.

We tested a range of agentic workflows running entirely on-device, using Muse Code powered by Muse Spark Open, including shipping real iOS changes to Ice Cubes (an open-source Mastodon client) — bug fixes, new features, full build — and driving DaVinci Resolve end to end, with the model reviewing footage frame by frame to find the strongest moments and crop them vertically.

That’s the Xserve pitch, rebuilt for 2026. Apple killed the Xserve in 2011 because nobody wanted a Mac in a data center. The Mac mini came along and provided some new use cases over the years. Now, a couple of Mac Studios can host a model that would otherwise require a rack of Nvidia hardware and a power budget to match, and it does so quietly enough to sit under a desk. Apple wasn’t trying to compete with OpenAI, Anthropic, or Nvidia. It was building the infrastructure for everything except the frontier model, and it looks like that’s where the market is going. A company like MacStadium has to be loving this future as well.

The Mac Studio story is the headline, but what matters most to most IT teams is at the other end of the lineup. I had Terence Pae, co-founder and CEO of Osaurus, on the Apple @ Work podcast last week. Osaurus is a free, open-source AI tool for the Mac. It helps manage local models that work offline, but it can also call a frontier model when needed. A really cool feature, when it does this, is that Osaurus runs a small local model first to find names, phone numbers, and account numbers in whatever you pasted, and swaps them for placeholders before anything goes to Claude or OpenAI.

Osaurus has no servers and no customer database. If the company went out of business tomorrow, the app would keep running until macOS broke it. Individuals use it for free. Workspaces, the paid tier, is for teams who want to share agents across their own Macs. There’s a Windows beta as well, which I think helps Apple’s case more than it hurts it. When the same app runs on both platforms, the Mac’s unified memory is the difference.

In talking with him, Terence mentioned he wouldn’t be surprised if a local model matches what today’s frontier models can do by this time next year. I believe him, and that’s the point. The frontier will keep moving, but good enough keeps moving too, and good enough is what most employees need most of the day. Apple spent the AI race building memory, bandwidth, and a framework instead of trying to match the frontier, and the narrative was that they were behind.

Now the most capable open-weight model in the US is optimized for the Mac.
